div.head: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.
div.p: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.
COCKNEY EPITAPH FOR A COOK.-1 hashes."
." Peace to his

Luc END OF Lrier..—The end of man's life is glory. The end of woman's life is about two-and•thirty. Win is a man ascending Vesuvius like an Irish- man trying to kiss a pretty girl?—Because he wants to get at the crater's mouth. y9iY_is Lord Hill, giving each of his children a agvereign, tike the rising sun 1-lle tips the little hills with gold. Do you know mathematics, sir ?—Can't say I do; I know Tom Mattocks of the Guards, but no Matthew—Tom's brother probably, eh 7 PARTY Cohoußs.—The colours at most of the Irish elections were black and blue—worn princi- pally on the legs and arms of the contending parties. PROGRESS OF TEMPERANCE. —lt is a remarkable and very gratifying fact that not a single bottle-nosed whale has been seen in the Clyde this season.

WE notice the marriage of Mr. John H. Strange to Miss Elizabeth Strange ; an event that is very strange, no doubt; the next event in course will be a little stranger. AN IRISH VIVAT."—An earl-marshal was found fault with by his sovereign for some mis; arrangement at a coronation. " Please your majesty," said he, "I hope to do better next time." SOME women think they clean their children when they wipe the dirt off thsir noses and rub it into the corners of their eyes. This is a mistake, and shows but a limited knowledge of the laws which govern soiled pinafores.

"So—there is another ruption on Mount Vocifer- ous," said Mrs. Partington, as she put down the paper and her spectacles; "the paper tells us about the burning lather running down the mountain, but it does not tell us how it got on Ere." RIVALRY IN INGEN C ITT. —A Gascon having made a portfolio into an umbrella, a Norman, in order that he might not be behind in ingenuity, made a snuff-box in toe shape of a pistol, and, by means of a slight spring, fired the snuff up his nose!

MACHINERY has reached a state of perfection. We saw some burnt peas put into the hopper of a eoffeemill the other day, and in less than two minutes in was occupying a place in a grocery window, labelled "Fine eld Mocha." A QUEXR-LOOKING customer inserted his head into an auction room, and looking gravely at the "knight of the hammer," inquired, "Can I bid, sir? "—" Certainly," replied the auctioneer; "you can bid."—" Well, then," said the wag, walking off, "I bid you good night." A GENTLEMAN residing in Salisbury, while walk- ing one morning in the market-place, having on a napless hat, met a friend attired in a wide-awake. " Well, friend," said he, "you look very wide- aveke this morning."—" Not so much as you do," replied the other, 'for your hat never had a nap."

A COUPLE of pedestrians, "gents from town," passing through a toll-bar, attempted a joke at the expense of a young woman who stood at the door, by asking what the charge was for passing through the bar. "uf you are gentlemen, nothing; if you are donkeys, a penny each," replied the damsel, much to their discomfiture.

A TEACHER in a Sunday-school was lecturing a class of little girls on the influence of pious instruc- tions-in the formation of youthful character. " Miss Caroline," said he to one of the class, " what do you think you would have been without your good father and pious mother ?"—" I suppose, sir," answered Miss Caroline, "I should have been an orphan." A FEW days since an attorney at a county court deemed it necessary to shake the testimony of a Mr. Butterworth, by impugning his veracity. The wit- ness being called, the lawyer commenoed :--"Do you know Mr. Butterworth ?" —" Yes."—" What is Butterworth?" "Thirteen - pence a pound, although I have paid as high as—"—" That will do, sir. You can take you seat." DR. BEESWAX, in his Essay on Women, remarks with some truth, that "beauties generally died old maids. They set such a value on themselves," he says, "that they don't Sad a purchaser until the market is closed. Out of a dozen beauties, who have come out within the last eighteen years, eleven are still single. They spend their days in working green dogs on yellow wool—while their evenings are devoted to low spirits and French novels."

ON one occasion when John Kemble played Hamlet in the country, the gentleman who acted Guildenstern was, or imagined himself to be, a capital musician. Hamlet asks him, " Will you play upon this pipe?"—" My lord, I cannot."--" I do beseech you ? —" Well, if your lordship insists on it, I shall do as well as I can ;" and, to the con- fusion of Hamlet, end the great amusement of the audience, he played "God save the King." COLONEL Landmann rela.,es that in the early part of the present century, while at Plymouth, then the scene of much excitement, be noticed one of the many ingenious ways devised by drunken sailors to get rid of their•pay and prize money. A foremastnian, who had just received £7OO, and twenty-four hours' leave of absence, hired three carriages and four—one for his hat, another for his stick, and a third for himself—and in this fashion rode about the streets of Plymouth, from public-house to public-house, until morning. DIME is a story told of a Carlisle "boots" and a Scotch drover. It was Sawney's first journey southward; he was in eestaciee when "boots" brought him his shoes in the morning, blabk and polished as he ha.l never seen them before. Sawney took them in his hand, turned them round and round ; could not enough admire them. "They're vera bonnie indeed ; thank ye, my mon," said he. But " boots " was not to be put off in this way, and he immediately rejoined, "None of your thanks, you owe me twopence." ASKING TOO Munn. —A young couple were sitting together in a romantic spot, with birds and flowers about them, when the following dialogue ensued : —" My dear, if the sacrifice of my life .would please you, most gladly would I lay it at your feet." —"Oh, air, you are too kind I But it just reminds me that wish you'd stop timing tonacco."—"Can'S think of it, it's a habit to widen I am wedded."— " Very well, sir' since tbat is the way you lay down your life for me, and as you are already wedded to tobacco, I'll take good care you are never wedded to rue, as it would be bigamy." SollETßltia SUBSTANTIAL.—An Intelligent cor- respondent who to witness the sun rise, had climbed up the aidge to a position a thousand feet above ordinary mankind, and remained there enjoying nature, and "nothing else," until he was half starved; is forced to the conclusion that, " in such a case, you will find more real genuine com- fort in a cold cut from a country-cured ham, or a slice from a well-buttered loaf, than you could by any possibility derive from the fragrance .of ten thousand flowers—from the sight of the most temptingly-spread landscape—or from a sunbeam— stewed, fried, or roasted ! "—American Paper. A Plan:um—A fair young girl is leaning pen- sively on the casement, gazing with thoughtful brow upon the scene below. The bloom of-fifteen summers tints her soft cheeks, the sweets of a thousand flowers are gathered upon a neck of per- fect grace, the swimming eyes seem lighted by the tenderest fire of poetry, and beauty hovers over rer as her own most favoured child. What are her thoughts? Love cannot stir a boson: so young, nor sorrow yet have touched a spirit so pure. Innocence itself seems to have chosen her as her own. Alas ! has disappointment touched her youth- ful heart? Yes it must he so; but hist ! she starts; her bosom heaves; her eyes brighten; her lips part; she speaks : listen—" Jim, you nasty fool; leave off scratching that pig's hack, or I'll tell mar."

The New York Tinies heard a story the other day of a distinguished politician from the rural districts, who came to New York, and resolved to give a splendid dinner to some of his party friends. In order to make sure tha.t, everything should be of the best quality, he went to mar-et himself, and bought first a turtle. After taking great pains to sel-et one of the finest specimens in the lot, and ordering it to be sent home, he said to the trades- man by way of making it quite right—" This is a right-down genuine turtle, ain't it ?"—" Oh, cer- tainly," was the reply ; "one of the best."— " Because," he added, "although I ain't been in the city long, I ain't to he humbugged; it won't do for you to try to put MI any of your confounded mock turtles on me l" T'le turtle-dealer stood astounded at his customer's sharpness.

div.head: "CAPITAL" CHAT.
div.p: "CAPITAL" CHAT.

" Guido " will feel the death of her mother ke.nly. They had seldom been apart duringlheir lives, and were deeply attached to each other, though the novelist's methods of attaining realism were not always to her mother's liking. It is said of her that in the old days she used occasionally to invite young officers- of the Guards and young gentlemen of a sporting tendency to dine with her and her mother. After dinner, then they had lighted up, she used to tell them to suppose that her mother and herself were out of the room. "Smoke and drink as if you were at the club," she said. "Talk as if you were in the smoking-room. Never think about us "—and they did so.

In the days when England was dotted with monastries and abbeys, the good monks grew excel- lent grapes and produced wine of quite passable quality. It is possibly due to Lord Bute's sympathy with the ancient faith of these isles that has deter- mined him to become a genuine British wine grower. The marquis does not, of course, aspire to be the purveyor of those somewhat mysterious compounds familiar to cbrildren at Christmas parties, under the denomination of "British wines,' but is con- vinced that there is a chance of England produc- ing something more nearly approaching to Chateau Margaux than vin ordinaire. So far his success is encouraging, and a keen competition resulted in good figures being realised at a recent sale of some of the Cardiff brands.

The Rev. Alexander Connell, who occupied his newly-acquired pulpit at Regent-sq. for the first time on Sunday evening, is a mere stripling of twenty-seven who was raised at Ballachulish,under the weird shadows of Glencoe. It is only ten years since he crossed, for the first time, the portal of Edinbugh University, whence, on attaining his M.A., he removed to the Free Church College in the same city, completing his course with a brilliant B.D. Although the best Gaelic preacher amongst his colleagues, be • forsook his native heather for Ilabylon, and for three years has been rushing into a reputation at Westbourne-grove. Regent-sq. Presbytery is to be congratulated upon baying made this time a choice that this is likely to stay.

"The happiest man in London," as a magazine recently described the Rev. Forman Horton, MA., was 38 years of age on Mbnday. The rev, gentle- man who is one of the most eloquent and popular Congregational ministez s in London, began his min- istry at Hampstead in 1880,after his Nonconformist views had resulted in his exclusion from a profes- sorship of New College, Oxtord, where he had been a fellow and a tutor. Within four yeals his success as a preacher necessitated the building of a larger church, and the congregation assembling there have the distinction of contributing more to religious and charitable purposes than any other church -in Lon- don. As a theologian, Mr. Horton has somewhat broad and advanced views, and his works have been much niscussed. By the way, he is president of the Hampstead Liberal Association.

The announcement in Tuesday's cable message from Melbourne that Sir Matthew Davies, the pro- secuted chairman of the defunct Mercantile Bank of Australia, is going to conduct his own &fence because he cannot afford to pay for counsel, is a startling illustration of the ups and downs of life. When Sir Matthew was a millionaire in 1886, and entertained on a lavish scale in conutztion with the Indian and Colonial Exhibition in South Kensing- ton, the aristocrats of the West-end who shared his hospitality, never dreamed that in seven years he would be a penniless bankrupt, facing a criminal charge. At that time he was regarded as the most successful of colonial financiers; and it was mainly on the strength of his name and reputation that a series of speculative companies were floated in the City. Nearly all of these have come to grief, and many a British investor laments the day on which he first beard of Sir Matthew Davies.

Mr. Albert Stanley. the agent of the ten thousand miners on Cannock Chase, who has sacrificed his all to provide food for his starving men, is one of the best examples of the second class of labour leaders whom the Miners' Federation has the credit of rais- ing. Sprung from the mine, and endowed with a great power of native eloquence, Mr. Stanley wields an immense influence over the men of the hilly dis- trict in which he lives, who have sent him to his county council as the first direct representative of labour there. Secretary of the Midland Miners' Federation, an organisation which int'ades the coalfields of North and South Staffordshire ad War- wickshire, Mr. Stapler, in spite of his youth, has already been mentioned as a miners' man for Par- liament. Prior to the last election he received from the Trade Council of Stafford—the constituency of the late Mr. Alexandsr Macdonald—an invitation to contest the borough, but Stafford is a shoemaking town, and not a mining constituency. and Mr. Stan- ley wisely decided to stand aside from the Parlia- mentary struggle for the present.

Mr. Wynne of Peniarth, whose evidence before the Welsh Land Commission is regarded with so much satigaction by the opponents of the Land Court, is one of the most popular landowners in the Principality. He is/ tall, fair man, still handsome,a good landlord, and justified in boasting that he never has a cross word with his tenants. His library of Welsh books and manuscripts is believed to be the finest in the world. Mr. Wynne himself is a scholarly man, but the credit of this famous collec- tion must be given to his father, who was one of the most learned and enthusiastic bibliophiles in in the country. The library was catalogued a few years ago by Professor Rhys, of Oxford. Mr. Wynne once made a bid for Merioneth as a Tory, but failed His ancestors had often represented the county. A story is told that one of them found the difficulty of travelling to London so great, that he refused to attend the sittings of Parliament. A Sergeant-at- Arms was sent to fetch him to the Bar of the House and got as far as Dolgelly. but when he saw the lonely roads over the mountains to the then resi- dences of the Wynnes,he lost heart and returned to town without his charge.

Now that Mr. Coningsby Disraeli is fairly. launched on the stormy sea of politics, and occu- pies his famous uncle's house at Hughenden, it will be interesting to see whether he will continue to adopt his present evident policy of following in the footsteps of Lord Beaconsfield. He begins as a landed proprietor, an ambition which Disraeli was only able to satisfy quite late in life, and which he accepted most seriously. Mr. Fowler, a .neigh bout of the late earl, published not long since, in a little volume, "Echoes of Old Country Life," a most amusing story in evidence of the spirit in which the Conservative leader acted up to his new posi- tion as lord of the manor.

Lord Beaconsfield was not merely anxious to be an authority an agricultural matterß,and talk crops and chemicals, but he once posed as a farmer, in full costume. At one of the meetings of the Bucks Association at Aylesbury, he amazed his constitu- ents by appearing in what he believed tobe genuine farming dress. He had discarded the traditional top-boots, but appeared in a brown velveteen shoot- ing coat, with a flapping waistcoat, and over his black trousers he had drawn a pair of long dark brown leather gaiters, with wooden enttonm covered with leather, reaching from his dandy Wellington boots to his hips, and fastened there with leathern straps to his brace buttons.

The earl's head, we are told. was covered with a black billycock hat, a bird's eye blue silk handker- chief was tied loosely round his neelr,and he carried a 'nig stick with a spud at the end of it. In fact,he looked like a well-dressed gamekeeper. Everyone was screaming with laughter, but, adds Mr. Fowler, "he thought he was paying us agricultural folk a compliment by wearing what he considered to be the typical dress of the British farmer. lie must have been surprised to find many of the real article dressed in the best modern style, and several with coats by the well-known Mr. Poole of Savile- row."

The debate on the diplomatic vote recalls the fact that Lord Savile still receives a pension of £1,700 for diplomatic services. It was thought at the time of his retirement from the Embassy of Rome that he would forego his pension. He had just inherited the Rufford estates of the Saviles in the West Riding, which now bring in a rental of at least £40,000 a year. lie preferred, however, to draw both the rental and the pension. and may do so for many years, as he is a sprightly old gentle- msn of seventy-five, which is comparative youth for a pensioned peer. Lord Savile is a modern Mtecenas. While in Italy he tempered diplomacy with archasological research, and was able to pre- sent a valuable collection of Roman remains to the Nottingham Castle Museum.
Another peer who ekes out a substantial living with the aid of a diplomatic pension IR Lord Sack- Tire, the owner of Boole. Lord Sackville inhelited

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 23, 1893.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 23, 1893.

, . the title about three years ago, although to his dis- gust, everything that could be alienated from it was left to the,Queen's maids of honour,Lord Sack- retirement from the diplomatic force would hardly have suggested a pension. It was his inju- dicious interference in one of the American presi- dential elections that almost led to a breach between the two countries. Lora Sackville was withdrawn from Washington. his errors were repaired as well as possible by Sir Julian Pauncefote,and the British taxpayer signifies his satisfaction with his career by paying the diplomatic bungler £1,300 a year.

Lord Sack Ville recently attained fame by attempt- ing to screw a small rent out or the people of Strat- co; d-on-Avon for the Sllakespearo fountain ;pre- sented by Mr. George Childs. The fountain stands in the Market-place,add the people of Avon showed Iris lordship that they would as soon pay rent for the sub-soil of the parish pump or the ground occu- pied by the gas lamps. Upon that the agent wrote Oat if they would admit Lord- Sackville's right to !Ivy rent on the fountain be might not feel disposed to enforce it. Up to the present,however,they have not done so, and Lord Saukville is probably sorry by this time that be ever made the attempt.

Edna Lvall, the novelist, is slight of stature, with a small thoughtful face, quiet reflective eyes, broad fore- head, and a firm little mouth. The rich brow n hair, arranged according to the prevailing fashion, gives an added dignity to the face._

According to Mrs. Belle M. Perry, the first newspaper to publish the American Declaration of ladepende nce was edited by a woman. The only newspaper that did not suspend publication when Boston was besieged by the British was published by a woman.. San Franscio rejoices in the possession of an athletic young woman, Miss Alice Brennan, otherwise known as the " Queen of the Bay." She is a slender, but strong girl of 19, who works hard at telegraphy. She is an ex- pert oarswoman and swimmer, and the admiration of all the boatmen on the bay. She finds in rowing her rest, tonic and beautifier.

Mdme. Sarah Bernhardt's littlegrand-daughter,Simone is now six years old. She and the curious pets that frisk about the great tragedienne's abode are fast friends She has absolutely no fear of snakes and tigers, and talk to them incessantly in a baby edition of the great Sarah's wonderful voice. A celebrated London dealer in tailor-made costumes for ladies has confided the following to a letter in " Home Sweet Home :—" Ido not for one moment doubt that all lady cyclists in this country will ultim- ately wear the same dress as men. The barriers between man's distinctive costume and women's ditto have been greatly broken down in all ways of late years. When Ellen Terry was married to her second husband, Mr. Craiz, whose name is pronounced as though it con- tained no" I,' 'they spent their honeymoon in a seaport town that was famed for its two great headlands— Ailsa Craig and Gordon Graig. When Ellen Terry gazed on these headlands for the first time she exclaimed im- pulsively : "If ever I have any little Craigs of my own these two great Craigs shall be their godfathers.' Subsequently Miss Terry proved true to her word, for I her two children, the girl is named Ailsa, and the boy is 'Gordon Craig. Mrs. Mackay—whose husband says that he never has more than three suits of clothes—gives magnificent receptions, adorns her house with flowers to the value of thousands of pounds, and possesses jewellery valued at £500,000. Mrs. Johnson-Foster is another million- aire lady who spends largely on social pleasures, as does her sister-in-law. Through the peerage it is the same, says "Home Street Home," and the tradesmen know well that it is not his lordship, but her ladyship, who puts the money in circulation. Mrs. Elizabeth Brown Davis, who computes the ephemeris of the sun for the "Nautical Almanac," is a woman less than 30 years old, and a remarkable mathe- matician. She competed for a place worth £240 a year in the office of that paper, and beat a dozen male rivals csmspicuously. The Germon Empress having such a passion for Eng- lish-made gowns, has followed the example of her husband's aunt, Princess Louise, Marchioness of Lorne, and has had two exact models of her figure made. By this means a perfect fit is *secured without the trouble of "trying on." .

div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting of the above Board was held in Widnes Town Hall on Tuesday, when there were present Mr. 11 Wade Deacon (chairman), Revs. Father Clarke, and Dean Finegan, Dr. O'Keeffe, and Messrs. C. Flynn and S. Quinn, and Mr. G. H. Denby (clerk).

div.head: GENERAL PURPOSES COMMITTEE.
div.p: GENERAL PURPOSES COMMITTEE.

Dr. O'Keeffe proposed and Dean ?mega,' seconded the adoption of the minutes of this committee which recom- mended that caretaker fiaguo, of the West Bank Board School, have an increase of salary. Dr. Olieeffe explained that the proposed increase was from 255. to 275. 6d. The old caretaker had 275. 6d. per week, but when the new caretaker was engaged he received a smaller salary until it was seen that he gave satisfaction. —The minutes were adopted.
DISTRICT EDUCATION COMMITTEE.-DECRBASR IN THE

div.head: NUMBER OF SCHOLLRS.
div.p: NUMBER OF SCHOLLRS.

The adoption of this committee's minutes which reported, that during the month of August (five weeks) the number of cases summoned before the committee, were the following, viz :—Application for free places, 51; for contravention of Education Act, 323; total 374. Free places granted in 51 cases. Refused, 0; number of prosecutions before the magistrates, 41; number of con- victions (including 2 iettendanct orders), 41; was moved by Rev. Father Clarke and seconded by toe Rev. Dean Finegan.;—The committee also reported the work ot the committee during the year to be as follows .—Cases summoned before the committee, 2.994; application for payment for fees, 424: fees reconamend,d for payment, 420; prosecutions before the magistrates, 336; fined five shillings including coets, 307 ; withdrawn, 18 ; attend- ance orders, 8 ; committed to industral schools, 2; chil- dren in truant schools, 3; averale number on the rolls, 6,5873; average atteedarice,s,Bol.4 .; percentage 85'0. Rev. Father Clark said that there were fewer on the rolls than last year, although the average attendance was higher. There was only one year previously when there was a higher percentage, viz., 1889. No doubt the fine weather would have something to do with it.—Deari Fines:as : The committee hope that the line weather will continue.—Mr.H.Wade Deacon was sorry that there were so many prosecutions,although it was shown that the cases had been properly bilt-cl by the committee when there were 307 coati( tions. He also regrett- d that the number on the rolls had decreased for the first time. This was not Batista, tory to contemplate as it looked as though the population was tending t go down. A report had been issued by the Education Department showing that there had been an increase in the average attendance for the whsle kingdoth of 322 the average attendance for infant schools being 87.08 P.C. and for the eider schools 82.88 p.c. He would like the committee to ascertain hov. the matter stood in Widnes. He had great pleasure in thanking the committee for the trouble they had .taken. —Dean Finegan said that the average attendance which was the great thing would compare favourahly indeed with other t iwns.—The minutes were passed.
SCHOOL MANAGEMENT commirm.—THEr TEACHERS' RE-
QIIICST FOE A HOLIDAY.

- Dean Finegan moved and the Chairman seconded the adoption of the minute, of this Committee, which recom- mended (a) that the res'gnation of Miss M. Woodall, certificated assistant, West Bank Schools, be accepted : (b) that the School Management Committee be and is hereby authorised to open evening continuation elapse!. at the Simm's Cross Schools, and if necessary at the Warrington-road and West Bank Schools, and to appoint teachers and to provide books,apparatus, etc., for carry- ing on the same; (c) also that the Committee report that they had the petition referred to them by the last board meeting respecting the teachers having an extra week's holiday, and that they beg to recommend that the same be not granted.—Dean Finegan referring to minute (b) said that they had selected Simm'a Cross school as being the most central. So far as the Committee could avoid it, they would not entail much expense. He hoped the public would appreciate the schools, if they did not it was useless to maintain them. He might mentithi that at Warrington last year the continuation schools only cost £7, to the ratepayers and at Runcorn a school was carried on with 45 pupils which was almost self-supporting.—Mr. Deacon said that the Committee must exercise a little proctiee in the matter, and the schools would become a great success. He was glad that the age for attending the schools was not confined to those under 21 years of age. There was also no examination now, and he thought this was a great inducement to many of the young people of the town. He urged strongly upon the Committee to make arithmetic a strong point, as a number of people were very deficient on the subject that was so necessary for other technical subject. —With reference to minute c, Dean Finegan said that the Committee were of opinion that the teachers had enough holidays as with the extra holidays during the year, the total number of holidays during the year amounted to 811 weeks. He also thought the children snent little time enough in the schools, and the more holidays they had, the greater cramming they had. The Committee had no objections to allowing the teachers to choose a different time for their holidays.— Mr. Deacon said that it must be considered that the teachers had every Saturday during the year as a boll- day.—The minutes were passed.

div.head: RUNCORN VOLUNTEER SHOOTING CLUB.
div.p: RUNCORN VOLUNTEER SHOOTING CLUB.
GOLD MEDAL COMPETITION.

The eighth and final competition for 1893 took place at Runcorn Heath, on Saturday, under Ris- ley rules, seven shots each at '200; 500 and 600 yards. The atmospheric conditions were fairly favourable, although the light varied considerably. However. the two principal competitors succeeded in putting in the very respectable totals of 91 and 90 respec- tively. As previously intimated, the gold medal 0, the club has now become the absolute property o Sergeant W. H. Harvey, who is to be congratulated on the success that has crowned his persevering efforts during the seven years that the medal has been in competition. The medal, which is a handsome specimen of the goldsmith's art, had to be won by the same person three years in succession, or four times in all. lip to the commencement of the year Sergeant:Har- vey and Sergeant D. Edwards had each held the coveted jewel for three years, but neither of them in succession, consequently which ever of these two won it this year took absolute possession. Hence the unusual haterest attached to this year's struggle. That Sergeant Edwards had struggled manfully for the honour will be seen from the following records of the six best shoots (upon which the decision rests) made by the two competitors : lot. 2nd. 3rd. 4th. sth 6th. Tat. Sergeant Harvey ... 84 ... 83 .. 82 ... 93 ... 84 ... 91 ... 517 Sergeant Edwards... 86 ... 81 ... 83 ... 85 ... 78 ... 90 ... 503 Now that the medal has ceased to be the property of the club, the committee would be grateful for the offer of a cup, medal, or other articles to be competed for in the future. As before stated, the club has justified its existence by the marked improvement manifested in the shooting abilities of those who have become members. This footnote was inserted at the close of the report of the last competition, and in consequenee a private gen- tleman in the town has suggested that an article not ex- ceeding £5 in value should be procured each year by a few gentlemen contributing ss.or 10s. each and he kindly offered 10s. if the remainder could be obtained. The challenge should be promptly attended to.

div.head: LADIES' LETTER
div.p: LADIES' LETTER
MY DEAR NELLIE,

With little evidence of the lateness of the sealon there is apparently no justiscation for talking about winter dress, but a glance at the calendar will assure you that the cold weather will soon be upon us. You will be glad to learn the latest fashion intelligence, and it is appalling for those of limited means—that all who can afford them will have velvet garments this winter; shot velvet by preference. How thick and rich the new patterns seem! The peacock shot with vieux rouge, the petunia with scarlet, the orange with brown, the emerald with yellow. How well they will combine with old laces, which are more and more valuable as the demand increases for them. But in velvet there are still greater novelties—the shot brocades in large arabesque patterns. On examining the weaving at the back, it becomes apparent that light green, dark green, and brown are employed; but the surface only shows a rich compact whole, which assumes varied aspects in different lights. Doubtless you, in common with many of our sisters, are searching for a costume for autumn wear. Well, there are some extremely effective styles in which any fancy or plain material may be used, and either ribbon or piece velvet employed for trimming, the latter cut on the bias. Five toad a-half yards of double width stuff and one and a-half yards of Vel-Vel will be ample for a costume, or six yards if the skirt reaches under the deep flounce.

Chine silks are the height of the mode, and a number of light-tinted shot moires, with white, cream, lightesi; pink, and faintest peach, are covered with close-set horizontal cords of contrast- ing colour—green on pink, tilleul on peach, pale blue on White, gold on cream, with large bouquets of chine flowers scattered all over, and exquisitely coloured. If anyone contemplates a stylish dinner or evening gown, she should bestow special atten- tion on this range of novelties, or some of the moires covered with pin spots of contrasting hue. One silk which is singularly distinctive is a rich shot glace, covered with what appears to be wire grounded black net; this is thrown on light pink shot with peach, diversified by the conventionalised bloom of a minute primula in the peach tint. It is equally pretty in gold, shot) with grass-green, and it has richness, substance, and colour. An extremely pretty child's dress of homespun has been shown to me. Perhaps I should rather call it a pelisse, for, although at one time this word applied only to a costume for "baby," we elders have now generally adopted the term, so I may use it without fear of being misunderstood. A pelisse, then, explains exactly what I mean ; and although this model may be copied for a tiny mite, i; is really intended to be worn by quite a big girl, say, of 10 to 12 years. Made of homespun, and trimmed with 'broad black or brown military braid, it makes a charming walking costume, or for smarter occasions it could be copied in a plain. fatted cloth, and edged with fur.

The newest varieties of brocades are singularly Lovely, displaying beautiful satin grounds with sparsely scattered flowers, that appear to be hand embroidered. A primrose, with its leaves in natural colours, is thrown on light petunia satin, the peaeh-linted primrose on grey; and a deep orange bloom on atone. Grass-green satin is beflowered with yellow blooms, petunia with rose- red, and tea-green with bright pink—nothing gloomy in tone is tolerated. Another variety of brocade is of two tints of the same colour. Light green roses appear on dark green satin, light violet on blush pink, the rose being of silk, the leaves outlined with the colour. Feathers and serrated leaves in waved weaving are worthy of all praise. Head gear is always a pleasing topic amongst women, and you will like to know that felts are coming into the market in large quantities. The shapes are excellent as a rule, and some compara- tively inexpensive examples are easily procured. Colours are neat and multitudinous. •

Out of a yard of soft bright silk and a-pair of fleeced cork soles a charming pair of bedroom slippers can be made in a few hours. Fust, "We" of dressmaker's canvas lined with the silk is fastened to the sole. Then the soft silk is folded all about the sole and is fastened to it by stitches between the folds ; it covers the toe, and is tied in a loose, soft bow on top. Each slipper requires half a yard of silk. Such slippers are very warm and comfortable for badroom wear. Believe ion, your ever loving, JENNIE.

Miss Maggie Davies, known throughout Wales as the " Little Nightingale." is the principal soprano at the Cheltenham Musical Festival. She is a native of Wales, and very young and pretty. Swedish women often work as farm labourers. Those that have babies carry them on their hacks in a leather bag, as squaws carry their young. This plan permits the mether to use both hands at her farm work. Princess Sybilla of Hesse-Cassel, to whom the Citarewitch will be formerly engaged, is a bright and pretty young girl, with a special gift for music. The little princess is rather young for the position that awaits her having not yet attained her 17tt, year. Has the revolt of women really driven men to find oecupation and refuge in fancy needlework ? At any rate, there was a young man the other day in a railway carriage working, in bright green end violet coloured wools, a canvas kettle holder I And Voltaire said the Worst use you could put a man to was to hang him !

div.head: Pickled Nasturtiums.
div.p: Pickled Nasturtiums.

Gather ripe pods on fine days. If only a very few are ready together, put daily conectings into a well-corked dry bottle. Wipe seeds clean. One pint vinegar, 1 oz. salt, 6 peppercorns, and nasturtiums to about fill. Bung up and seal, or resin the tops. Pickle will be fit 10 or 12 months hence.

div.head: Hot Hands.
div.p: Hot Hands.

Carbolic acid, one part ; burnt alum, four parts; starch, two hundred parts; French chalk, fifty parts ; and oil of lemon, two parts. These ingredients made into a fine powder and applied to the hands will be found useful, or it may be sprinkled in the gloves. Another remedy, and often recommended, is the application,with friction, of belladona liniment. Care, however, is needed with this, as it is poison.

Elderberry Syrup. Gather elderberries, pick off the stalks, and put the berries into a preserving pan with a cupful of water to warr. . Press all the juice from the berries through a bag made of cheese cloth. To each quart of juice add one pound of loaf sugar; boil for twenty minutes. Put a few cloves into a piece of muslin and boil in the syrup. Leave the syrup in the preserving pan until cold ; then, to each gallon of syrup, add one gill of rum or brandy, and bottle or barrel for use. when using the syrup, pour a little into a tumbler with lump sugar and boiling water, and drink hot.

div.head: Vegetable Marrow Preserve.
div.p: Vegetable Marrow Preserve.

Ingredients :---One vegetable marrow, sugar equal in weight to marrow after it has been pared and cored, one large lemon,, and at least two ounces of root ginger. Mode : Slightly bruise the ginger and enclose it in a thin muslin bag ; lay this in the bottom of a large basin. Cut the marrow into pieces about an inch square, and lay on the top of the ginger. Next slice the lemon into the basin, and then heap the sugar over all. Cover with a plate, and leave to soak 24 hours. Then drain off the syrup which will have formed into the preserving pan, putting in also the Ringer and lemon. Boil until the sugar is quite dissolved, then pour the boiling syrup over the marrow in the basin, and let it remain until cold. When quite cold, return to the pan, and boil till tender, stirring frequently. Then remove the ginger and lemon and pat once. The marrow, when done, should have a clear appearance.

div.head: DARK WOOD.
div.p: DARK WOOD.
A TALE OF LONEMOOR.
BY MRS. HARRIET LEWIS, Author of "Her Double Life," " Old Life's Shadows," "Lady Kildare," etc.
CHAPTER LXVIIL CONCLUSION.

Miss Norreys retreated before Lord Darkwood's outstretched arms, eyeing him with a haughty dis- daM, under which lay a great and awful agitation. " Stand back !" she cried. " I am Sicily Nor- reys. Clare Markham is dead !" But the marquis, with frenzied pleading, called that name again. "Clare ! ''My wife ! My wife—"
"You are mistaken, sir.
You had no wife I"

"To see her before My eyes, and yet so far off I" groaned his lordship. "Glare, hear me ! We were legally married. They told me the same lying tale they told you. My father believed it. Captain Tollish adhered to it, so that even I was staggered. When I heard his story, I hurried back to our lodgings. My father and Captain Tollish had just depiirted, and you also were gone. I searched for you. I hurried to Yorkshire. You had not been there, and I would not betray our secret until I had found you. I hastened back to London, and my father told me that you had been found drowned in the Thames. He had had the body buried. There had been a body found, iden- tified as yours, and buried. I thought you had destroyed yourself. I remembered your spirit and your pride, Clare, and I believed that you would not survive dishonour."
"Do not call me Clare," said the heiress haughtily, "else I will, not listen to you. lam Miss Norreys." . .

Lord Da-rkwood's features contracted with an expression of despair. "Believing her dead, tortured, agonised, I left London. I determined to prove Captain Tollish's statements. I went to Berlin. I found the Eng- lish actor still there. The man confessed to me that Captain Tollish had employed him to person- ate a clergyman, and that Captain Tollish had paid him a liberal sum for the wicked imposture. He had intended to keep his agreement, but at the last his courage had failed, and lie had feared to com- mit a felony. He had, therefore, at the last moment employed a clergyman of the Church of England to perform the ceremony! The marriage was true and lawful. Clare Markham was my lawful wife !"

A strange sobbing cry came from Squire Mark- ham, who still stood upon the threshold unheeded. "I returned to England with proofs of the mar- riage. I was too late. My wife I believed dead. I heard that Squire Markham had left England. I found it hard to forgive my father, who had been an instrument in the hands of Captain Tollish, with whom he had a deadly quarrel after my return, forbiddim; him his house and presence. I quarrelled with Tollish also. I could have killed him. He had destroyed my life, my happiness, my wife !" His lordslisp looked at Miss Norreys imploringly. Her expression wavered. She looked uncertain, moved to the depths of her soul. " Last night I found my child," said Lord Dark- wood. " Gwendoline, my daughter, come to me !" Gwen quitted her lover and walked to the mar- quis's side. " Gwendoline, plead for me," said the noble lord entreatingly, his gaze not swerving from Miss Norreys's face. " I was to blame for the fatal weakness of concealing our marriage. But have I not been awfully punished for my weakness? Clare, forgive me. I love you more than I did years ago. You are my life, my soul. Clare, wife, take us— your husband and your child! Come to us, wife ! "
Gwendoline took the marquis's hand and drew Matto Miss Norreys. . .

The heiress.s face softened into an ineffable beauty, sweetness, and tenderness. Her eyes were irradiated with a love that struggled through all the bitterness and darkness and misery of years, that had underlain the passionate sense of wrong and desire for revenge and still survived, deathless, unalterable, the principle of her being. She moved towards him. He released Gwen, and took her in his arms—his wife !
And still Squire Markham stared at the heiress, his features working, his breath coining in gasping sobs,
The marquis, forgetful of the wondering eyes upon the most sacH,l meeting, rained kisses and tears upon Miss ~;orreys's face, and thanked heaven for its great goodness to them both.

_ Then he drew Gwen also to his embrace. There was a profound silence for many minutes, broken cnly by those low sobs. Miss Norreys—Miss Norreys no longer—was the first to recover herself. She gently disengaged herself from his clinging arins, but still his armt mowed her, ana his proud eyes moßea iove ann tenderness upon her, as she said—

"Lord Chilton, Mr. Sutton, friends, there is some explanation due to you. I am that Clare Markham who was supposed to have perished on the Yorkshire moors seventeen years ago--" "Clare Charteris, Marchioness of Darkwood Interposed her husband. "How I escaped death that night upon the Lone Moor Ido not know," said Lady Darkwood. "I was picked up by some belated farmer who crossed the moor that night, and took me to his home near Staley-bridge. I was very ill from exposure, and he sent me to a hospital in Manchester, where for weeks I was nigh unto death. When I recovered From my derangement, it was long before I could ask the question that was uppermost in my mind. After I was transferred to the convalescent ward, I asked my new nurse for my baby. She knew of no baby. She made inquiry, and told me that my child was dead. My visit to Lonemoor seemed to me the merest vagary .pf a dream, and yet my father's curse hung upon me like a living terror. I could not go home. What was Ito do?

"I had been known by a very ordinary name in the hospital. They had not known my real name, and had conferred upon me the name of Mary Smith. I was discharged from the hospital ; hut one of` the doctors, who had interested himself in me, offered to procure me a situation as child's nurse in a family going to India. "I had relatives out there. I was eager to get away from England. I accepted the proffered situation, and went to India. "There I found my mother's brother, General Norreys. I told him of my disgrace, my father's curse—which, although I thought it a dream, seemed yet so terribly real—and he and his wife pitied me, and took me to their hearts. They had recently lost their only child, my cousin Sicily. They gave me her name, and adopted Inc as their daughter. They procured masters for me, and I remained in the school-room another year, having a dread of society and being fond of hooks. I entered society a year later as their daughter, and was supposed to have been fresh from my studies, as I was, indeed, and from a lifetime of seclusion. My new mother died. General Norreys, my dear second father, died also less than two years ago. 1 He wished me to return to England, to make for myself a home, and I promised to do so.
"I came to London. Beekiliniont was for sale. I sent an agent to look at it, and bought it without seeing it, and without knowing that Dunholm Castle was so near.
"The rest you know. I have found rank, posi- tion, honour—l have found my husband and my child. But one desire remains to me—to see my dear old father yet once more, and implore his for-
giveness-- " Spire Markham tottered forward. _

"'Here he is, Clare !" he exclaimed; "your hard old father, who cursed you! Can you forgive me? I can never forgive myself !" Clare, with a glad cry, sprang to his arms, and they wept together. " Gwendoline," said the squire, humbly, a little later, "can you forgive your old grandfather? , I know lam past all forgiveness— ' But Gwen, too, came to him and kissed him, her pale lace radiant with joy. Upon this scene a servant intruded. " Is Squire Markham here ?" he asked. The old squire raised his head. How genial his happy old face had grown ! His tears had washed out all the grimness and hardness of the past eigh- teen years. " I am here !" he answered. "Au old person, who has just arrived from Lon- don, insists on seeing you, The servant was pushed aside by the gold person " herself, Mrs. Quillet. She had, npon recovering from the shock of the discovery that the body which had been found upon the Lone 'door was not that of her nursing, followed her master to London, hoping to see him before his departure from England and tell him the astounding news. _ _ .
She had learned of his departure for Beeehmont, azd had followed him thither. Fe„,a.ring lest she atint`,Ll 1.):;

appeal to inm yet once more on nenair or Ms daughter, who might he alive, she had pushed her way into hid very presence. " Master," she said appealingly. "I must see you. I have something of great importance to stsY. to you--" . .

_ She stopped, staring at Gwen. Could it be that the squire had found his grand-- ' daughter, and intended to adopt her? " Nurse I" said a soft, low voice at her elbow- . "Dear old nurse, have you forgotten me?" . Mrs. Quillet faced about. "Mrs. Quillet," said the squire, proudly, " this . lady is my daughter, the Marchioness of Dark- ' wood--" " Miss Clare !" cried the old nurse. ~ My 10St lamb ! Oh, my darling, my pet !" . The old housekeeper was overwhelmed. There was imminent danger that the shock would produce a second " fit" ; but her nursling's caresses and embraces warded off the peril. When they had all grown calmer, what experi- ences they rehearsed, what happiness and mill". content possessed them !
Is them more to tell? Shall we describe the joy of the reunited husband and wife, of the old squire, of the lovers, of every member of the group? Shall v describe the 11,-- to Min"
iliall we the happy home going holm Castle, the grand rejoicings of the tenantry, the seven days' wonder of the county?

Nay, it is not necessary.. The reader will understa.nd that which our pen is inadequate to describe. But we will state that Captain Tollish,s humble funeral took place the day after the reunion. S° great was the detestation of the villain among the Darkwood tenantry that the landlord of the ino could not be prevailed upon to allow the bedy remain longer under his roof. He lies in a secluded corner of the churchyard, and no one, not even his daughter, mourns his death. Miss Tollish, shorn of title and honours, Nv3! sent to school by Lady Darkwood, hut completea her own misery six months later by eloping will, strolling player, who abused her shamefully, an° of whom she stood in mortal terror.

Six months later ! Ali, that brings us to the vied; ding of the Lady Gwendoline Charteris and 1,001 Chilton—a grand affair, chronicled in the Court journals with great descriptive details! And the Orkneys, in rage, read how the bride was dressed, and gnashed their teeth that the great prize had escaped their brother. Mr. Orkney had long since lost his situation at Lonemoor, and was living upon his savings at Penistone, devoting his time to strictures upon the conduct of his family, and making the life of wife and daughters a burden to them. We have only to add that Lord Chilton presented a comfortable living to Mr. Myner, and that Mr-, and Mrs. Myner bless Lady Chilton every day their lives. And the Rev. Mr. Myner "assisted the bishop and other reverends at the marriage 0f our hero and heroine, an honour which he will ever regard as the greatest of his life.

It seems that some time in 1889—in the winter, tie' doubt—Mr. Strong, of Leicester, was taken down witb influenza, often called the grip ; and truly a strong grit' it has when it once takes a hold. Well; lam glad to sal he was able to fight out the battle and get the best of it• But the best wasn't anything to brag of. The influeorn hadn't exactly beaten Mr. Strong, but it left him in fi very bad condition. And here is where you and I pro- rerly pick up the thread of the story. His meals didn't tempt him ; the most savoury °f dishes had no charms for our friends. He had lost bis appetite, and in the long run a man had better lose Ina money. He forced down something of course, but,, "i: gave him such a pain in the chest that he wished " hadn't swallowed a mouthful. Then, naturally, he /P 4 so weak and nervous he couldn't sleep o' nights. Thie' as everybody knows, is the straight road to the grave- yard, through the madhouse. Lots of people area-faking that trip all the time. We mast eat and we must eleeP- If we don't we are done for. Neuralgic pains, ton,inad: matters worse for Mr. Strong. He saw a doctor, what did did the doctor do ? This is what the patient sal, on that point t " This doctor gave me all kinds strengthening medicines, but none of them did me Of, good, and I continued to suffer for month afte. month." Just what we might have expected. Mr. Strong ther says : "In October, 1890, my friend, Mr. Jan/'" Webster, of 28, New Walk, Leicester, advised me to a medicine called Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup, and followed his advice. The first bottle gave me great re lief, and I began to digest my food and to have an petite ; and after I had used three bottles 1 was eui9-0 another man. I was completely cured. All me ecben and pains left me,my strength returned,and I have all right ever since. What astonished me was that t" Syrup cured me so quickly,and I shall never cease that'll°. Mg Mr. Webster for making it known to me. YOU are at liberty to publish any case for the benefit of otberl• Yours truly (Signed), W. STRONG, 41, East Street, cester, December 30th, 1891. " Now, was there a mistake in this matter, and if: what was it ? Yes, there was a common mistake inn It is an old and seemingly hopeless blunder. "The doctor," says Mr. Strong, " gave me all xo- of strengthening medicines." Open wide your ears and remember what I'm going W. tell you now ; remember it for the hour of your 011.,, helplessness and pain : There is ne such thing as stile', ening medicine, neither in the earth nor in the eatit,%, which are under the earth. This is the truth ; 511 to. high class doctors know it. As for the others--ire there ! the less.said about them the better. , and Mr. Strong took " strengthening medicines,' der what happened to him ? Why, ht "continued to snd, month after month." Did you ever see a horse niaoff stronger and fatter by spurs and lash-whips ? leaving the oats and hay? I think you have not. And that; what " strengthening medicines "do, and all the ° inf So-called tonics are like making, a sick man wel and fast by kicking him at every other step. ° Nothing under the sun but digested food lrePa strength ; no drug ever does. of And herein is the perpetual success and victo rgease. Mother Seiyers Syrup; it cleanses the system of dis poison and leaves nature street and free. The stonaco then cries, "Feed me," and so power and health se7; back like the green grass after a shower. Doprn_ture Mother Seigel proclaims " I destroy disease ! ' responds, " Only do that, and I can take care self." Strong The disease is indigestion and dyspepsia. Mr. had it and was badly treated. Should you have it 1.4" the Syrup first—not last, for I have told you why- London, March, 1592.

MR. SAM WOODS' SALARY AND EXPENSES. Fully 3,000 persons assembled at Gars% ood, near St. Plelens, on Wednesday, to hear an address from Mr. Sam Woods, M.P., an additional attraction be- ing the hope that the Rev. W. J. Melville, rector of Downall-green, who had replied through the Press to Mr. Sam Woods, and who had been chal- lenged by the latter to appear ori‘that platform, would be present. Mr. Woods, however, read the following letter from Mr. Melville ".Ashton Rectory, Wigan, Sept-amber 15, 1893. " Sir,—l am in receipt of your letter of the 13th inst., and wrote one letter to the Liverpool Courier with the object of correcting a gross mis-statement of yours respecting the action of the colliery masters in relieving the distress. I wrote a secend letter which was simply to point out to the colliers a better means of having something to live upon in times of a strike .or other distress than their present plan. My third letter was simply a reply to yours, in which you accused me as you do in your present letter, of siding with the masters against the colliers. I deny emphatically that I have ever said or done a single thing which to an•honest, un- prejudiced mind could be interpreted in this light. I have taken no side at all. I have striven to relieve the distress by every insane in my power, and if at any time I tbink the colliers are being advised by you or anyone else to their own disadvantage, either immedi- ately present or future, I shall not fail to try and check it. On these grounds I see no reason why you should ask me to justify myself at your mass meeting, which I cannot attend, even though I were in such a state of health as to warrant me in doing so.—l am, sir, yours faithfully. "W. J. MEtvitte. Mr. S. Woods, M.P. " P.S.—As you have sent to the Press your letter to me, I shall do the same with my reply if I think it necessary." • Mr. Woods then stated that this explained the absence I of the rev, gentleman, whose statements and attack lie I (Mr. Woods) would deal with later on. (Cries of "Re dare not come 'I" "Give it him Woods and j laughter.) Mr. Joseph Hayes, a miner, said they had been battl- ing eight weeks against the unjust demands of the ' masters and against the hostile criticisms of persons who knew little or nothing about the real issue. Asking them to accept arbitration was like asking a condemned man it he would accept the guillotine. (Laughter.) Mr. Ned Walkden, of Brynn, district secretary for the : miners, proposed a resolution to the effect that themeet- ing approved of the efforts to bring the crises to an end at an early date, but strongly protested against any ' reduction, believing that wages were low enough to maintain themselves, their wives, and children in a respectable manner. The meeting also condemned any I outside interference with the negotiations, believing that men's reprerentatiyes and the employers' representatives were very well able to take care of their own business. The speaker said the Rev. W. J. Melville had criticised the spending of the funds of the Miners' Union, and had said they were frittered away on agents and expenses. That was not the fact, as he (Mr. Walkden) was in a position to say what it had taken to keep Mr. Woods in Parliament and in going up and down the country. They were told it was impossible to return Mr. Woods to Parliament, but they diri return him.. (A voice : "And will again," and cheers.) They were told by the Conser- vative Press and a certain section of workingmen that if :they would look to their own business instead of making a great noise outside it would be better, as to keep Mr. Woods in Parliament would mean a levy of 2d. per member per week. That (Mr. Walkden said) was purely imaginative, for it had taken nothing of the kind. When :Mr. Woods was only a miners'. agent it was costing 2.9. per member per Year, and now he was in the House of ' Commons and working both at Bryon and London, and they had an assistant agent, he found the full cost to be less that ls. a year. (Loud cheers.) It was less than id , per week for each man. Was that money frittered away. (" No, no.") If Mr. Woods had done nothing more than what he had for Messrs. M'Corquodalels printers he had earned his salary. Mr. Joseph Haves seconded the resolution. • Mr. woods will was greeted with loud cheers,' said the hostile criticism he had received firm a section of the Wigan "Press would not interfere with the close con- fidence which existed between him and the electorate of I the division. He cared nothing about the opinion of critics. So long as his conduct and language were , approved of bv those whom he had the honour to , represent he should simply fht his finger at them. It ' was said he had fallen foul at the magistrates at Feather- I atone. That might be so ; and where was the man with I one principle of human nature and ono principal of , Christianity that would not fall foul of a Man who ordered a troop of soldiers to fire and shoot down I unarmed men with scarcely any justification whatever? In the interest of the working men of the country they must put an end to that sort of business. He thought, : it was abominable that magistrates could be found to , order men to fire on a crowd without justification. As long as he could speak, and as long as their influence could be felt, he should not leave that case until the I man vihn gave the order had either been committed or 'prneed clear by a searching investigation into all the e.ircumstanees (cheers). If they would not get such an inqiiiry during the autumn session of Parliament, he and others would move the adjournment of the house in I order to call attention to the matter, in vindication of the rights and liberties of the working people. The , miners were fighting for a living wage. Some said in ' effect, "You must. work, no matter what wages you get" hut that was done in the days of slavery, andatbey did net intend to have the taskmasters over them with , the whip in the nineteenth century (cheers). They were trying to upset the old order of things, and were trying to get living wages and honourable treatment for the people who were making the wealth and making the , character of the country as great as it was. He Woods) had incited the people to work fora living wage for honest work; and he had incited the people resist the aborninallv unjust and Unreasonable reduction of 25 per cent. Would anvnne say that the miner shonld not have a fair wage, and should not resist the reduction (a Voice, "If there is, kick him out ") ? He was then griing to deal with the Rev. W. J. Melville (laughter:) That humble head of his had been heaped with vindictiveness and calumniation ; but he had tried to bear it, and he was there that day with a stronger desire to serve the miners and the country than even at the beginning of the struggle. He would not in- dulge in disrespectful criticism ; but as the rev, gentle- man had charged him (Mr. Woods) with ignorance, he weiild charge Mr. Melville with intelligence. (Laughter.) As an instance, he (Mr. Woods) spoke at Ashton-under- Lyne. and said only one employer in his neighbourhood willtaasisting the destitute families. Mr. Melville thought I he had snelcen et Ashton-in-Makerfield. and contradicted , him. When Mr. Melville found out his error about the town, he said if he had known Mr.Wo.:,ds had spoken at Ashton-under-Lyne, he would not have written it.. That was something for his intelligence. He (Mr. Woods) I stuck to his statement that the coa.lowners were trying to break up the Federation by starving the women and children. Mr. Melville had said that Was a libel, as he knew four employers who were largely contributing to the necessities of the Women and children. When he (Mr. Woods) wrote the letter, so far as he knew then there was only one employer that was giving anything. 'end that was at Garswnod Hall. Did Mr, Clark, of Park-lane, give anything before the sth of September ? (A Voice: "Yes.") Let the man give the time and 1 place whore Mr. Claidt gave it, and to whom it was I given. (Thine was na reply, and apparently someone pushed the man.) Mr. Woods said they would have no "purrine." They were having a fair, upright fight,ancl I didn't believe in kicking. They were face to fare with ( criticism, and had an honourable MUM (A Voice : 1 "That we have.") Had Mt. Stone, of Garswood. given anything before the letter was written ? (No r"Piy.) Perhaps he had given it to Mr. Melville, because the latter apparently knew I about it. Ile thought they ought to know from I a Christian minister, when he had made a , statement, when and where and who had received it. , If he did not answer through the Press who the three ' emplovera where be (Mr. Woods) should consider him ri liar. That wee straight. He (Mr. Woods) stuck to the I statements he had made. The masters were trying to 1 win the battle by starving the woman and children. His (Mr. Woods) meaning was deeper and far more reaching than that. lie believed the employers were wanting the men to go to work at 25 per cent, reduction and bring them down to starving wages so that they could not 'lmport their union. Mr. Melville did not compre- hend the meaning, and that was another evidence of his intelligence. He said the agents had made extravagant statements, hut. he (Mr. Woods) had made no statement which was not hatted unon NOR since the commence- ment of the struggle. Mr. Melville had stated that the agents were running away with the money that ought to be for the support of the men. Every penny he Mr Woods) had received in the way ef wages he considered he had worked for (hear, hear.) Not a man there would say he had nnt. -("No.") He had dents all that lay in mortal man to do, both before the strike and diming the strike, and both before he went to the House of Cotnmons and since he had been in the House of Commons. If a manager of a colliery WAs entitled to £1,500 a year, he was entitled to his £5OO a year, nut of which he had to pay railway fares, ex. penees in London, telegra ma, postage-s. and other ex- penses. (Hear, hear.) He had never received a penny except with the unanimous approval of the whole organi- sation. And they could discharge him when they were tired of him. He wished it were so with Mr. Melville. If they could have a ballot on Downall Green they would shift Mr. Melville from his church in less than a fort- night. If the power were in the hands of the parishioners he wnuid not atop in the place he was in. (Hear, hear, and applause.) The motion was unanimously adopted. A vote of sympathy was passed with thn relatives of those who was killed and injured at Featherstone. and: the meeting closed with cheers for "the miners' cause." During the meeting rain fell heavily. Mr. Woods re- marked that, being a Baptist he did not mind the wet, 1 And as the downpnur had not ceased when the proceed- ings closed no time was lost-in dispersing.

SNATCHED FROM HIS GRAVE. "Lancashire Evening Express." Aug. 7. 1893.

We are all sceptical in believing that which on the surface appears to be impossible. But when enquiry ; comes to be made into it our incredulity begins to waver. , We have to ultimately give in and believe the evidence , of our senses, because facts are stubborn things. , Such a fact is the case of Mr. James Henry Brogden, ' who lives at 27, Spring Street, Rislaton, a flourishing little town of six thousand inhabitants, three miles and a half from Blackburn. Three years ago he was going to the grave with no elow or uncertain step-40-day he is as well as ever he was, and, fit for the hardest work that may chance to his hand! Such is the fact, and in! an interview with ac" Express man had with him a few nights ago, he explained how it all came about. His occupation is for the most part out of doors, and some three years ago he caught a succession of severe colds. No end of evils spring from colds, simple though they appear, and one immediate result of Mr. Brogden's chills was sciatica. By and by he got worse, and as he went on he became worse still. He consulted,doctors, but there was no relief for him. His health did not improve, and as a consequence he got into quite a des- ponding condition, and his nerves were attacked. When our representative saw him, he looked as hale as man could wish to, and he was quite willing to tell the " Express " man all about his cure. "It was this way," he explained. "I had tried no end of doctors—three of them, and four herbalists be- sides—but none of them did me any good. Well, one day my brother came from Burnley. He had a news- paper with him, and in this paper was an advertisement which stated what complaints and diseases Dr. Wil- liams' Pink Pills for Pale People were good for." Then Mrs. Brogden took up the narrative and said, " He was reading the advertisement over,when he said, " Eh, lass, this is just the same as me !" Mrs. Brogden continued to explain that they went home and thought aboat it. They had tried everything—doctors, patent medicines, and the hundred and one things that are al- ways recommended by well-meaning friends and neigh- bours—and it occurred to them that they might as well try Dr. Williams' Pink Pills. However, it took some time to come to this conclusion But they decided at length to try a box, and, said Mrs. Brogden, "It wor a God-send." Of course, her husband was not cured by the first box. His disease had got a firm hold on him, and it wanted same moving. But he felt some benefit front the first hex, and this naturally enough gave him faith in the pills. He tried a second and a third box, and up to the present time he has taken the contents of eleven bores with the result that be feels as well as ever he did in his life. "See," said Mrs. Brogden, "I got to quite dislike him. He would come home and row over nothing at all. He got to such a colour too—first yellow, and then worse, almost brown—that I quite took a dislike to him. Be seemed to have no use in his legs at all. He used to diag them about as though he could not walk. Why he actually spoilt one pair of boots in dragging his legs after him; he never wore them out by walking in them.' "The wife used to have to hold me when I went up- stairs," said Mr. Brogden," forA I, hadn't got strength enough to get myself up." "And how do your legs feel now f" asked the " Express " man. "Well, you may guess" replied Mrs. Brogden. "Only last Sunday he walked nineteen miles, and he could not have dents that unless he was strong." Then the good woman went on to tell of 'other circum- stanceis connected with her husband's cure, for she is quite enthusiastic about it, and frankly admits that iss ttsr tired of sounding the praises of , the pills. What with the worry she had through' , her husband's illness, together with his nervous attacks, and her difficulty in keeping the house going out of her single-handed earnings, her own system got out of order. So seeing the benefit he had derived from the pills she I started taking them herself; nor did she end there; for she,gives half a one to her children sometimes, when her I little ones require them. And if the pair of healthy-leeking boys who were called in for our representative to look at were any guide, there could be no doubt that Dr. William,s Pink Pills had left their mark upon them as ' well as upon their parents. Bt Mrs. Breeden went even further than this. " I'm not a bit selfish," she said. " When I know of a good thing myself tans only too glad to tell someone else of I it." . And such is the case. When Mr. Brogden had the first box, Dr. Williams' Pink Pills were unknown in Rishten. But not so now. Others, on her advice, have : taken them, and have felt the benefit, and there are scores of people in Rishton to-day who not only know what Dr. Williams' Pink Pills are good for, but who are I quite willing to believe all that is to be said in their ' favour--for have they not the marvellous cure of James Henry Brogdes before their very eyes? "People could hardly believe their own eyes," said Mr. Breeden,'" when they saw me Walking about on the high road to recovery. I was nearly in my grave, and quite broken down, but lam all right now, and it's a 1 : lowing to the Pink Pills." "And," put in his wife, "I'm expecting him to go and earn 22 per week now, and give me a rest." Whereat both laughed, and Brogden expressed his perfect willing- ness to do so if the chance offered. After hearing mudl more that Mr. and Mrs. Breeden had to say in favour of Dr: Williams' Pink Pills for Pale People, our representa- tive went to Mr. Parker, a local chemist, and there ob- tained substantial evidence of the truth of the Brogdenst experience, and also of the fact that others were now taking the pills who had not known of them before. With such facts as to the results of taking Dr. WU_ hams' Pink Pills, there can be little doubt as to their extraordinary merits. div.head: 111 E EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 2;-3. 1893. RUNCORN BOARD OF 141ARDIANS.
div.p: 111 E EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 2;-3. 1893. RUNCORN BOARD OF 141ARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting wos held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday. Mr. Knowles presided, and there were present the Mors. J. W. N. Tanner, land J. Hanby, Messrb. Baxter, C. 0., T. Lea, D. H, Jones, S. Yarwood, Weir, Aaron, Stokes, Whitley, Lewis, Heywood, Brandreth, Williams, Bratherton, Woodward, Parkinson, Baxter, John Jones, Ford. S. Houghton, John Whitlow; J. Ashton (clerk) and G. Ashton (deputy clerk). ' -

_ _ . TIER ROYAL INFIRMARY. The Local Government Board wrote consenting to the Guardians increasing their subscriptions to the funds of the Manchester Royal Infirmary from £3 3s, to Le es. per annum. THE SCHOOL FEE QUESTION. The Clerk read the following communication " Education Department 18th September 1893. Sir,—l am directed to express their Lordships regret at the long delay in replying to your letter of July 26th. The delay has been caused by their Lordships being unable to ascertain the number of free places the volurtary schools in the Runcorn school district. In repl) to your statement" the Board require 49 free places in the ' township of Runcorn in denominational schools, " I am again to paint out that the law does not give a right to free education in Public Elementary Schools which are entitled under the Elementary Education Act, 1891, to continue to charge fees. I am therefore to inquire whether the Guardians wish to represent to the depart- ment that there is an insufficient amount of public elementary school accommodation without payment of fees for these 49 children, and I am also to inquire whether the Guardians have applied to the managers of the Holy Trinity Church of England school, (at which school there appears to be a considerable:number of free places) for admission of these 49 children without pay- ment of fees.—l have the honour to be, sir, your obedient servant, J. W. J. STRPRENSON."—Mr. Brandreth moved that the board apply to lloly Trinity School to find free places for these children. He thought as the Guardians had to pay, that they ought to have the choice where the children went to. If the parents paid they could send the children where they liked. As to the whole question of school fees in Runcorn he had not altered his opinion in any way. Free places ought to be found at the whole of the denominational schools for a certain of children. These schools received the grand and the capitation, besides fees, and if they could not find room for one or two poor children it looked very bad.—Mr. Woodward said Mr. Brandret h's proposition would not help the matter at all, because there were children of all denominations affected, and to apply to Holy Trinity would not meet the case at all. The Board must fall back upon the resolution already passed, that the representatives of those children should appear before the Board.—Mr. Brandreth : Yes, that has been passed.—Mr. Stokes asked had they any in- formation as to what was done in other parishes.—Mr. Woodward said it was unfair that other parishes should pay any proportion of the charge for the Runcorn folks. —Mr. Stokes said in the parish with which he was con- nected children of poor people were admitted to school free, and these schools were struggling to maintain their position. Extra efforts were being made to obtain subscriptions to keep the schools going. There was a charge of so much per quarter made for the children of tradesmen and farmers and others. If a church having poor members sent their children back from the school, fern few coppers,he was astonished. Be was a church- man himself, but he would take an extra collection in church himself before he would call upon the rate- payers.—The Rev. Mr. Tanner said in his school every child was admitted free.—Mr. Aaron: The church school at Weston is totally free—books, paper. etc.— Mr. Lea said they had a meeting of Runcorn School Inquiry? Committee on Friday night, and they passed about half-a-dozen cases • so the Board was paying school fees yet.—Mr. Brandreth : You are, but the Board Is not.—Mr. Lea: You are paying from this Board.—The Rev. J. Hanby inquired if there were 49 free places at Holy Trinity, would the Board 'firing pres- sure to bear upon the Wesleyan or other parents to send their children to that school.—Mr. Brandreth said he would rather bring pressure upon the Wesleyan school to admit them free. —Mr. Hanby stid AS an educationa- list he agreed with Mr. Brandreth, but tile committee of the school had decided that it should not be a free school, and they were acting under the protec- tion of 11. paternal government. Mr. Woodward asked would the committee so far consider their position as to find free places for the children lof their own poor adherents.—Mr. Hanby replied 1 that the Committee had decided that it should be a fee paying school, and the law said the Guardians should pay for the children of parents who were too poor to pay. The Board must not take the children from that school and compel them to go to Holy Trinity school or any ether school.—Mr. Brandreth's motion was car- ried.—Mr. Lea inquired what was the position of the Runcorn Inquiry Committee, were they to refuse these fees or pa 7 them out of their own pockets.—Mr. Wood- wood.: The position is exactly this, those children who have received fees, their representatives must appear before the Board.—Mr. Lea said he strongly objectedto bringing parents from Runcorn to that Board on such an errand.—Mr. Aaron thought it would be a most cruel course to pursue.—Mr. Lea asked who called Runcorn Committee together.—The Clerk : The inquiry officer. —Mr. Jones read a post card calling the last meeting, which was signed John Ashton, Clerk. (Laughter.)—The Clerk said he had not sent it out. It had nct come from his office.—The subject then dropped. , TAKE COUNTY ASYLUM. The Rev. J. W. N. Tanner reported that the Commit- tee appointed by the Board had visited the County Asylum at Upton, Chester, accompanied by Mr. Ashton, the Clerk. Forty-one patients, costing 7s. per head per week; Of which the County Council repaid 4s. per head, were presented to the Committee by Dr. Davidson, Medical Superintendent, 22 of those were males and 19 ' were females. The Committee were sorry to report that the whole of the patients with one exception were nope- less lunatics. They were well cared for and treated with the greatest kindness and attention by the officials connected with the institution.—Mr. Brandreth said the said the cost of the inspection was £2 10s. 6d.—The re- port was adopted. RUNCORN AND SMALLPDX. Mr. Brandreth said the Committee appointed to deal with the claim of the Runcorn Commissioners for the maintenance of certain smallp par patients in their hospi- tal, had held a meeting, and alter considering replies from a number ot unions as to their method of dealing with such cases, had passed the following resolution That it did not appear to be the practice in other unions to pay for patients taken into an infectious diseases hos- pital, and that the removal thereto of such patients fs for the purpose of stamping out direase, and the general good of the district within which the disease has broken out, and that in the cases charged for the patients were not taken into the hospital at the request of the Guar- dians or under an order of the magistrates, the Commit- tee therefore cannot recommend payment of this account:" Be moved the adoption of the Committees resolution.—Mr. Woodward seconded. Passed. It was stated that the account was for £B3.

NEW VAGRANT WARDS. For the erection of these wards the following tenders were opened ;—R. W. Collin, Warrington, £375 ; Win. Beckett, Northwich, £357 ; Joseph Houghton, Whitley, £3581-Thomas Davies, Frodsham, £335. It was unani- mously decided to accept Mr. Davies's tender. UNPAID CALLS. It was reported that the following townships had not paid their calls : —Alvanley, Frodsham, Kingsley, Kings- wood, and Preston o'th Hill. THE CONTRACTS. ThP tenders for the supply of provisions, &c., to the Workhouse were opened, and ofter consideration the fol- lowing were accepted for the ensuing six months : Drugs, Mr. J. H. Weston, Runcorn ; clothing, Messrs. .Unsworth Bros.. Runcorn ; drapery, Messrs. Thomas Leach and Son, Runcorn ; general carting, Mr. William Grounds, Aston; groceries, Mr. Edward Gregory, Run- corn ; potatoes and straw, Mr. John flankey, Orford ; boots, Mr. John Hobson. I,lAntwich ; coal, Meilsrs.W.sed J.Richardeon, Warrington ; meat, Mr. William Gill, War- rington ; and cartage, Mr. ll•nry Jackson, Runcorn.
