div.head: ST. HELENS CORPORATION AND THE UNEMPLOYED.
div.p: ST. HELENS CORPORATION AND THE UNEMPLOYED.

On Wednesday afternoon, a deputation of the un- employed, headed by Mr. Peter WRinley and Mr. David Rimmer, waited upon the Paving Committee of the Sr. Helens Corporation, to ask if they could at once commence public works which were in con- templation, chiefly paving and sewering certain streets, the extension of the main sewer, and the erection of deposit tanks at the Double Locks. —The Town-Clerk informed the committee that he had had a conversation with Mr. WKinley on the subject, and had informed him that the Corporation were not in a posi- tion to push on with those works, on account of ordi- nary formalities, such as givieg notice, Sze., having to be gone through.—lt was decided to admit the deputation, and Mr. M'Kinley stated their ideas.—Councillor Hatton mentioned that two contracts had been given to local firma that afternoon.—Mr. Ritnmer thanked them for letting the contracts to local contractors, as it would be I a great help to St. Helens men in finding employment.— Mr. M•Kinley remarked that he was glad to see there was a prospect of a settlement of the strike, and hoped it would be settled the next day.—The Chairman said he did not think they could say anything to the deputation, but the matter would be considered.—Mr. M`Kinley asked if they might depend on works being pushed forward.— The Chairman said that would have to be discussed. —The deputation then withdrew, and Councillor Greenough remarked that the building trade was never so busy as at present.—Councillor Hatton asked how that could he if they could not get bricks or coal.—Coun- cillor Greenough repeated that they could not get a bricks, tter or joiner in the town.—The Town7Clerk said he had explained to Mr. M'Hinlev that it was impossible for the Corporation to comtnence the works at once.— The matter was allowed to drop.

div.head: COMMITTEE.
div.p: COMMITTEE.

At the conclusion of the business at the police I c,Jurt on Monday, Chief Constable Hunt said that he bad received a letter from the Town Clerk, with refereono to the licensing question. The question was whether it should be made public.—lt was thought advisable by the magistrates to have it read, and the magistrates' cltqk (Mr. H. B. White), thran read the letter which was as follows :

Town Clerk's Office, Warrington, Sept. 15th, 1893. Dear Sir,—l beg to acknowledge the receipt of your letter on the 13th inst., referring to the objections to the removal of certain licenses, and suggesting that I should engage counsel in support of such objection. It appears that the Watch Committee yesterday during my absence from town passed the following resolution :—Reselved that this Committee regret that the magistrates appear to have acted with a want of courtesy, by issuing in- structions to and employing the police without in any way consulting the Watch Committee, and that the same be not acted upon without instructions from this Commit- tee.—Apart from the above resolution, I think I ought to inform you that by the terms of. my appointment of Town Clerk, I am precluded from engaging counsel without the express direction of the Council. It does appear to roe that if the objections to the licenses are being raised byithe licensing committee, the person to instruct counsel is the Magistrates' Clerk.—Yours, etc., J. L. Whittle.—Mr. Samuel Hunt, Chief Constable.:'

Mr. White : I can say by the terms of the Municipal Corporation Act, the duties of the police are defined as follows .-45 and 48 Vic. Municipal Corporations Act, 1882, ch. 50, clause 191 (2),a police constable shall obey all such lawful commands as he receives for any justice of the peace by jurisdiction in the borough." There is nothing about obeying the Watch Committee.—Mr. Hunt: I have not shown the letter to anyone before this morning.—Alderman Harrison : It can do no harm. —Mr. Bunt: It does not encourage us in our duties.— Mr. Monks : Mr. Hunt has not acted upon the instruc- tions given. I presume; the notices have not been given. —Mr. White : The notices were delivered before this bombshell exploded.—Mr. Monks : I am quite certain there is no discourtesy towards the Watch Committee. It is most desirable that the Bench and Watch Committee should work harmoniously together.—Mr. White: Seven of the magistrates are on the Committee.—Mr. Monks : According to the Municipal Corporations Act, I don't think there is the slightest justification for the action they have taken. It seems to me that the con- stabulary are more under the authority of the Bench than of the Watch Committee.—Mr. White: Entirely so. When they make their declaration they swear to obey and serve their sovereign lady the Queen,and the magis- trates are the representatives of the Queen, and not the Watch Committee.—Councillor Roberts : I take it that the resolution has been passed by the members of the Watch Committee, they having an entire misconception as to the position of the Chief Constable, and that if the Town Clerk had been present such a resolution would never have been passed. When the Chief Constable was requested by the magistrates to submit a report, he was bound to do it, and, therefore, the resolution of the Watch Committee is absolutely worthless.—Mr. White : The Chief Constable would have been liable to ten days' imprisonmentif he did not obey the magistrates.(Laugh- ter.)—Alderman Harrison : I was at the meeting of the Watch Committee when this resolution was passed, but I declined to vote for it as I was in doubt as to vi hether they were acting with commonsense in the matter. I used that expression at the meeting,—Councillor Roberts: There never was the slightest intention on the part of magistrates when they asked for this report to bring the Chief Constable or themselves into anything in the shape of a conflict with the Watch Committee. Quite the reverse.—Mr. Hunt : There were three members of the Watch Committee present when I received instruc- tions to make a report on the back doors of the public- houses of the borough. To receive such a letter as I have was astounding.—Councillor Roberts : This is a case 'of those who are dressed in a little brief authority play- ing their fantastic tricks.—Alderman Harrison : Which makes the angels weep.—Mr. Hunt : The Liverpool police have received a round sum of £lO from the Watch Commi,tes for the duties they have performed in this direction. List year they received Llb. It is a very arduous and distasteful duty, and in the case the off licenses, I think it very near to encroaching on the liber- ties of the subject, but we have met with great civility last week.—Councillor Roberts : The investigations of Mr. Hunt and his confrirs have been carried out with the least possible friction.—The Court then rose.

WYCLIFFE COCKEIEDGE MISSION.

The anniversary sermons in connection with the above-named mission were preached on Sunday in the schoolroom, Brick-street. The room had been tastefully decorated with flowers and plants for the occasion. The Rev. John Yonge preached at the morning service, and the Rev. John Davies, formerly pastor, but now of Rishton, near Blackburn, preached in the evening. A Children's service of praise was given in the afternoon, at which the Rev. J. IV. Varley, of Latchford, preached. Special hymns and anthems were given by the choir under the leadership of Mr. R. Travis. There were good congregations at each service, and the collections realised over a. MARTINSCROFT WESLEYAN CHAPEL.

The anniversary services of the above *chapel were held on Sunday afternoon and night, the preacher being Mr. S. B. Stringer, of Warrington, who preached from Psalm 31.19 in the afternoon and 2 Corinthians, 6.4 in the evening. The choir which was reinforced by the members of Rixton choir under the leadership of Mr. William Shaw rendered the anthems "Blessed is the man," and "I know that my Redeemer liveth! A quartette entitled "Sweet Zion" was sung by Miss Clark, and Messrs. J. Bate, W. Bate and J. Thomas very effectively. The collections for the day amounted 0 £3 15.5. Bd. which is to be devoted 0 decorating the chape!. At the close of the service Mr. String* thanked the Rixton choir for their services during the day, arid before the congregation separated " God be with you till we meet a/2ain waa sung with much fervour. THE P.S. A. AT WYCLIFFE CHURCH. •

A mo;Csuccessful and inspiriting P.S.A.,meeting was held in Wycliffe Church on Sunday afternoon. It being the quarterly meeting of the society, it was thrown open for the attendance of women, and the church was filled to overflowing, about 1,200 persons being present. The president, the Rev. J. Yong% conducted the service and in the course of a short address said it gave him infinite pleasure to see Wycliffe Church full that afternoon. He was perfectly sure that everyone belonging to that P.S.A would also feel gratified. They had been having grand meetings and everyone, more or less, had been a success, and he felt sure that theso P.S.A. meetings had not only been a means of gratification, but they had told upon the lives and characters of the men who attended them. Ile was glad to hear testirnonies from the men them. selves of the benefit they had derived from them. He was always glad to know that there were workshops in the town which were healthier now than they were before the cornmercement of the P.S.A. Miss Bessie Dutton, of Moore, then gave an admirable address on " Life" which was most attentively listened to. Mrs. R. H. Pearson sang as a solo with great effect" Listen to the children " (Clifton Bingham). The duet •' Love Divine" was sung by Mrs. Pearson and Mr. A. Grifiths, Mr. E. Wallington and Mr. A. Lang took part in the ser- vice, Not the least interesting feature of the service was the baptism of an infant son of one of the brethren of the society who had requested that Mr. Yonge should perform the ceremony at the quarterly meeting. A col- lection was taken in aid of the working expenses of the P.S.A. and realised £6 3s. 2d. The membership has now reached 836. ST. ALBANS R. C. CHURCH.

On Sunda"s:,•the---a-Wiei-vei'S-ar-v- services Of; St. Albans Roman Catholic Church, flowsey-street, were conducted in the morning he the Rev. T. J. Brown, S.J., of St. Francis Raviers, Liverpool, and in the evening by the Rev. Dr. Larkin, 0.5.8. In the morning High Mass was celebrated after which the Rev. T. J. Brown preached from the text " There stood by the cross of Jesus. Mary, his mother," St. John 19,21. He said that that day as his congregation was aware, they were com- memorating the seven sorrows that pierced the heart of Mary the Mother of Jesus, fulfilling the prophecy of Holy Simeon. On two occasions the church brings ! them before their minds. The first time was at Easter I which was at a time when their hearts were too much. taken up by the sufferings of our blessed Lord to dwell on those of his mother. They were too apt to allow their minds to lose hold of what had been done for them j in the past, to allow their memories to forget the sacri- fices and sufferings which were the source of the rich treasures and blessings which were their lot in the pre- sent, until the solemnities of the church brought them !before them, and assuredly they could not dwell too often upon what. their salvation had cost then. There was nothing which tended more to increase their devo- tion and reverence to the Mother of God than the study of her sorrows. That study brought to their minds her union with her Divine Son, in the great work of the redemption, and also showed that they were in unison in all that was done. The preacher then went on to , eloquently depict the sorrow and woe of Mary when she saw Christs' troubles, and finally- klie greatest sorrow of all when she saw Him crucified. He concluded his sermon by an earnest appeal for funds to wipe off the debt still remaining upon the church. In the evening the Rev. Dr. Larkin 0.5.8., preached from the words "Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart." lie said that when God created man he created him so that he conld intelligently love 'him and serve him, a!though man had at the same time the right !of free will. He could love God or he could hate him. it was the duty of man before everything to honour God, and his neighbour second. At the present time this was generally reversed, and man loved his neigh- bour before God; He was ever ready to do good works, and no doubt that appeared at first sight to be the right thing as , suffering humanity was ever present and work done to alleviate them had visible results. God was in- visible, and therefore men did not do so much for Rim as they ought to do. He urged his hearers to show their love for God by csntributing liberally to the funds in aid of UM !muse. No doubt times were had with the coal strike, and those liberally inclined would give to- wards the suffering, but he urged that God had the first ' claim—The concregations at each service were very attentive to the eloquent addresses of the two minister 4.
IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
MONDAY.

In the House of Commons on Monday Mr. NAOROJI gave notice that he intended to move for the appoint- ment of a Royal Commission to inquire into the civil and military administration of India. Replying to a question, Sir E. GREY said there were two and would soon be three British warships in Rio harbour for the protection of our sabjects and property. Trade was paralysed owing to the revolt, and merchants would do well to remember that they sent goods at great risk. .The neutral ships would endeavour to prevent the bombardment of the town by the insurgent vessels. The House then went into Committee of Supply. Dis- cussion followed on the cost of our embassies and their help to trade, and also on the attitude of the Govern- ment towards Uganda. With regard to the latter ques- then, Sir EDWARD GREY said nothing would be decided till the autumn session—till the subject had been consi- dered by the House. After debate on naval armaments and works many votes were agreed to, and finally the ssork of Supply was completed.

TUESDAY. In the House of Commons on Tuesday Mr. Fowler gave gratifying assurances as to the decrease of cholera. Report of Supply was then considered. Discussion followed with regard to our policy towards Mashona- land, and also on naval armaments. Exception was taken to the purchase of shells from foreign firms ; but Sir U. Kay-Shuttleworth said the Government had a right to go to the cheapest market, and in this purchase were making no new departure. On the report of the vote for the Admiralty, Mr. A. Morton moved to omit the sum of £7OO, the salary of Prince Louis of Batten- berg as naval adviser to the Inspector General of Forti- fications, but the amendment was negatived. The Post- office service and the action of the Government in relation to telephonic communication were commented upon. Many votes of supply were agreed to or carried on a division, and the House adjourned at eleven o'clock.

The House of Lords met on Tuesday. Several bills were advanced. The Light Railways (Ireland) Bill passed through all its stages, and the Savings Bank Bill was read a first time. Their Lordships adjourned till Friday.

div.head: WEDNESDAY.
div.p: WEDNESDAY.

In the House of Commons on Wednesday, on the motion for the second reading of the Appropriation Bill, Mr. JAIHIS LOWTHER called attention to the recent dis- turbances in the mining districts of Yorkshire, and said it was incredible that such lawlessness should have been permitted. Mr. ASQUITH again explained that it was the duty of the local authorities to put down disorder. He might advise them in an emergency, but they were at liberty to accept or reject his advice. A grave state of things had existed in the West Riding, but he was bound to say that the riotous proceedings that went on for some days, the wrecking of collieries and the burning of buildings, met with no sympathy from the men on strike. Certainly Labour members had denounced him and circulated pitiful and ridiculous fictions against the Government, to the effect that they had deliberately sent the forces of the Crown to take the side of the masters and crush the men, but where were the mem- bers who had made those charges? Why were they not in their places in the House, face to face with the Minis- ter they had condemned and ready to fight the meter out. He thought it a most creditable circumstance that in the whole county of Lancaster, where a largo number of miners had been out, there had not been a single case of outrage or disturbance; and he attributed this peaceful state of things very largely to the restraining influence exercised by the miners' leaders and organisa- tions, for they had kept the men within the bounds of moderation and good sense. He promised an inquiry into the Featherstone disturbance, and appealed to the leaders of the men to put an end to the deplorable dis- pute in the coal industry. After some discussion of the foreizn policy of the Government the Appropriation Bill was read a second time. The debate on the motion to go into Committee on the Indian Budget was interrupted by the half-past five o'clock rule, and the House adjourned.

_ THURSDAY Questions were asked on Thursday in the House of Commons chiefly with regard to land purchase in Ire- land and the situation in Mashonaland. Mr. BUXTON said the Government policy towards the latter country had been neither uncertain nor variable. Any grave disturbance in Mashonaland would certainly involve the peace of Bechuanaland and have far-reaching results in South Africa. The Government were therefore bound to take care that a war with Lobengula was not lightly entered into. But the British South Africa Company had entire freedom to take measures for resisting any attack by the Matabele,s. It was decided that the House shauld meet on Friday and adjourn till November 2. On the motion tn go into Committee on the Indian Budget the condition of the people of India was dis- cussed. Mr. G. W. RUSSELL said the Government were quite willing to inquire by the means at their disposal into any greivance, but they could not consent to the appointment of a Royal Commission as suggested by Mr. Naoroji, for it would be a vast undertaking and could have no practical result. The House went into Committee, and Mr. GEORGE RUSSELL explained the Indian Budget. In 1891-2 there was a surnlus of 480,000 tens of rupees; in 1802-3,a defi- cit of 1,100,000rx. ; and in 1893-4,a deficit of 1.600,000rx. He spoke on the loss caused by the fall in exchange and the steps taken by the Government of India. Bespoke of the condition of the railways as satisfactory. He next turned to the moral and material condition of the people. In spite of the gloomy statements made, he maintained that there was a distinct advance in the material prospe- rity of India, though he could not say so much for the , educational improvement of the people. After discussion the usual financial resolution was agreed to, and the House adjourned at a quarter past eleven o'clock.

div.head: RUNCORN REVISION COURT.
div.p: RUNCORN REVISION COURT.

On Thursday, Mr. Colt IVilliams barrister opened a court at Runcorn Session House for the purpose of revising the list of parliamentary and County electors in Runcorn and outlying townships. Mr. W. Handley, assisted by Mr. Clement Handley, appeared for the Liberals and Mr. Alfred Lightburu represented the Conservatives.

A MISLAID CLAIM. Mr. Hughes said on the 18th July he posted to the Overseer of Sutton a claim for Edwin Charles Leventon, of Oakfield, Roby in respect of leasehold bone works land and cottages, and the claim was not published by the overseers. He wrote to the overseers in August informing them that he had not received from them a copy of the ownership claim list. He was then informed that no claim had reached the overseers. He again wrote to the overseers enclosing a duplicate of the claim and asked them to forward it to the Clerk of the peace and he (Mr. Hughes) would explain the circumstances to the revising barrister. On the previous day (Wed- nesday) the overseer found that the claim had been mislaid and had fallen behind a dresser its the kitchen. The postal marks sh•wed the date. He (Mr. Hughes) was afraid in the face of the decision in Bennions case 'at Wharton that he would be unable to induce his ' honour to allow the claim—ln reply to a question, Mr. Robinson assistant overseer for Sutton, said he had not published the claim.—The Barrister though this case and the Wharton case were on the same footing ; the basis of his ruling was that there had been no publication which was necessary: If the overseer had published the claim but not in proper time he might have considered the claim. But there must be publication in order that the public might know and have an opportunity of objecting ; otherwise they might have persons coming there and obtaining votes and no one would know. He did not wish to blame the overseers but there ought to be extreme care taken of these official documents and should not be allowed casually to slide behind dressers. He did not say there had been carelessness in this case, but it was only right he should express his opinion about it.—Mr. , Hughes said the carelessness was on the part of the over- seer's servant, and it would not be wilful neglect but jnad vertence.—The Barrister said great injustice might , be done if great care was not taken.

div.head: FREI! LISTS FOR AGENTS.
div.p: FREI! LISTS FOR AGENTS.

- The Barrister informed the assistant overseers present that he had derided to allow the political agents copies of the lists free,instead of paying for them as heretofore. If the auditor made any fuss about the matter and sur- charged the overseers, Mr. flandley and Mr. Hughes had undertaken to pay for them as usual. He did not think there would be anything said, because a certain number of copies had to he printed and a couple more or less would make no difference. The agents assisted the overseers and assisted him very much, and he thought it only right and fair that they should have lista.

RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY A U THORII Y.

The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday. In the absence of Mr. Mclntyre through a severe cold, Mr. J. Knowles occupied the chair, and there were present the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Rev. J. Hanby, Messrs. Weir, Aaron, Stokes, Whitley, Lewis, Heywood, Brandreth, Williams, Bratherton,Woodwood, Parkinson, Baxter John Jones, Ford, S. Houghton, John Whitlow, J. Ashton (clerk), G. Ashton (deputy clerk), J. Farrington (nuisance inspector), and Dr. Adams (medical officer.) Mr. Aaron moved " that Mr. James Farrington be re-appointed Inspector of Nuisances and Inspector under the Dairies Cow Sheds and Milk Shops Order 1885 for one year ending Vie 29th Septsinber 1894 at a salary at the rate of £l5O per annum, being an increase of £lO per annum on his present mlary, arid that he be re-appointed Inspector of Canal Boati for the same period at a salary of £lO per annum." Mr. Farrington said his salary was only equal to that of his predecessor, and yet his duties had increased more than two fold. He then retired. Mr. Aaron said Mr. Farrington's work had quad- rupled since he was engaged, and he pointed out that he had now to attsnd five parochial committees. If Mr. Farrisgton were his own servant he should give him £2OO a year willingly.—Mr. Wiliiams seconded the , motion and remarked that Mr. Farrington was the only man who was acquainted with the whole of the drains and sewers of the district and if he were to leave them they would be in a awkward fix—Mr. Weir moved as an amendment that Mr. Farrington be re-appointed at the old salary. tie considered that although Adr. Farrington did good service he was well paid for it, and in his opinion this was not the time for raising salaries. Farmers had hard work to make end's meet.—Mr. John Whitlow seconded—Mr. Brandreth suggest d that it would be better to give Mr. Farrington a gratuity than to raise his salary. He mentioned that during the present year he had had a gratuity of £2O.

PROPOSED INFECTIOUS DISEASES IX OSPITAL. In reply to a request of the Authority, the Local Government board stated that it would be contrary to the board's practice to instruct one of their inspeci,rs to visit a district in order to advise a local anthority as to the site for an infectious diseases hospital. It was for the authority themselves with the aid of their profes- sional advisers to select a site and to prepare plans, etc., and in the event of a loan being required for the erection of the hospital the board would then direct one of their inspectors to hold an inquiry. The officers of the board's medical and architectural departments would be quite ready to confer with the Rural Sanitary Authority's professional advisers on the subject, if the authority wished them to do so.—Mr. Williams said the Hospital Committee considered that this was a backhanded way of dealing with the matter. The authority had to go to a lot of expense and trouble and then somebody would come down from London and perhaps wipe it all out. The Committee had resolved that the owners of land adjacent to the workhouse be applied to for land as a sits for an Infectious Diseases Hospital, and be requested to state upon what terms they would be prepared to sell. The two owners interested were Sir Gilbert Greenall and the Aston Estate.—The resolution was adopted.

div.p: PORT SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The Committee appointed to consider this matter had resoived with reference to the article in the order of the Local Government Board, setting forth that the ripa- rian authorities should contribute towards the expenses incurred for any year in proportion to the registered tonnage of the vessels discharged within the respective districts, that it be pointed out to the Local Government Board that the increase in the tonnage of the rural dis- trict had been caused by the Runcorn docks being closed on account of the construction of the Manchester Ship Canal, so that all cargo bound for Runcorn had to be unloaded at Weston or S iltport, and also that although the tonnage had been increased in the rural district, the assessments have not been altered, those of the Runcorn Docks being £6,000 and those of %Veston and Frodsham £550 ; and that therefore the expenses for the the years ending December-31st, 1893 and 1894, should be charged on the basis of the tonnage bound for Runcorn, although unloaded at Weston or Saltport. It was also decided that inasmuch as the stamping out and the preventionof the spread of the disease was lon the general good of the community at large, all expenses with reference thereto should be an Imperial cliargrr.—Mr. Williams moved the adoption of the resolution which was carried. div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.
KILLED BY A "BOGIE."

At the Ship Canal liosoital on Saturday, an inquest was held by Mr. 11. C. Yates, coroner, on the body of Thomas DAintith. 42 yeurs., of age, 8, Stamford-street, ‘Varrington a labourer on the Ship Canal, who was killed on the Arpley Works the previous Friday. Mrs. Ward, sister of the dece,asen, said her brother left home at. 5 30 on Thursday morning to go to his work at the Arpley deviation of the Ship Canal; at 8.30 she was Informed of his injuries. She went to the hospital, and her bother told her that the waggons between which he had been crushed should have been "scotched." He afterwards said he was not sure whether they were "scotched" or not. De had not time to get out of the way. He had been fire works at the job, and worked in three shifts. Thomas Tremble, foreman waterman. Runcorn, said some men were emptying a dredger at the Arpley works, and one wagon load not being hoisted high enoogh, it struck the" bogie" and knocked it against some light waggons. Degeassd was standing between the "bogie" and the waggons, and was caught between the buffers and badly crushed. Witness attended to him, and had him taken away on an engin° to the hospital. Deceased was stooping to pick "1' a waggon On at the time he was ciught..-:-.Dr. Walker said deceased died Oil Friday from injuries to the abdomen and shook to the systern—A. verdict of " Accidental death "was returned.

Federation, there are not wanting symptorns which show that, if the struggle be prolonged: there might easily be a further disastrous spreaa_ of the strike policy. Already many thousands e French miners have thrown down their tools. The Frenchmen have, to some extent, done this 00t of sympathy with their English fellow-worker* though no doubt their main motive is a feeling that the present is a favourable time for extorting concessions from their own employers. A stril`e. in France or Belgium can be regarded with CO siderable equanimity in this country, but the sasie cannot besaid, at the present juncture in partial" lar, of a cessation of work in the great coal centre of Northumberland and Durham. That such an event is within the range of possibility is t°l3: gathered from the fact that on Wednesday a 181:6' meeting of delegates representing Northllmbrno d Durham collieries declared in favour of a striO if terms, which have been rejected by the masters; were not conceded. If that resolution 1)0 'late upon before the present dispute is settled, ths results are bound to be disastrous in the extrenle'

IT may now, we believe, be said The Great that there is a silver lining to the Dispute. black cloud which has, for the last eight or nine weeks, darkened the social and in- dustrial life of a large part of this country. The period of discussion and conciliation seems to have arrived in the stupendous labour dispute which has filled so many fair English counties with con- tention and misery. An invitation to a confer- ence has been thrown out by Mr. ASIITON, the secretary of the Miners' Federation, and the masters do not seem to be indisposed to accept it, though unfortunately their acceptance is not of so cordial a character as it might have been. Of course, even a meeting together of the repro- sentatives of the opposing parties does not mean an end of the lock-out. But it may mean the beginning of the end; and, at all events, it is an almost necessary preliminary to a settlement. Even as it is, the present week has seen a slight limitation of the struggle. Miners have gone back to work in Staffordshire, Nottinghamshire, and Warwickshire on the old terms; that is to say, the employers are not insisting upon the twenty- five per cent. reduction. This is a policy that may spread. The miners' leaders are understood to be favourable to it, and at present it is the majority of the men themselves that are standing out against it. It is, however, a policy which, once initiated, is likely to win converts rapidly. "Divide and conquer is an old and well established fight- ing maxim. By "going in" at the old, wages wherever they have the option, the miners not only help to break down the combination of the masters, but they also provide themselves with the sinews of war. The men who work an contribute towards the support of those who " play," seeing that—from the miners point of view—the working and " playing" are alike for the good cause.. While conciliation is, let es hope, making headway in the district a the Miners'

It is not surprising that the shooting of mieety in Yorkshire by soldiers is to be the subject 191,e special investigation. It has been Mr. AsQuirL/5, misfortune rather tha» his fault that he has,clerin:„ his brief tenure of the Home Office,had to deal %Iv various embarrassing questions raised in conneetlell with disputes between capital and labour. libel may certainly be two opinions as to the readiees with which the military has lately been called '9: to the scene of strikes, but we do not seehow en't one can , question the judiciousness of the P31„1 played by the Home Secretary. When lecho authorities have declared that they could net:„ responsible for order in their districts if t; repressive forces at their disposal were not anrt, mented, is Minister of the Crown would by reie'; ing such appeals, even if ho had the P°ll,per' be taking much more upon his shoulders than could be fairly asked of The lesson that is taught by this calling military is not, as some would have us belielol that Her Majesty's Ministers are on the side the capitalists, but rather that the whole sYstetr, of appointing magistrates, and especially elle; magistrates, is out of harmony with the times .o which we live. It is the magistrates who 0113 the military, and as the magistrates are, for t,11,1d most part, employers, their decisions are bet,l-,1 to be looked upon with suspicion. The time 70 come when either the power of the rnagletr3tAi in the case of strikes, must be restricted, Benches—county as well as borough,--tne4 democratised. In this respect the killing 3n/i maiming of miners at Featherstone is not unliker; to be fraught with useful results. Thereilt many matters in regard to that tragedy yr`4r, need clearing up, and the annonneetuent of Asourru that he intends to cause a special ii) gation to be made should meet with gene approval.

ROBBERY FROM WIDNES BMWs. At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, before the Mayor and Mr. Deacon, Geo. Costley, of Beamont-st., aged 16, and Alfred Ellis, of Terrace-road, were charged with stealing a jacket and a pair of shoes, the property of Samuel Bate, of Charlotte-St., from the Widnes Bathi, on Friday afternoon. The prisoners pleaded guilty and were dealt with under the first Offence Act and bound over to appear for judgment when called upon.

- - MIL BANTOCIC PIERPOINT. Mr. Bantock Pierpeint, says the "Sun," the well- known baritone, is a native of Runcorn,in Cheshire. A t a very early age he revealed a wonderful talent for music, and while still young, became organist at the lirdependant Chapel. Soon he came to London, and en- tered the Royal Academy of Music, but after gaining his bronze medal there, he left for the Guildhall School, to study under M. Visetti, a little later becoming a pupil of Mr. W. Shakespeare. ' POPULAR SIMON° CLASSES AT RUNCORN. The twelfth session is announced to Commence on Thursday evening next in Ellesmere-st. School-room. During the past eleven sessions over 900 students have received instructim in vocal music and the various branches of musical theory, and of these. a goodly num- ber have succeeded in passing the exaininations of the Tonic Solfa College. Prospectuses with full information are to be had from members of previous classes and also from the teacher, Mr. J. Holford, 123 Greenway-road.

RUNCORN MUSICAL SOCIETY. The first rehearsal for the present season in connection with the above society took place on Monday evening in the Bethesda Lecture Ball. There was a large attend- ance of members. The pieces practised were " Rest, soldier, rest," " The sea bath its pearls." and the " Gipsy's Chorus," as well as part of the oratoria " Samson." It may be remarked that the two former selections were sung by the competitive choirs at the 1892 Royal Eisteddfod, held at Rhyl. The conductor, Mr. Crossley, expressed his thanks to the members for turning up in,such strong force. '

MARRIAGE OE A RUNCORN FOOTBALLER. On Wednesday afternoon a large congregation assem- bled in Bethesda Congregational Church Runcorn, to witness the celebration of the nuptials of Mr. Samuel Houghton, of Irwell-lane, and Miss Annie Warburton, daughter of John Warburton, of Irwell Cottage. The oeremony was performed by the Rev. J. S. Simpson. The bride was accompanied by Miss Louisa Warburton (her sister) and Miss Hongliton (sister of the bridegroom). Mr. Walter Warburton acted as best man, and Mr. Charles Houghton as groomsman. After the service the guests were entertained at the , residence of the bride's father. The happy pair were the recipients of many pre- sents. rhe bridegroom is the popular full-back of the Runcorn team, with which club he liqs been associated for three years, during which time he has performed brilliant services. He has also been selected to play in all the matches for his county : and he has taken part in the competitions North and youth of England and England against Ireland.

OBSTRLICTING A COUNTY COURT BAILIFF AT RUNCORN. At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Mr. John Brundrit and Mr. Charles Reynolds, John Jones, Ben., and John Jones, jun., of Suffolk-street, were sum- moned for attempting to rescue goods from Alfred Torrie, county court bailiff, while levying execution.— Mr. F. A. Lake appeared fcr the complainant, and said on the sth inst. f orrie was entrusted with an execution to levy on the goods of the elder defendant. About four o'clock he levied the execution, but stayed in the house some three hours in order to give the eldef defendant time to raise the money. At the end of that time the defendant refused to pay the money, and Torrie and his assistant Arkwright attempted to remove the goods. The elder defendant said that no goods should be re- moved, and threatened that if they were they would be covered with blood. Terrie seized a chair, but both defendants wrested it from him,and the elder defendant knocked him over a round table, against the wall. Ulti- mately P.C. Booth arrived on the scene, and the de- fendants again obstructed the bailiffs, but an the con- stable warning them they allowed the goods to be re- moved. Mr. Lake mentioned that these proceedings were taken under the County Court Act, 1888, and said the duties of a bailiff were wit of the most pleasant or easiest kind, and the officers of the court should be pro- tected in carrying out the orders of the judge, and he asked the Bench to inflict such a penalty as would be a 'yarning to the defendant§ and others.—The defendants did, not deny the charge,but the elder defendant alleged that the goods belonged to his eldest son' and he was only a lolitter in the house.—The Bench fined each defendant ss. ard costs 103. 6d., and also allowed the advocate's fee of 103. ed.
When In want of a CHASTE and ELEGANT WEDDING or BTEDAT PRIONNT go to PRITCHLRD'S, 61, High-et.—Advt. A DROWNING MYSTERY AT RUNCORN.

Mr. Won: ley, the coroner, held an inquest at Runcorn Cemetery Office, on Saturday, touching the de .th of Thomas Roberts, aged 18 years. of 34 Cartwright-st., Liverpool. It appeared that deceased was a fireman on board the steamship " Ant," of Liverpool. At ten o'clock on the night of the 9th inst. a sailor named Caleb Davies saw the deceased with a numer of the crew. The deceased was under the influence of drink. The deceased was not seen alive again. On Friday even- ing his body w-s taken from the Fenton dock by a lock keeper named John Pendlebury, of 14 Clarence-st., who informed the jury that it was possible the young man might have fallen off the gate in crossing to his st?amer. P.C. Williams said there were no marks of violence on the body. The police had no reason to associate foci play with the death.—Mr. Shaw, seamen's missionary, said the man's mother had made a suggestion of foul play, and asked if someone might not have pushed him into the water. She received from him 103. a week, and was expecting her usual allowance that day.—The coroner said he did not coincide with the theory of foul play. In his opinion the young man was under the influence of drink when returning to his vessel, and unfortunately fell into the water. The jury in giving an open verdict of found drowned would enable the police to investigate the matter further if they had any reason to suspect anything wrong.—The jury returned a ver- dict accordinglv.—Mr3. Roberts, the mother, who had remained in the room throughout the inquiry, was greatly distressed, and at the conclusion she fainted and was carried outside and attended to. The deceased was buried in Runcorn Cemetery on Monday alt.rnoon. About twenty captains and sailors were present as a mark of respect to the deceased. .The Rev. A. J. Jame- son conducted the service. PRITCHARD'S have now stood the test for fifty years, and quality and fir Et-class Workmanship are still guaranteed.— Advt. THE LATE MR. J. CLIFFE, OF WHITLEY. The service in church was conducted by the vicar, the Rev.J.G. Bryant, the burial service at the grave- side being read by the Rev. L. D. Lyon Bennett, of Little Leigh. div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY. SEPTEMBER 23 1893.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY. SEPTEMBER 23 1893.
RUNCORN IMPROVEMENT COMMISSIONERS AND . THEIR LOAN.

Aswill be seen from an advertisement in arrither column, the RuneJrn Improvement Commissioners are issuing mortgages for the purpose of paying for the waterworks which they are purchasing from the Runcorn, Weston, and Halton Waterworks Co. The issue is for £69,000 in the 31 per cent. mort- gages tor cloirty years. The mortgages are being offered by the Manchester Trust Limited, at £lO per cent. on application, and £9O per cent, on allot- ment. The security for this loan will comprise a, mortgage of the water revenue, the district fund, and general didrict rate of Runcorn. Thc water revenue is estimated to produce at present £2,600 per annum, after paying working espenses,and the rateable value tor rating purposes is £52,779 us. 6d., and the district, rate for the current year t;m,nitit. to 24. 101. in the .C. The mortgages will be issinitl in multiples of £lOO. and will. be regis- tered in the name of the proprietor. The list, will opeu on Saturday. the 23rd inst., and close on or before the following ;Tuesday.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND -SEEN AT.
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND -SEEN AT.
RUNCORN.
BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.

11 uncorn Guardians are still floundering about on the kehool tee question. As was anticipated. the Education Department have replied to the question addressed to them in regard to denominational schools, that free education cannot be claimed at schools which are entitled by the Act of 1891 to charge tees. The Department further pointa out that there are a good number of free places at Holy Trinity school and ask if the Board had applied there. The Board had not deciaed to do so on the proposition of Mr. Brandreth, who has taken the lead in the agitation.

This step, however, is hardly likely to advance the question one step further towards solution. 'lf the Holy Trinity managers are willing to find accommodation for the 49 children,. the Guardians have no power to compel the parents to send their children there. The parents have a free and un- fettered choice as to which elementary school they will send their children, and the Guardians, if the parents are too poor to do so themselves, must pay a fee not exceeding threepence. Therefore, the application to the Trinity managers will be futile.

e The Guardians evidently think this is the fact, for. Mr. Woodward again introduced the idea of compelling the poor parents to go to Dutton Work- house to apply for the tees, and this scheme of har- assment appeared to meet with considerable ap- proval. Mr. Aaron rightly characterised such a course as cruel, and Mr: Lea entered his protest against it. If the parents are too poor to pay a penny fee they cannot afford to ride to Dutton Workhouse, and must perforce walk a distance of 12 miles. Surely the Guardians will not enforce the resolution which, the Runcorn Inquiry Committee to their credit, be it said,have hitherto ignored and have granted school tees in the usual way in de- serving cases. Nor is it to be thought that the threat of surcharge will cause them to relinquish their position without a struggle. The alternative placed before the parents is plainly this : Send your children to the FCIIOOI we choose, or walk to Dutton Workhouse as often as we may desire it. Is this procedure likely to bring abont the alteration in the law the Guardians wish? No oce for a moment would argue that it ; then spare the poor people the toil and discomfort of a tramp to the House:

The revision of the Widnes voters lists has been 'one of the quietest held for many years past and the number of claimants for votes was very much ' less than formerly. He Mr. Foard said this apathy was most extraordinary and inquired how it was to be accounted for. Mr. Madge put it down to the strixe, but Mr. Shores stated that most of the men he wanted had appeared. The teal explanation of the tailing off in the business will I think be found in the fact that the lists were better prepared. The throwing out of the Tory declarations resulted in serious loss to that party.

During the recent election of Runcorn Com- missioners the sanitary or insanitary condition of the town was the most fruitful topic under dis- cussion. The ratepayers will therefore be interested in learning that Mr. Edwin ltnison has been elected chairman of the Health Committee. Mr. Lightburn has occupied that position since the Committee w&á first formed some ten years ago.
Congratulations and best wishes to Mr. and Mrs. R. W. Pierpoint, and Dr.and Mrs. Larkin.

Next week will be commenced the fourth session of the evening continuation school classes in con- nection with Runcorn Boar.' School. Provision is made for girls on the present occasion, as the school magazine edited by the head master Mr. Moulton states " The purpose of these classes is to enable young persons to continue their education after leaving the day school, and to provide a series of preparatory classes to those in connection with the Science and Art Department." This useful little magazine further states that " the classes will be made as attractive as possible by discussions, com- petitions, and lessons illustrated by the oxy-hydro- gen light. Capable lecturers will probably be engaged to give short, well-illuitrated lectures on subjects taught in the school." The curriculum included reading, writing, and co mposition, arith- metic, algebra, mensuration, English grammar, geography, book-keeping, the life and duties of the citizen, and vocal music. Prizes and certificates will be awarded for regular and punctual attendance and for success at the examination. The classes have been phenorninally successful in the past. and 1131. Inspector has on eadh visit expressed his warmest appreciation of the work carried on. In the financial aspect also, the ratepayers may Con- gratulate themselves, as the classes have practically been self-supporting. There also commences next week the Science and Art classes, and the Commit- tee present an extensive syllabus of subjects to be taught there. Besides the usual list of science and art subjects, tuition in French, shorthand and dressmaking may be obtained. The fees are fixed at a very reasonable figure, and youths who have a desire for self-improvement should not fail to take advantage of the opportunities the School Board are offering of obtaining a most useful education. It is as true now as ever that knowledge is power. The race is not only to the swift and strong but to the educated. Intending students should endeavour to be present on the opening nights as only classes will be formed in those subjects where a sufficient number of pupils express a desire to learn.

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.

DISTURBANCES.—During the past week rumours have been circulated in the. village of attempted burg.laries at several houses in the neighbourhood. Several farms have been visited, and the inmates of one house were roused at midnight by someone prowling around. Last Saturday night two young fellows returning from War- rington, were set upon at Penketh Lane End and one of them received a cut in the region of the temple, from 1 the knife of one of the assailants. Robbery seems to have been the motive, but happily they were foiled. At the same spot a cyclist was also waylaid but managed to evade the men. The absence of the local policemen at the collieries, is a source of much alarm to many of the , villagers. THANKSGIVING SERVICES.—On Monday evening the harvest thanksgiving services were continued at St. Mary's Mission Church, Penketh. There was a crowded congregation, over 200 persons being present. The edi- fice was beautifully decorated with flowers and fruit contributed by friends. Some very fine oranges pre- sented by Mrs. E. Bolton being specially prominent. Lovely baskets of maiden hair fern, &c., hung from the roof and a large motto "Holy is the Harvest" sur- mounted the chancel rail. The preacher was the Rev. J. J. Langham, M.A.,vicar of Pads,,ate, and he preached an excellent sermon. The anthem "And God said, let the earth bring forth grass" was well rendered. Mr. E. Foster officiated at the organ. The collection amounted to £8 Os. 4d. and will be devoted to church expenses. WINDOW AND COTTAGE GARDENING.—Lo,st evening week, a meeting was held in the Wesleyan Schoolroom to consider the advisability of staiting a Window and Cottage Gardening Society. There was 'a moderate attendance of gentlemen interested in the subject, and also Mrs.R.Garnett, whose project it was. The meeting was opened by Mrs. Garnett, being voted to the chair. Mrs. Garnett then explained her scheme, which was to form a society to promote the culture of flowers, etc., in the village, and to hold an annual exhibition, and give prizes for the best specimens. A committee was formed of the following gentlemen :—Messrs. J. Newcombe, G. Clarke, W. Moores, J. B. Aitken, and others with power to add to their number. Mrs. R. Garnett was unanimous- ly elected president. It was decided to call the society "The Penketh Window and Cottage Gardening Societe" with an annual subscription cf 23. for members. Mr. George Clarke, of Sankey, was elected Secretory, and Mr. John Jackson, Treasurer. It was resolved to offer prizes for the following classee : The best arranged flower garden, the best bunch of cut flowers, best dish of potatoes, vegetables, window plants. &c. It is hoped that befote long the society will be in better shape. The townships of Penketh and Sankey will only be included this season.

div.head: WARRINGTON MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS.
div.p: WARRINGTON MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS.
PROBABLE CONTESTS.

It seems pio-I;it-b-ln-t-h-ai-, se-v-ei.ai:ifiTiOt all, of the nine wards into which Warrington is divided will be contested at the coming municipal elections. The members of the Council who retire this year are as follows;

Town Hall Ward, Councillor Fleming (L)./ Whitecross %%lard, Councillor Roberts (14. Bewsey Ward, Councillor Shaw Green (L). • Orford Ward, Councillor James Walker (L). St. John's Ward, Councillor W. J. Shaw (C). Fairfield Ward, Councillor F. Dixon (14. Howley Ward, Councillor Arthur Browne (L). St. Austin's Ward, Councillor James Hepherd (C). Latchford Ward, Councillor Joseph Ashton (C). The elections of three years ago when all the retir- ing candidates of this year—with the exception of Councillor Shaw—were elected, was signalised by remarkable Liberal victories. The, town had just previously divided into the nine wards, and as the result of a very vigorous; and, with the exception of Bewsey ward, an all-round contest, the Liberals secured a balance of two seats. Mr. Fleming ousted Mr. James FairclOugh from the Council in Town all ward, and Mr. A. Browne defeated Mr. N. B. Percival, a retiring candidate, in Howley ward. One of the seats—that of St. John's ward—was towards the end of last year regained for the Tories by Mr. W. J. Shaw, a vacancy having been caused by the election of councillor Blackhurst as an alderman.

At a meeting of the Conservative Council held on Monday evening, it was resolved that all the Libe- ral seats should be contested, but as yet no headway has been made in securing candidates During the week a deputation of ratepayers have waited upon Councillor Shaw Green to ask him to. stand again for Bewsey ward, but he has not yet we believe,givena final deciAion. In regard to Orford Ward it is not yet certain whether Councillor Walker- will seek re-election, and failing Mr. Walker, Mr. Holmes has been spoken of as a suitable candidate.

A meeting of Conservatives was held on Thursday evening at St. Barnabas' Schools to choose a candi- date for IV hitecross Warta , and a formal invitation was tendered to Mr. R. T. Smith, Lovely Lane to' stand for the ward, but he destined to accept the invitation. The meeting was then adjourned until Monday. It is, in face, rumoured that the ward will be uncontested. Councillor H. Roberts has already organised a strong canvassing party, and his re- election is practically assured.
In respect to the appointment of ,layor for the en-uing year, it is expected that the present Mayor (Alderman E. Greenall) will be invited to hold office for another twelve months.
WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

Houghton, E. Aukland, Win. Balharry, S. Davies, Wm. Fairclough, Wm. Gill, J. Hibbert, J. Hill, J. Houghton, A. Jolley, A. .J. Jolley, J. Kilshaw, H. J. longton. T. Mather, J. Muir, W. J. Shaw, T. Smith, J. Swinton, and J. Turton ; also Mr. J. O. Sutton (clerk), Mr. S. Sutton (deputy clerk), Mr. Ward (master), and Mr, Mines (superintendent df schools.)

div.head: SCHOOLS COMMITTEE.
div.p: SCHOOLS COMMITTEE.

At a meeting of the Schools Committee, tenders hav- ing been examine() for laying pipes and connecting the pump with the reservoir by means of wrought iron pip- ing, it was recommended that the Messrs. It was recom- mended that two sewing machines be purchased from the Singer Manufacturing Company, on the terms speci- fied in their letter of the 15th September, at a cost of £ll. The Superintendent was instructed to procure tenders for four clarinets, one piccolo, and one flute, as additions to the band.—Mr. MUIR explained that the £ll did not pay for the machines, they had also to give two old ones in exchange.—The minutes were adopted, on the motion of M. Wm. HOUGHTON seconded by Mr. S. DAVIES.

div.head: RESIGNATION OF THE SCHOOLMISTRESS.
div.p: RESIGNATION OF THE SCHOOLMISTRESS.

Miss Mary Houghton having resigned her position as schoolmistress at the Padgate Industrial Schools, Mr. AMMAN° moved that the resignation be accepted, and that advertisements be issued asking for applications for the post. This was seconded by Mr. Smiw, and carried.
PRESENTS.

Mr. WARD acknowledged the receipt of a parcel of " Tit Bits" from Mr. Dolan, Church-street. for the inmates, and a quantity of flowers from Great Sankey Church. The Superintendent acknowledged the receipt of a hamper of apples for the children from Mr. William R.4yston, Paddington.

div.head: iCCLAIMODATION WANTED.
div.p: iCCLAIMODATION WANTED.

The CLERK read a letter from the Stockport Union asking if the Warrington Union could accommodate a number of old inmates and children from their Union. The Clerk had replitd that the Warrington Workhouse was full.

div.head: ABOLITION OF El-OFFICIO MEMBERS.
div.p: ABOLITION OF El-OFFICIO MEMBERS.

Mr. Munn wanted tn know when the act would come int, force which abolished ex-officio members from Boardiof .Guatdians.—The Clerk . There is no such act. -Mr. Muir : But there is an Act of Parliament which ban been passed. It was at the recommendation of the Local Government Board I think. Mr. WILLIAM GILL : You mean the Parish Councils Bill which has not yet been passed.—The CLERK: Yes. That is one of the provisions in the Parish Councils Bill.—The Clerk then stated that it was a subject which would come up for debate in February next when deputations from Boards of Guardians and local authorities would assemble in London at the conference. THE PURCHASE OF MEDICINE. —A "SCENE." .

...- Mr. CLARK E moved that the contract for supply of medicines be transferred from Dr. Watkins, the medical offcer of health, to Mr. Brown, druggist, of Earlestown. He did so because he thought Dr. Watkin's charges were too high. He charged a shilling per battle, while in Warrington the medicine was supplied at ninepence per bottle.—A discussion then ensued as to the advisability of carrying out Mr. Clarke's pro iti Ihrinsivr asked : Is there no other druggist besides Mr. Brown who could supply the medicine ? The people from New- ton would have to walk to Earlestown.—Mr.R.urcurra : I don't see any necessity to discuss that now.—Mr. HIBBERT : .You want to take the bit of a contract into Earlestown, I suppose. (Cries of " Order" and "Jealousy.") —Mr. ItnacrAFFE: I don't ; I don't.—Mr. lIIEBERT : But I know better.—Mr. RATCLIFFE : I won't stand this any longer. I won't stop here to be insulted. —Then speaking to Mr. Heaton, the vice-chairman Come and take this chair. I won't stop here.—Mr.FlEa- I TOW : Oh, sit down, it's all rig'ht.—Mr. RATCLIFFIt : But it isn't all right.—After a little further altercation, Mr. Hibbert apologised for making the imputation against the Chairman,which he said was only done in jest.—The question of supplyingthe medicine was further discussed. Several members said that Dr. Watkins often delivered the medicine, and that, no doubt, justified the extra charge. Upon the motion of Mr. BALHARRY, Mr. Clark's motion was rejected.—Mr. Clarke said he should bring the matter up at some future time.

div.head: WORKINGMEN'S GOSPEL TEMPERANCE MISSION.
div.p: THE WORKINGMEN'S GOSPEL TEMPERANCE MISSION.

A bible discussion Was held in the mission Hall, on Friday night, at which an adjourned conversation on the second Epistle of Peter was much enjoyed by the members of the mission. Mr. A. Horrocks presided. On Saturday night last an open air meet- ing was held on the ground at the end of Be wsey- street. Al r. R. Storey conducted and was supported by Mr. J. Drury, and Mr. H. Taylor, P.C.M. There was considerable interruption by a drunken man. On Sunday evening a public meeting was neld at the same place, conducted by Mr. J. Drury. Addresses were delivered by Messrs. J. Rigby, J. Tanner, J. Coldercot, A. Horrocks, H. Taylor, P.O.M. Councillor Dixon and Mr. R. Storey. A few hun- dreds of people were present. A numbersigned the pledge. The meetings were very successful. A well-attended band of hope meeting was held in the Temperance Hall on Monday night, the programme consisting of singing, reciting and speaking by the children, and a very pleasant meeting was spent. --On Thursday night the members of the Gospel Temperance Mission held a service of praise and thanksgiving for the decision of the magistrates at the adjourned licensiag sessions held that morning.

div.head: DISTRESS IN WAIiIIIN GTON.
div.p: DISTRESS IN WAIiIIIN GTON.
POSITION OF THE WORKS,

The state of things in Warrington owing to the prolonged coal strike continues to grow worse, and the papers are eagerly scanned to see it there is any appearance of a settlement.. The nuMber of people out of work is something appalling. such a num- ber have probably never been known previously. The smaller works of the town are for the greater part completely closed, and the larger works are almost in as bad a position. The only large works ' which are going full time are the Sankey 1% ire Mills of Messrs. W. D. Houghton and Son.. Monks' forge is'practically stopped, and at Dallam and Bewsey forges only half the men are working. Ilvlands Wire Works are working three hays a week, and there is a probability of this being still further reduced. At Whitecross Wire Works, all the mills are stopped, and the wire department is only par- tially at work. The Waggon Works of the Cheshire Lines Committee in Battersby-lane are only Work- ing three days a week, and all the extra hands are completely stopped. The Cock beige Mills employees as was reported in the " Examiner 'last week have adopted the wise course of contributing a penny in the shilling of their wages towards meeting the advanced price of the coal. But foi this arrange- ment 1,500 people would have been thrown out of employment at these mills. In order that those out of work might still be well posted with the news of the day, the cocoa-rooms of the town have opened free newsrooms tor those who are in enforced idleness. THE SOUP KITCHENS.

Since Thursday in last week, the work of dealing out the soup has been performed under new arrangements. It, will tid remembered that at the Towns' meeting held On Tuesday week a general relief comtnittse was fermod which should take the place of tie previous emergency committee. On Thursday the town was divided into districts with a suli-commlttee for each district in order that the distribution of soup could be carried on with ,much less difficulty. This was most desirable as some persons had to wait for hours at the , Drill Hall before they could be served so great was the ' number. The General Committee have opera d soup kitchens in the following places No 1 district com- prising St. Johns Ward (soutn of C.L C. Railway), Fair- field Ward, Howley Walcl, and Latchford Ward, is supplied from the mission room, Lower flank-street, at which place relief tickets are disrtibuted, and all arrangements for the day are made at ten o'clock in the morning by the sub-committee. No. 2 &strict, com- prising St. Johns Ward (north of C.L.C. railway), Orford Ward and Bewsey- Ward, is supplied at Buckley, street Schoolrootn. No. 3 district, comprising Town Hall Ward, Whitecross Ward, and St. Austins Ward, is supplied at the Drill Hall. Great credit is dee to the indefatigable secretary Mr. Stanley Wilson for the excel- lent arrangements that have been made in connection with this distribution. All the soup is made at the Drill Hall under the supervision of Mr. Powis, the Town Hall keeper, who is an experienced cook. When the soup is re- quired it is placed into zinc tanks which will hold from ten t e fifteen canons. There are about 285 ga'lons of soup used daily and also 1,600 loaves. The tickets which are given are available for the whole or part of a week, and entitles the holder if beer, she is an adult to a pound of bread and a pint of soup, and children under twelve years of age to half that quantity. An appeal has been made by Mr. F. Monks J (chairman of the executive committee) and Mr. Stanley Wilson (secretary) for further support as the number of destitute people is increasing. About £75 per week is required for the present needs. The gifts of money are requested either to be forwarded to the secretary at the Town Hall, or to paid at the local banks. Any gifts of food should be taken to the hall keeper at the Town Hall. It is satis- factory to know that subscriptions are coming in much more freely than they did previous to the present com- mittee being formed. . _ . . .

Mrs. Carleton has for some time been supplying 50 children attending St. Mary's Mission School,Bank Quay, with free breakfasts, and her kindness has been much appreciated. Since the division of the town into districts, the em- ployes of Messrs. Monks, Hall and Co., have combined with the general relief committee, and it has, therefore, been found necessary to open a soup kitchen in Liverpool road. On Monday, the soup kitchen was opened at the Mr. alien's cycle shop, and there is a new sub-commit- tee to superintend this also. Mr. Charlton Parr J.P., C.C., has sent the following letter to the Mayor " I send you cheque for £2O for 3-our relief distress fund. lam truly grieved to know there is so much suffering in Warrington.—Yours faith- fully, J. Charlton Parr." The collections at Cairo-st., Chapel on Sunday realised £l2 4s. 4d.

MEETING OF THE COMMITTEE YESTERDAY. A meeting of the General Relief Committee was held in the Council Chamber of the Town Hall, the chair being occupied by the Mayor (Alderman Greenall). There was a very large number of the committee pre- sent including a number of ladies. The Mayor said that as Mr. Monks knew all about the business of the committee. he would leave everything in his hands. Mr. Monks said that be knew he was expressing the sentiments of everyonein the room in congratulating the Mayor on his recovery to health. It would be a satisfaction to the Mayoress to be amongst them again and taking her share of the responsibility in the work of the town. The Executive Committee had fixed Fri- day afternoon for the present meeting as being the most convenient time for the committee to meet, and he would suggest that the committee meet each Friday atternson at 2-30. He had a statement to make of Hie work which will have bemi done by SAturdav night. The amount of subscriptions receivii up to date was £341 7s. 3d. The amouitt expended by the emergence committee up to last Friday was £B9 7s. 7d. leaving the present committee with a balance of £2.51 19s. Bd. The amount which will have been expended by Saturday night will be £122 84., which leaves a balance of £129 us. Bd. With reference to the placard issued by the executive committee to the effect that £75 a week would be required to meet the distress,he was sorry to say that the condition of things revealed during the week was something appalling as to the extent of the distress prevailing in Warrington. By Saturday night 18,306 pounds of bread,and 15,181 pints of soup will have been given out, at a cost of between Ifl. and 10. per head to the people relieved. This I meant that at least 4,000 people were relieved every I day. If this expenditure was to 134 met the committee would require at least £l5O a week. He most earnestly ' appealed to his fellow-townsmen to meet this exped,ture in as liberal a spirit as they had done before. Be and the I executive committee had spent some time VI at morning in one of the districts in which the expenditure was most heavy, and they were very well satisfied that the com- mittee was doing its best to get the large number of ! people relieved in as satisfactory a manner as possible. (Applause.) He most earnestly pressed upon every re- ligious congregation and upon those workmen who were at present in employment, to do what they could to , mitigate the sufferings which was so acute amongst I them. He would venture to say that he had never seen such distress since 1847. The distress then was very acute and very long standing, and after the distress there was an epidemic of typhoid and typhus fever due Ito some extent to the privation which the people had suffered. The sanitary condition of the town was now 'infinitely better than it was then' but he urged the necessity of guarding against such a state of sickness 'again. Although there appeared to be a rift in the cloud, that the strike wnuld soon be at an end, he was not going to say. He did not say that the position of things would warrant them in looking forward to an early termination to the strike. And even if time strike came to an end it would be a week before the :nen re- ceived their wages. They would also not be able for some time to earn their full wages owing to their ph ysm- I cal condition. He did not think that if °they had £5OO ! they would have more than would be absolutely re- quired. Next Monday there would be another boiler so that the soup would be supplied in larger quantities. Later on in the meeting Mr. Monks gave a statement of the amount of provisions supplied at each district. No. 1 district used 2,700 lbs. of bread and 1,840 pints of soup per week: No. 2 district, 10,106 lbs. of bread and 8,538 pints of soup; No 3 district, 5,500 lbs. of bread and 4,808 pints of soup. He concluded his speech by moving on Saturday a double allowance of bread be given to tide Sunday over. Councillor Smethurst seconded the motion. Rev. Owen Watkins, Mr. Malkin, and the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton also supported the motion. The Rector (Rev. F. W. Wilds) asked for a modificatinn in the manner of giving tickets, and whether it would not be desirable to have the names at the works published at which tickets were to be ob- tained. There were some from the Ship Canal works who had come to him saying that there were no tickets given of the works and lie gave them some. rhe Rev. J. Yonge thought that as everyone had a better dinner on Sunday than other days, the poor peo- ple ought to have at least as good as other days. Accord- ing to the present motion, they were only to have bread He thought they ought to have some soup as well. The Rev. Owen Watkins said in reply that there had been a difficulty in that, but as there was to be a new boiler they would perhaps manage it. In reply to the Rector he would, as secretary of No. 2 district, describe how the tickets were given out. The Committee met at ten o'clock in the morning, and there was a representa- tive from the works who knew those who worked there. The people came for tickets, and if anyone lived in another district they transferred that person to another district.

Mr. Monks said that the relief was not intended to be for the Ship Cant) employees,as if they did, they would not be able to supply them. The Rev. J. Kirtlan said that in No. 3 district the tickets were given to the managers of the works to 'us- tribute and that plan acted very well. After a long discussion in which Mr. F Monks, Revs. J Yonge, Father Feeney, W H Drummond, F Slater, and Owen Watkins, took part, it was decided to give bread and soup on Sundays at 12.15 p.m.
" i

Rev. Owen Watkins next brought up the question of the congestion in administering relief is no. 2 district. There were 20 per cent, more persons than the united number of the other districts. He suggested that the employes of Bewsey forge be taken over by district no 3. A long discussion ensued, and a large number of suggestions were thrown out. Mr. Watki us was willing to keep on with the mme number provided two places were provided for Vie administration of relief. .
_ Councillor Sinethdr+t thought that Bewsey district should be added to no 3 district.

Councillor Roberts thought that the Bewsey portion of the district should he added to district 3, as it had been shown that no 2 district was almost overwhelmed with tile numtair of those wanting relief. fle might say that that district had done their work in a magnificent ins nrier. Imposition was reduced to a mini in In. It was finally decided to leave the committees of the two districts to thrash out the question among them- selves.
FREE BREAKFAST FOR CHILDREN. THE OLD COMMITTEE DISSATISFIED.

An open air meeting of members of the emergency comteittee who were dissatisfvd with the doings of the central committee fer the relief of the distress, was held in the fair ground on Wed eesday night. There was a good number present. An improvised platform was made by means Of a lurry, upen which the members of the eommitree mouuted. The ChairMlll was Mr. George Urinston who was supported by Mr, Malkin, Mr. Price and others, and amcngst the audience was Mr. Diggle, , who during the proceedings frequently interjected his views of the matter, much t , the amusement of the majoritF and the dislike of the few. The Chairman in- troduced himself and those upon the lorry as tie work- ing-man's free breakfast commnittee, and said that they were the working-men who started the soup kitchen a fortnight last Mouthy. As the gentlemen of the town saw that the distress in tier town was increasing, they formed a committee, and took the matter out of the hands oi the previous committee. He (t he chairman) was glad that the richer people had come to their assis- tance, as the working-mei without the funds w ‘mild have been unable to grapple with the distress ie the town. The gentlemen had a perfect right to do what they had done, hut the old committee found that there was no relief for SundaY, and they, therefore, decided to give a free breakfast On Sunday morning to the poor children of the town.—Mr. Malkin proposed the following resolution ; That this meeting is of Opinion that time working-men's committee are doing the right and pr. ,per timing in providing free breakfasts on Sunday morning for the starving children of Warrington, and we pledge ourselves to render all the assistance in our power IT the carrying out of the same. He said that they all felt the need that the little children of the town should be-fed, and they thought when the soup kitchen was opened that the poor children would be provided for. Last Sunday morning they (the breakfast commit- tee), had fed 600 children. If the general committee were prepared to act properly for the Sun- days as well as the week days, they would only be too willing to give way to them.—Mr. William Allen seconded the resolution.—Mr. J. Price in supporting the motion said that it was an unthankful job to please everybody, and they would always find that if the workmen in any town tried to benefit their own class, it was put down that they were doing it from personal motives. The committee had no personal motives whatever. If they were satisfied that the general committee would provide for the little ones, they would give them every assistance. Mr. Price gave a number of instances of poverty which he had met, after which the resolution was put and carried.—Mr. Diggle wished to speak, but permission was declined, and a vote of thanks was passed to the chairman by Mr. Bate, .seconded by Mr. Price, after which the meeting was de- clared to be at an end. This was not so however, for Mr. Diggle by sundry pushings and pullings had been hoisted upon the lurry. After a brief show of resist- ance, Mr. Diggle was allowed to proceed, the committee leaving the whole lorry to him, and mixing in the crowd. Mr. Diggle wished to know what any one mem- ber of those who had spoken that night had done for ' the poor. He (Mr. Diggle) had given a large amount of provisions away.—Asked for proof of this, Mr. Diggle at once pulled a bunch of bills out of his pockets, and allowed one of the audience to read them. They proved to he bills for bread, onions, split peas, and sundry other kinds of provisions. Asked whether they were paid for, Mr. Diggle said that they were rmt yet, bu': as they wore in his name,so that he would have to pay for them. He then I waxed eloquent inhis denunciation of the" ragamuffins" who formed the emergency committee, and of the way they had treated him. " They have kicked me out," said he indignantly, and he suited the action to the word. Mr. Diggle now began to give his views of the present 'strike He was of opinion that the miners ought to have submitted to arbitration, when they would perhaps only have keen dropped 10 per cent. " Why don't you drop your rents 10 per cent. ?" shouted someone in the : crowd. "I would drop them 20 per cent, if tha'd pay the rates for me," answered the indomitable William. How long he would have kept on in this strain, cannot be said, but he was cut short by the lorry being taken away. Mr. Diggle continued his altercation with mem- bers of the committee upon the solid ground, and the shades of evening were falling fast before they separated.

div.head: FOOTBALL CLUB AND TUB DISTRE33.
div.p: THE FOOTBALL CLUB AND TUB DISTRE33.

,- - - The football match between the married and single tri-m of the club played on the 9th in,t at the football field Wilderspool Causeway realised £l5 for the benefit of the distress. Since that date, the club with that atnount,considerably augmented by a sum from their own funds have been relieving about 200 distressed people , per day at Mr. Ashton' s Bridge Foot Inn, The distribtl- tion has been made by the committee of the football club, and the amount distributed since Wednesday week has been 2,240 lbs of bread,and 6,000 lbs of potatoes. In an addition to this the committee have received the following provisions &C: Mr. Percy Davies, president of the club, two loads of potatoes and a Quantity of vegetables ; Mr. William Pierpoint. vice-president, 2i loads of potatoes ; Mr. Henry Whitlow. Hatton, two loads of potatoes : Mr. James Britch. Appleton Thorn, two loads of potatoes. The relief tickets are left in the hands of the members of the committee who distribute so many per day. This assistance to the distressed will be continued for at least another fortnight, if the present state of things continues.

div.head: CONCERT LAST NIGHT.
div.p: CONCERT LAST NIGHT.

Last night the Co-operative Hall, was crowded to excess on the occasion of a concert given in aid of the distress fund. The affair had been organised by the Y.P.S.C.E., Golhorne-st. Baptist Chapel, the chief mover in the work being Mr. E. Lloyd Jones, who rec,ived every aid from the members of the society. Se thronged was the hall that many people were reluctantly refused admission. The programme arranged was of an excellent character, the artists consisting of many of the leading local vocslists and instrumentalists, whilst the " special " artistes were Miss Parry, harp violinist, Liverpool. and Miss Lamb, Widnes, Mr. R. H. Pearson (violinist), and Mr. W. II Payton (pianist), and Mr. E. Balmford (violoncello), were the chief instrutnentalists, whilst a most enjoyable vocal programme was suhmitte 1 by Mrs. MEI Pearson, Miss E. Fieldhouse, Mr. Joseph M. Bate, Mr. A. Field house, During an interval Mr. E. Lloyd Jones. was requested to explain how the concert was organ- ised and he gave the credit to a committee of the Y.P. CE S. It was subsequently shown, however, that Mr. Jones had gone to an exceedingly great amount of trouble in organizing the entertainment :A very consider- able sum was, we understand realized by the proceeds.

div.head: SANKEY BRIDGES.
div.p: SANKEY BRIDGES.

On Saturday night 180 men sat down to a substantial tea, which was provided gratis. After the tea an en- tertainment was given, over which Mr. W. 13r0ugh pre- sided. A varied and interesting programme was gone through, the participants being as follqws i—Glee, " Wreath," Messrs. Mills, Bailey, and Entwistle ; song, "The outlaw„' Mr. W. Massey, who being ericored,sang " Plenty of bites " ; Mr. Schofield followed with a speech after which Mr. Mills sang " Dumb wife," who was encored, and sang "Let me kiss him for his mother " ; Mr. P. hardy, Lancashire recitation, "Bob and his wife Sall" ; song, "Up to date," and on his being encored sang " The forge " ; address by. Mr. W. Light ; song, " The sexton," Mr. Princep ; address, Mr. Woolley ; song, " Ora pro nobis," Mr. Mills. Mr. T. Brougdi, who has arranged all the concerts from the commencement, presided at the piano. During the afternoon previous to the tea, the men were provided with potatoes for their Sunday's dinner. On Tuesday another free tea was provided for 430 children. On Thursday night again there was a tea provided for 130 of the women whose husbands are out of work. To-night a tea will again be given to the men, and as has been the case before: an entertainment will afterwards be given, at which speeches, songs, etc. will form the programme.
