div.p: FRODSHAIf.

POLICE COI:MT.—At this court, on Saturday. before Mr. A. Thomas, William Mansfield, of no fixed address, was committed to gaol for seven days for beggiag at Helsbv.—On Monday, Charles French was sent to ganl I for lf days for sleering out at Wright's arm, Helsby, on Sunday night.—Matthew Sanders, Thomas Howard, H. Younge, and Margaret Turner were charged with drunkenness, and fined ss. and costs, or in default seven days, Sanders and Howard wore sent t..) gaol ; Young and Turner paid their fines. PAROCHIAL COMMITTEES.—The monthly meeting of the committees for Frodsham and Frodsham Lordship was held in the Town Hall on Friday evening, Mr. A. Thomas, IT., presiding. A certificate of occupation was granted to Mr. Bretherton for two new houses in Red-lane. It was reported that the Overton pump was again out of re:air, and after some discussion Mr. Farrington was instructed to procure a new one. It was resolved that a notice board be put up warning the public that 'anyone damaging the pump will be pro- secuted. The Nuisance Inspector reported that lie had visited the sewage tanks at Sea Flats, and averred that, notwithstanding the report of Mr. Wells, they were in a very unsatisfactory condition, and it was -resolved to ask Mr. Wells to meet Mr. Farrington and the committee at Sea Flats.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND BEEN
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND BEEN
AT WARR [NUTON.

I must say that, after all the defiant language that has been given utterance to of late, 1 was vastly surprised at the complete collapse of the liquor party at the adjourned Licensing •iessions on Thursday. The sweet reasonableness of the legal representatives of the brewers and publicans was almost enough to take one's broath away, consider- ing how militant and almost scoraftl was the at- titude that some of them took up at the previous sessions. According to some authorities Messrs. Walker and Co. had determined to flout the bench to their faces in regard to the side door at the Lion 1.13te1. But how different and, let me say, how much wiser was the conduct of the great brewing firm when it came to the test.lThe (I.e.:they ',rought down:struck quite an obsequious and deferential key in his address to the bench, and instead of heroically defying the magistrates to do their worst, he mildly suggested that, instead of clo=ing the side door completely, they might fall in with a suggestion that the door should be closed at six o'clock at nights. When the magistrates intimated that they intended to adhere to their original intention to close the door altogether, a promise to comply with the order of the court was very promptly given.

Then, with regard to the numerous side and back doors of other public-houses that have been objected to, we have hear 4 a lot outside about the ' supposed irregularity nnd illegality of the magis- trates' proceedings. One prophet even went so far as to predict that there would be a collapse. There was a collapse certainly, but it was the other way about. Nothing was whis- pered but the utmost submission to the wishes of the bench, and b-fore the licenses were renewed,all the owners and licensees undertook to carry out the *alterations that may be required of them. Owing to this unexpected turn of events the business of the Sessions, which was expected to absorb the whole of Thursday and a good part of Friday, was over in little more than an hour. As to the result the temperance party of the town are entitled to claim that they have won all along the line.

Now that the Licensing Sessions are over and have resulted in the full carrying out of theinten- tions of the magistrates, what is to be thought of , the action of the Watch Committee ? This Commit- . tee under the pretext that it had not been treated wi-13 proper courtesy —although it was palpable that no discourtesy had been meant—went out outs way to thrciw obstacles in the path ot the police and to decline to assist the magistrates in the usual way by engaging counsel. The result has been to bring the Committee into contempt. The Licensing Sessions were held,and the justices effected all they aimed at, while the Watch Committee and its re- diculous resolution were never even referred to. It is to be hoped that one of the outcomes of the municipal contests will be the re-construction of this Committee.

I am told that the decision of magistrates with regard to the side-door at the Lion Hotel was only come to by the casting vote of the Chairman. It appears that two of the magistrates—Mr. John Burgess and Mr. John Fairclough—who were originally in favour of closing the door entirely were " caught " by the proposal to close the door at six o'clock. The sub-committee of magistrates which has been appointed to confer with the brewers and publicans as to the closing of the back doors is compod of Aldermen Sutton and Fran- comb; Councillors Fleming and Roberts, and Messrs_ Monks and Fairclough.

At an inquest held in the Parade room a few daye ago, the foreman of the jury told the cot oner of the disagreeable duty the jury had had to perform in the viewing of the body. The person had been dead some days, and the smell arising from the corpse, was offensive, to say nothing of its being dangerous to health. The pity is that the law in regard to this matter as it now stands, compels twelve good jury- men to view the body previous to the judicial inquiry, and the risks incurred in so doing are great, especially in infectious cases. It is time this old law was amended, as the duty is unnecessary_ The doctor's certificate of death ought to be suffi- cient to meet the necessities of the case.

It is interesting to note what a palpable differ- ence has been made in the amount collected in the Park at the band performances toy the members of the Band Committee going round with the collect- ing boxes. For the first moath in the season it was left to the generosity of the public to drop their coins in the boxes. At the first performance, when there was one of the largest attendances in. the park, the public subscribed the handsome sum of 35., the Sonday following 3s. 101 and the third and fourth Sundays 954 I. and ss, 8L respectively. The first Sunday of go:lig round with the boxes realised £2 4s. 51. or more than double the amount received at the four previous -performances ! The result has been that the eight local bands woo per- formed have been rewarded with a well-earl:lei bonus.

There was a striking contrast between the attendance of the " great unpaid " at the Police Court, on Thursday morning, when compared with that of recent court days. On Saturday last the court was kept waiting for a second magistrate to appear until 10.25. The only magistrate who put in an appearance at the appointed time being Mr. John Burgess. Sergeant Chantler—that indispens- able officer—went in search of one and succeeded with Mr. R. Garnett, although it is only fair to state that it was not the day assigned for Mr. Garnett to undertake magisterial duties. A similar occurrence occurred on Tuesday morning when another half- hour was wasted by twenty or thirty persons through waiting for one magistrate. A better system of apprising the police, of their inability to be present, by those appointed to attend, seems Wanting. As things are now arranged, the police never know whether the required number will " turn up " or not, and it is only after ten o'clock that a search is made for a substitute.

Mr. Fleming's haystacks in Arpley fields appear to be the favourite trysting place for those persons who are so unfortunate as tr, be unable to find or pay for lodgings elsewhere. Almost every week some unfortunate individual is brought to the Police Court to explain their reason for spending their night under the open vault of heaven Last Sunday morning, however, surely the climax was reached for no fewer than ten were captured on or about the haystacks, and Constables Turner and Bell must have felt rather queer when they saw this little army of sleepers out. They are to he congratulated on getting them all safely down to the Police Station with a little assistance. The very next morning another three were captured by Sergeant Smith and Constable Clough, and again yesterday the same two officers captured four more in the same place. Seventeen in one week is a pretty large order, and Mr. Fleming has had to appear so frequently that when he appeared yesterday Mr. White, the magistrates' clerk, laughingly asked him if he had the same old story to tell. There is no doubt that the large number of this class is due to the coal strike which has caused such wide spread. poverty.

div.head: MERLIN. SHOCKING DEATHS OF BOYS AT ItTJNCORN.
div.p: MERLIN. SHOCKING DEATHS OF BOYS AT ItTJNCORN.

Andrew Whitlow, aged 3 years and nine months, son of Harry Whitlow, farmer, of Halton Gate Farm,Norton, met with a terrible death. On Wed- nesday night the deceased went to bed with a man- servant, and early next morning when the servant got up the boy went into his mother's room. Later in the morning Mr Whitlow took a cup of tea up to his wife, and perceiving a strong smell of whisky in the room,and found his son lying unconscious on the bed. He remained in this condition until Thursday night,when he died. It is presumed that the unfortunate boy had drunk some whisky from a bottle, which was in the drawers. John McEwen, aged 13 of Runcorn, went with tam school companions named Gilligan and Feeney to Run- corn Quarry after dinner on Thurs.-lap. When the school bell rang the two latter went to school, but McEwen expressed his intention not to attend school. As he had not returned borne in the evening, his father went in search of him hut could not find him nor !pm any news of his whereabouts. div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES,
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES,
A SUSPICIOUS FIND.

At Warrington Borough Court, OR Wednesday, Peter Bailey, a stranger in the town, and Samuel Hustage of Warringt m. were charged wit `l unlawfully offering in pledge at the skop of Mr. Joseph Houghton, a lady's silver demi-huntl. watch with monogram at hack, and gold chain, supposed to have been stolen. D.S. Mona- ghan said he went to Mr. flought-m's shop and there saw Bustage offering the watch and chain for pledge. In reply to questions he said Bailey had given it him to pledge and that he had found it in Shiel-road, Liverpool Inspect ,r Spinks said Bailey told him he came to War- rington to raise some money on it. Mr. Houghton said Rustage asked six shillings on it, and said it belonged to his cousin. Mr. Hunt (chief constable) asked for a remand until Saturday which was granted,

div.head: THEFT OF MILITARY CLOTHING.
div.p: THEFT OF MILITARY CLOTHING.

On Wednesday morning at the Warrington Borough Court, Martin Ryan, was charged with assaulting P.C. Robinson in the execution of his duty, and also with stealing two mi airy shirts, a coat arid cap value 19s. 6d the property of the military authorities. Illsoner pleaded guilty to stealing the shirts. P.C. Robinson said he WaS on duty in Marsh-house-lane when he met the prisomr. He noticed he had something bulky under his great coat. His answers not being satisfactory he (witness) took him into custody. The prisoner then became very rough and struck him in the face, and tried to getaway. The prisoner was wearing three shirts at the time. James Winstanley and John Wm. Roberts, privates, identified the coat and cap as theirs. Prisoner was fined 10s. and costs for toe assault m the policeman, or 14 days impris- onment, and one month's imprisonment for the theft.

THEFT OF A LOAF OF BREAD. At the Warrington County Pet ty4 Sessions, on Wednes- day, before Mr. Z. Armitage (in the chair), Major Pick. mere, and Mr. John White, a collier, named Ralph Hart. was charged with stealing one four lb. loaf of bread, value 4id., at Burtonwood, on the 12th September, the pr.:.perty of Mr. Peter Thompson, grocer, Earlestown. Mr. Bissell, a carter, in the employ of Mr. Thompson, said he was delivering bread in Burtonwood on the date in question. He was in Chapel-lane, when from infor- mation received he counted his bread and found one loaf missing. He afterwards gave information to the police. George Houghton, residing at the Chapel House Inn, 4leposed to seeing the prisoner take the loaf. P.C. Grundy said he apprehended the prisoner, and chargcd him with stealing the loaf. He said he took it and gave it to another man. The loaf was found in the prisoner's house. It being the prisoner's first offence he was bound over to appear when called upon.

div.head: BIG CAPTURE OF SLEEPERS-OUT.
div.p: BIG CAPTURE OF SLEEPERS-OUT.

At the Warrington Borough Court, on Monday, Patk. Dolly, Patrick Morris, Michael Gill, Michael Dolan, John C. Flannigan, John Riley, John Davies, James Burns, Wm. Gladder, and John Johnson, all strangers, were each charged with doing wilful damage to a haystack of John El. Fleming's, in Arpley fields, the damage amount- ing to 205., at 3.30 on Sunday morning.—P.C. Turner said he was in company with P.C. Bell on Sunday morning, and went to look round Mr. Fleming's stacks, where they saw nine of the prisoners lying round one of the stacks. One of the prisoners was on the top of the stack,where he had dug a hole a yard deep.out of which he had to be pulled. Assistance was procured and the whole hatch were taken to the Police Station. Each of them had pipe and matches in their pockets.—Mr. Fleming said that the damage they (lid on Sunday morn- ing was 203., but owing to the rain which had come since, the damage would be £5, as the prisoners had pulled the roof off the stack.—The Chief Constable said that all but Riley had money in their pockets.—The pri- soners alleged that they had been all over the town to find lodgings, but failed,and that was the reason they were found sleeping out in the fields.—The magistrates inflicted a fine of 58. and costs, or seven days imprison- ment upon each prisoner. Thomas Johnson. Thomas Jones. and Edward Jones, all of no address, were also charged with committir.g a similar offence on Monday morning at 1.10. at the same place. P.& Smith proved the case, and the prisoners were also fined ss. and costs, or in default seven days.

div.head: MINOIt CASES.
div.p: MINOIt CASES.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.
SATURDAY. —Before_Mr,John Burgess (in the chair) and
Mr. Robert Garnett.

DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Bridget Brown was fined ss. and costs or seven days for this offence in Froghall- lane, the previous night. IMPUDENT Tit-arr.—Mary Jane Hamblen, Silver-st., and Annie Bohen, 7. Silver-square. were charged with stealing from Sarah Darbyshire, in Winwick-road, the previous night, a sovereign, the property of William Kenwright, provision dealer. Barnblett pleaded guilty and Bohen, not guilty. From the Chief Constable's statement it appeared that the two defendants met with a man who was said to be a sailor, and he paid for drink for them at the Shakspeare Inn. They afterwards went with him to Mr. Kenwright's provision shop. He told the two defendants to ask for whatever provisions they wanted, and they did so to the extent of 4s. 10d. The man proffered a sovereign in payment and a girl named Darbvshire wa.3 sent for change. On returning with the silver, the girl was met by the prisoner Hamblen. who took fifteen shillings from the girrand gave her 54. in , payment for the groceries. The other prisoner remained in the shop with the man waiting for the change but left as soon as the girl returned with the 53. Information was conveyed to the police and the two woman were arrested by P.C. Dean, when it was found that they had divided the money between them. They were each sent to gaol for one month.

DRUNK AND DISCHIDARLY.—JuIia Ann Shielcis,3 Pilling's Court, and John Hall, no address, were dealt with tor this offence. A Man FREAK.—DUINKINH A QUART OF WHISKY.— Patrick Flannaghan, 59 Fetlock-st., Liverpool, was charged with being drunk in Marshhouse-lane on Satur- day night.—Prisoner had come ever to Warringt,n to see Ids son, whom he had not preyiously seen for nine years. His son is a soldier at Orford Barracks, and after seeing him, he went for a quart of whisky, probably to celebrate the event. When he came back to the bar- racks, he apparently fonnd no one with whom to share the whiskey, and therefore, drunk it all at once. This quantity of whisker of course quickly took affect upon him, and he lay in whiskey dead drunk, and re- mainad there until Constable Barnett came along, and as he could find no one to whom he was known, the officer brmght him to the police station. During Sunday the prisoner was very ill frc:n the effects of the whisky, and had to be attended to by the doctor. Prisoner's son came to the court on Monday morning, and said that he would pay the fine and the doctor's fee, and the magis- trates fined prisoner 53. including costs, and the doctor's Tar.rr n TRK OPFN STREET.—Jan Murray was charged with stealing in Friars Green on Saturday night, a black cloth, a pair of cloth trousers, a shirt, and a handkerchief valued at 10s., the property of James Clark.—From the Chief Constable's statement it ap- nea rid ihat Clarke, who lodge at Bruchemitc's lodging- house in Friars Green, was talking with some other men, in the street, and had the bundle by his side, Murray, -who is a stranger to the town came behind him, picked

Mr. Kent had not pleased Mr. Dyson, and a notice to leave was given him, which ha: expired, but he refused to go, although Mr. Dyson had tried every possible means to get him to go.—The order was granted. CRUELTY TO A HORSE.—Georee Thorpe, 38 Ormskirk- st., St. Helens, was charged with illtreating a horse by working it while in an unfit state, and John Aspinall, 128 Dunriding-lane, Ec.cleston, was charged with allow- ing it to he worked.—P.C. Bell said that he saw the horse at Bank Quay on the 10th inst. Thorpe was driving it, and it was very lame. Witness shouted to him to stop, but he refused but witness afterwards discovered that it was in the "Nag's Head" yard. and the horse was there examined by Mr. Dixon, veterinary curn.eon, and In- spector Dowty, R.S.P.C.A.—Mr. Dixon said that he saw the horse pass him near the park. It was going very lame, and on his examining it at the " Nag's Head," he found that the fetlock of one leg gave way and caught the ground, and it was very much cut in consequence. The horse was in a very had state, and the weakness appeared to be of old standing.—lnspector Dowty corro- borated, and said that Thorpe had told him that he had taken the horse back again to Aspinall after he had started out, but Aspinall told him to go on with it.—The Bench inflicted a fine of 404. and costs upon Aspinall and dismissed the charge against Thorpe who did not appear.

A WINDOW SMASHER. —Thomas Larkin was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Tanner's-lane, and also with breaking a coloured glass window at The Three Pigeons public-house, value 50s. From the evidence of the barmen it appeared that the prisoner came into the public-house and asked to he supplied with drink, hut on being refused he used abusive language, and picked up the water bottle on the counter. It was taken from him and he was put out. He returned and broke the window with his fist. div.head: RICH NEGROES.
div.p: RICH NEGROES.

A New Orleans correspondent sends to the " New York Times "Some particulars of wealthy Southern negroes, which is interesting as showing how rapidly these men, nearly all of them who are at one period of their lives slaves, have acquired at least an improved pecuniary position. One died recently leaving a million dollars hti had been a slave and learned the tailor's trade. The wealthiest negro in Louisians is credited with a fortune of 500.000 dollars, and the possession of one of the finest libraries of French, Spanish, and Italian classics in the State. He, like mauy other coloured men, received his education in Paris. In Arkansas there are some half-a-dozen neeroes, all born in slavery, and now worth 50,000 to ?50,000 dollars. One of these, a man of 80 years of ace, is in every respect self-made. Hit owns the entire street-ear system in a town of 12,030 people, a saw mill working El hands, two enod planta- tions, besides some valuable real estate. He is also a direct-n- in the bank. The writer speaks highly of the general rise of the negro race in the State.
A Mumbles boatman, Henry Smith by name, has saved 16 lives from drowning, but be has no medal to wear.

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMMIR 23, 1893.

WARRINGTON "A" v. WIDNES" A."—This match was I played at Widnes on Saturday, and the home team started tha leather, Mackley replying by dribbling into his opponents' quarters. Following some scrimmages, Cox and Emery broke away into the Warrington terri- tory, brit Bailey, Teare, Edwards, and Hatnpson retali- ated by dribbling splendidly down the ground. Here Westall, in the hose, forced the play right into the home line. Morris relieved the pressure S: me what,until Brad- bury and Westall again pur the Widnesians on the de- fensive. Warrington, however, lost the advantages gained by their very ineffective tackling,but Teare with a very fine brLakaway from a lino out again put his side in the ascendant. Some fine work by Houghton to Lally who ran finely down the field and threw to Lawless,gave Warrington a glorious chance of scoring, but the latter's pass was badly muffed and the chance lost. Then the home forwards got right away to the Warrington end, but Lawless getting possession recovered the lost ground in fine style. Good footwork by Monks, Nelson, Brad- bury, and Bailey, caused the Widnes back division some trouble, but the Warrington tackling was weak. and Anderson and Wright headed a dribble into the visitors' quarters, where a bad pass was made by a Warringtonion on the line, allowing Toohey to obtain a try. Half-time arrived shortly afterwards. Warrington restarted the fray by rushing into their antagonists' 25, some very smart work by Lally bothering the Widnes backs. Peters by a long kick, sent the warfare into the visitors' lines, Warrington having an anxious few minutes. Gib- son was the first to relieve, and this was followed by a nice bit of running and passing between floughtnn,Lally Edwards, and Bradbury, which transferred the game into the home quarters. After some rather inconsistent play on the part of Warrington, the game ended, the visitors being beaten by a try to nil,

WARRINGTON 2ND V. TRANMERE WANDERERS' `' A" TEAM.—Played at Wilderspool causeway. The visitors kicked off and immediately attacked, but a neat piece of play by Mason and Raybold took play to the visitors' 25, where Mason secured, and, eluding his opposing halves, ran over, the same player kicking a neat goal. From the drop-out Warrington again rushel the leather up the field but the visitors recovered owing to a late pass by Mather. Buckley scored for a line out, and Mason again cnnverted. Batty, for the visitors, got hold and kicked the ball to Coggins, who ran strongly along touch and gained the best try of the day, Edleston just missing from a difficult place. At half-time War- rington were leading by 2-1-3 to nil. In the second portion of the game play was more even, a dribble by Freeth ending in Lawless scoring, Mason's kick grazing the upright, and the game ended in Warrington winning by 2 goals, 2 tries, 4 minors to a minor.

div.head: RUGBY. WARRINGTON v.
div.p: RUGBY. WARRINGTON v.
WIDNES.

The first meeting of these teams this season, took place on the Wilderspool ground, on Saturday. There was a splendid gate, and the afternoon was not too hot. Barber kicked off for Widnes, but Potts was early on the offensive, and with a sharp pick up and punt he took operations into the Widnes territory, but the ad- vantage was not sustained,and Warrington again missed a good opportunity by faulty passing, and Drummond and Johnson troubled Ileesom considerably at full back. Wirkes at this period of the game were giving the Warringtonians a deal of anxiety, and Alford had hard lines in missing a drop goal. Warrington, however, speedily recovered, and Evans and Potts breaking away, the latter scored at the corner.. The difficult place was not improved, a:nd soon after kick out, Bate and Nevins were almost over the line again, but the danger was cleared. After a spell of open play, Dakin led off with a rush, and the Widnes defence was very severely taxed, but it proved equal to it, although Bate had very hard lines. Widnes now made a spurt but Barnes and Potts again came to the attack. Tnis did not last long how- ever, for Alford and Clarke put a different complexion on the game completely, hut their efforts to score were unavailing, and half-time arrived with the score of Warrington one try, Widnes nil. Turner re-started, and Warrington's eagerness lost them a point in the first minute. Heesom was early called on to defend his charge, and right well did he perform, a , ponderous kick settling the game at half-way. A mono- tonous series of scrimmages and line-outs, intermingled with free kicks, made the game drag somewhat, but the interest was revived when the 'Widnes men bore down on the home goal, and Clarke looked a certain scorer until he met Potts. The home forwards responded well to the calls made on them, Donohue ably leading the way. Barnes daringly saved a rush of Forster, Johoson and Kenyon, but Berry was to the fore with a single handed dribble along touch. Warrington continued to improve their position, and Nevins got his side out of difficulties with an excellent mark. Jolley got going from a p,,ss by Bate, but unfortunately he stepped into touch, and some mulling of the home three-quarters almost let in Widnes. Each goal was threatened, and though Widnes got dangerously near at the close, they were kept at bay, and the cunclusion was a victory for Warrington by a try (three points) to Widnes nil. Teams —Warrington : Beeson), back ; Barnes, Evans, and 1 Potts, three-quarters ; James Bate and Nevins, half- backs.; Fair Turner, Jolley, Donohue, Berry, Thorniley, Handles, Holmes, Dakin, and Higham, forwards. Wid- nes-: Brennan, bark : Barber, Aldford, and Clarke, three quarters.; Drummond and Wright, half-backs ; Johnson, Wynne, Hogan, Forster, Derbyshire, Whelan, Kenyon, Fraser, and Ridgway, forwards. Referee, Mr. S. Simp- son, Manchester.
RUNCORN v. WIGAN.

On Saturday, Runcorn raid their annual visit to Wigan. The match, which is one of the most popular that Wigan play, was witnessed by 5.000 people and shortly before play commenced the gates were thrown open, which considerably augmented the attendance. Runcorn had not their strongest team, owing to Cromp- , ton having gone svith Bradford to Huddersfield, and Abrams being indisposed. The homesters had whipped together their strongest team, but dispite this fact they had to undergo a defeat of two goals and two tries, to one dropped gcal. Alt through the competition the visi- tors displayed admirable combination. The following was the Runcorn team :—Houghton, back ; E. J. Morris, T. Warder, and J. Nickson, three-quarters ; J. Faulk- ner and G. Robinson, half-backs ; W. Faulkner, H. Williams, J. Langley, A. Taylor, J. Davies, H. Farmer, W. Jordan, J. J. Stubbs, and R. Reece, forwards. Mr. John Knowles (the president) kicked off for the home team. Grand passing by W.' Halliwell, Mitchinson, James Ilalliwell, Winstanley, and Roberts carried play to the line, a long kick by Trow adding a minor.. The drop out did not bring relief, the Wiganers playing grandly. Unsworth got over, as did Roberts, but both were ruled back. Faulkner and Warder were next in evidence, and the home quarter was reached, but Mitch- inson and Halliwell neutralized. Rigby and Roberts next got away, but a pass torward spoiled a splendid opening. The play was fast and open, Runcorn show- ing up well with some fine running and passing. A minor to each side followed, the players being well matched. From a line out Wigan got away, and the ball was headed by Unsworth, but Warder saved nicely. Mitchinson initiated a fine pass- ing nuivement between Winstanley, Hailiwell, and Whitehead, Houghton stopping the latter. Rigby next dribbled down, Robinson kicking behind to avert disas- ter. From the ensuing pack Houghton landed the leather in touch at the quart ,r mark. Wigan were hav- ing the best of the argument, but could not pass Hough- ton, who plaved a champion game at full back. Nickson kicked, and, following up, again secured the leather, but was nulled down on the line. Trow, the home full back, received an injury to his leg, which necessitated his re- tirement for a while. Play was subsequently located at centre, and neither could claim any advantage. Half- time': Wigan, nil; Runcorn, nil. In the second half Halliwell, la,t year's full back, took Trow's place, but his loss at threequatters considerably weakened the home side. Winstanley, however, dropped a gaol for Wigan, but Runcorn soon scored a try by Warder, through a splendidly cninbined piece of passing, and again another try immediately after by Morris, which Warder im- proved. Houghton then came out with a short kick in , his own quarters, and by again getting possession secured a try, from which another goal was kicked by the youthful c,entre. Another try was obtained in the last minute of the game through the instrumentality of Davies, hut the goal kick was futile. The Runcorn score was got In the last twenty minutes of play. They, how- ever, were much bet:er in combination than Wigan, and fully deserved their victory. Houghton, at full-back, for Runcorn, was th,- hest man, and Winstanley, at three-quarter, arid Rigby, forward, were the most pro- minent for Wigan. RUNCORN VICTORIA V. BIRKENHEAD Sr. EDWARD'S.— These teams inPt on the ground of the former on Saturday. The Vies. wet e t.hort of Nevitt, Nicholls,and Christie, but the visitors were well represented. After a well contested game the result strod—Birkenhead, one goal ; Runcorn Vies., one goal cdropped).

div.head: RUNCORN FOOTBALL CLUB. THE TRANSFER OF J. A. CROMPTON.
div.p: RUNCORN FOOTBALL CLUB. THE TRANSFER OF J. A. CROMPTON.

A special meeting of the Cheshire Rugby Union was held on Monday evening at the Adelphi Hotel, Liver- pool. Mr. J. W. H. Thorpe, president, in the chair. Mr. W. H. Wallace, hon. secretary, presented the financial statement for last season, which was unani- mously adopted. It was decided to play the Yorkshire match at the County Ground, Birkenhead ; Cumberland match at Runcorn ; Durham match at Stockport. The County trial games were arranged to be played on October 11th and the lath, the first one Dukinfield, the second at Birkenhead Park. The transfer of J. H. Crompton to the Br.,dford club was considered, when the meeting decided not to grant the transfer, and a committee was appointed to investigate the matter. Crompton is debarred from playing until the matter has been investigated. There was la ry strong feeling at the action of the Bradford club playing Crompton before having the transfer of the Cheshire County Committee. There is every probability of a searching inquiry being made in the matter.

A special meeting of the committee of the English Rugby Union was held on Wednesday night at the West- minster Palace Hotel,Mr.Cail presiding, to consider the objection by Cheshire against Crompton playing in Brad- ford. As Runcorn, the club to which he formerly be- longed,had signified their consent to the transfer,the coin- tnittee decided that there was nothing to prevent Cromp- ton playing witn the Park Avenue team.

div.head: ASSOCIATION.
div.p: ASSOCIATION.

EARLESTOWN V. MlDDLETON.—Earlestown having a couple of open dates, arranged home and home fixtures with Middleton, the Manchester junior cup holders. The first match was played on the Earlestown ground on Saturday, when Middleton turned up with a strong team. Peat, the Earlest-iwn captain, won the toss, and Midd:eton kicked off down hill, with the wind in their favour. Playing with some dash in the first half, the visitors soon put on two goals to their credit. Several times Earlestown were very dangerous, Conway in par- ticular having the goal at his mercy two or three times, but owing to bad play could not manage to score, and half time arrived with the score as above. On changing ends Earlestown had the hill and wind to favour them, 1 and speedily began t) press, placing two goals to their credit in quick time. The game then became very rough, and although the Middleton players played a strong game, their tactics were not rough. Earlestown n- tieued to press most of the second half, the visitors seldom crossing the line. Towards the close of the game Middleton broke away, the outside left putting in an oblique shot, which completely beat Sudworth. After this the visitors packed their goal and effectually pre- vented Earlestown from scoring, the game ending in a win for Midd!eton by 3 goals to 2. PADOATE V. ST. ELPRIN'S RESERVE.—This match was played at Padgate on Saturday. Padgate won the toss, and St. Elphin's started against the wind. Williams getting possession of the ball sent across to Bradskaw, who ran up the field and passed to Dennett, that player defeating the Padgate goalkeeper, Weston re-started for Padgate and a good effort was spoiled by a poor shot by Howard. Just before the call of half-time, Dennett again scored for the Saints' the ssore being to nil in I their favour. After the interval, Westen sent the ball going, and the Padgate forwards getting possession raced down the field, and Hughes being pressed sent the ball through his own goal. • Dennett again scored 1 for the Saints. The final result being St. Elphins three , goals, Padgate one. WARRINGTON V. EVERTON (COMEINATION).—This well- known association team played Warring ton A.F.C. at Arpley on Tuesday night. The game was an exhibitioni game. There was a large attendance, and the field was in excellent condition. Appended are the teams : Warrington : Goal, Carter; full-hacks, Mather and Fran- comb ; halves, Phillips, F. Williamson, and Linaker ; forwards, Read, Norman, Connor, Fennelly, and G. Williamson. Everton : Goal. Jardine ; full.backs, Lind- sey and Arridge ; halves, Walker, Jones and Stonier ; forwards, Pilule% Murray, Hartley, Reay, and Elliott. Mr. W. Sugg referee. The final rbsult was Evertou four goals, Warrington nil.

The top hats were quite 'respectable when first put en, but before the termination of the match, nearly every hat was disfigured beyond redemption, some being without crown, and others minus the rim. div.head: 'COAL TRAIM CRISIS.
div.p: THE 'COAL TRAIM CRISIS.

AN ALARMING OUTLOOK AT CREWE WORKS. Notices were issued at the London and North-Western Railway Works. Crewe, on Thursday, stating that on account of the scarcity of coal, some more of their work- shops will be closed to-night until further notice. The forges have been completely suspended. The coal stop- page is having a disastrous effect on the North-Western Company, and unless the situation speedily improves, their great works will have to be closed altogether.

div.head: WORK RESUMED IN SHROPSHIRE.
div.p: WORK RESUMED IN SHROPSHIRE.

On Wednesday intsnse Pat's( action was expressed am .ingst the starving ironworkers and colliers of Stafford- shire at a general resumption of work at the old rates in many parts of the Shropshire coalfield. The blast furn- aces and collieries of th.. Lilleshall Strel'and Iron Com- pany, one of the leading coal and iron concerns of the kingdom were also set going. The furnaces had been damped down, and unless the men had resumed on Wednesday they would all have been blown out and not relighted until after ChriAtuas. PROBABLE STRIKE IN NORTHUMBERLAND. __ _

The Central News Newcastle correspondenttelegraphs that a conference of the representatives of anout fifty Northumberland and Durham collieries was held on Wednesday night in Newcastle, when it was resolved that increased financial help should be given to the Mid- land miners. A resolution was also adopted calling for a conference of the leaders of all the counties. An impor- tant motion was subsequently carried in favour of striking on the refusal of the Northumberland and Dur- ham coalowners to grant the advance asked for. As the masters have already intimated their refusal, the confer- ence thus decided upon a strike, but before any action Is taken the interegted unions will be communicated with. THE COAL-OWNERS DECISION.

The special meeting of the Coal-owners -Federation called to consider the resolutions passed at the Miners' Federation meeting at Nottingham, took place in London on Thursday. Alter tho communication from the miners secretary, Mr. T. Ashton, had been read, the coalowners passed a resolution in which they expressed regret at the fact that the resolution passed by the Miners' Federation was to the effect that no reduction In wages was to be agreed to. This . was described as merely a repetition of the suggestion made to the coal- owners in August, and the coalowners were not prepared to encourage false hopes by accepting a meeting on such a basis. At the same time they were quits willing to meet the rePresentatives of the miners to discuss the proposed reduction, and they authorised the Executive Committee to meet the miners representatives at such time and place as the secretaries for the two bodies might agree upon. Mr. B. Pickard, M.P., president of , the Miners' Federation, wss questioned on Thursday , night as to his views on the decision of the masters. He said the fact that the owners were still demanding the 25 percent. reduction showed that they intended to fight the battle out to the bitter end. That being so, it devolved upon the Miners' Federation to find out them- selves the means of escape from the present. deadlock. When it was a well-known fact that the miners of Lan- cashire, Yorkshire, Derbyshire, and Nottinghamshire were to-day as determined as ever they were, it was certain there was a terrible struggle in 'front of them. The owners apparently intended to have their pound of flesh, and whether there were to be any bones left for the men remained to be seen. OUTRAGE AT ST. HELENS.—A COLLIERY FIRE- MAN'S HOUSE WRECKED.

Following close upon the incendiary fire at St. Helens and the committal of two miners to prison for assaulting the police who were keeping order, and the arrest of a number of miners for stealing coal, there comes from St. Helens the news of 'another outray.e. Thomas Jones, a fireman in the employ of Messrs. Richard Evans and Co. at their Havannah Colliery, who resided with his wife and flie children at 8, Chancery-lane, Parr, was awakened by hearing a loud report. He at once jumped up and went and looked out of the window, but saw no one about. On coming ilow.nstairs, however, he found that the stone window•sill had beed smashed, and that the frame had been blcwn clean out. The furniture in the house had been damaged, and lay broken in all directions. The fanlights or the windows in No. 2 and No. 4 were broken, and the windows in No. 8 were also broken. The circumstances surrounding the affair point to the perpetration of an outrage,the explosive employed being roburite used in collieries. When Jones awoke he smelt roburite fumes, and on examination afterwards a yard of spent five and the wood of a match were found near the window. The object of the outrage was undoubtedly to prevent Jones from going to work at the colliery. It appears that from the beginning of the strike Jones had been working at the Havannah Colliery but after the strikers had marched on Ashton's Green and Bold Collieries a fortnight since, and intimidated the few men who were at work, Jones remained at home. Early last week, however, he was sent for, and requested to resume work. He did go on Wednesday night, and on Thursday and Friday, but did not go on Saturday. Mrs. Junes and her baby had a providential escape. The child was taken ill early in the week, and the mother up to and including Friday night had slept with it under- neath the window Which was blown out. Had she been there on Saturday she and her baby must have been killed, as the sofa was broken up. Theaffair has caused great excitement in the neighbourhood.
THE UNEMPLOYED AT ST. HELENS.-DEPUTATION
TO THE OVERSEERS.

Mr. Henry Martin, J.F., and Mr. Robert lielsher,over seers for the township of M,indle, on Monday morning received a deputation of unemployed at the Overseers' offices, St. Helens Town Hall. Mr. APKinley said the overseers would be aware of the renly of Mr. Fowler (President of the Local Government Board) to Mr. Kier Hardie, in which it was stated that under an old Act the overseers had power to purchase fifty acres of land in each parish, and establish works thereon for destitute able-bodied men. He suggested that the overseers of St. Helens should take fifty acres of land with crop coal in each parish, and find employment for those men at such remunerative prices that the ratepayers would not be at any loss by it. The guardians had previously put 500 men to the task at Whiston Workhouse, but since then he had seen the Guardians twice, and they were unwilling to allow miners to do task work. The syston carried out now was that when a man applied for relief he had to get a character from his employer, and if he got that the house was offered to him and his wife and family. He would have to break up his home, which was unfair to the poor half-starving people—Mr. Martin, speaking on behalf of the overseers,expressed deep sym- pathy with the unemployed, and reminded the deputa- tion that as individuals, they (the overseers) had shown their Sympathy practically. Mr. M'Kinley had quoted from the first speech of Mr. Fowler, but he had subse: quently stated most distinctly that after consultation with the Law Officers •.f the Crown, he found that the powers given to overseers by an old Act of Elizabeth had been superseded, and vested in boards of Guardians by the Act of 1834. It was the duty of boards of Guar- dians to provide labour for the unemployed at. the public expense.—Mr. D. Rimmer thought as the Guardians had refused to allow miners to do the task,they should write to the Local Government Board and ask for yes or no to the question—" Has a lockout man a right to be treated as any other man P"—The deputation then thanked the overseers ft,r their courtesy and withdrew, the result being communicated to a large body of unemployed who were waiting outside. MR. SAM WOODS AT HOME. •

- A correspondent RVs: -I had occasion on Wednesday to call at Rose Villa, 'Bryn, the house of Mr.. Sam Woods, M.P., a labour leader who has come into great promin- ence during the present great strike of colliers. Rose Villa has an appearance of comfort which is generally associated with the better class and more thrifty mechanic or artisan. It is semi-detached, and has its lobby and rooms of fair proportions, with a small garden plot in front. 'Me back room on the ground floor is devoted to a study. There are several hundreds of books arranged in cases, books having apparently been the most luxurious hobby of the hardworking member for Ince. Over the mantel there hangs Mr. Wood's certi- ficate or proficiency as a manager of mines, and on either side of it an illuminated address. One is from the North Wales Miners' Federation thanktrig him for his devoted- ness to the miners' cause, an4i hailing with satisfaction his presence in Parliament. Mr. Woods received this at the hands of Mr. Osborne Morgan. The other is from the Baptist Sunday school at Bryn, with which Mr. Woods has for, many years been connected.. A present of gold accompanied this address. Mr. Woods has also a gold chronometer from the Burnley miners. the inscrip- tion beasing testimony tn the services he had rendered in re-establishing their union, and a combination diamond ' scarf-ring from the Garswond Mill miners and other friends and neighbours. Mr. Woods said he had always taken great interest in the organisation of his class, and for the last fifteen years has been specially set apart for the work, Flip hon. member referred with pride to the tokens he had received, and, pointing,to the mass of correspondence, intimated that his work just now was of a most arduous nature, and. he could almost do with a shorthand clerk. The miners in the neighbourhood are manifesting every confidence in their leader, and do not hesitate tow that whatever is the result of the struggle they believe Mr. Woods is doing his utmost to gain for them a victory.

MARRIAGE OF MISS LIGHTI37,IIN .OF RUNCORN.

A marriage in which great interest was displayed took place at Runcorn Parish Church. on Wednes- day morning, the sacred edifice being well filled. The contracting parties were Mr. Frederick Charlea Larkin, F.R.C.S., of Rodney-st., Liverpool, surgeon of Stanley Hospital, and Miss Helen Alice Light- burn, youngest daughter to Mr. John Wilson Light. burn, of Heath House, Runcorn. The bride was attired in a travelling dress of beaver coloured habit cloth, with a hat to match, and she wore a gold diamond brooch, the gift of the bridegroom. She carried a shower bou- quet of white roses. The bridesmaides were Miss Ada Timmins, who wore a dress of heliotrope habit cloth, with hat to match, and Miss Gladys Jolley (the young twice of the bride), who was costufned in white broche velvet, and wore a white beaver hat trimmed with ostrich feathers. Each bridesmaid wore a gold brooch the gift of the. bridegroom. Miss Timmins carried a shower bouquet of yellow marguerites, and Miss Jolley held a basket of choice blooms. The bride was given away by her father, and Dr. Robert Edwards, of Widnes acted as best man. The officiating clergy were the Rev. Canon A. Maitland-Wood, M.A., Vicar, and the Rev. H. J. Wilcox, of Cockshutt Vicarage, Ellesmere, Shropshire cousin of the bridegroom. At the conclusion of the ceremony, Mr. and Mrs. Larkin, received the hearty congratulations of numerous friends, and rice was plen- tifully showered upon them during their progress to the carriage at the entrance gate. Subsequently breakfast was partaken of at Heath House, the guests comprising the members of the family and Canon Wood. There was a magnificent array of valuable presents. In the course of the afternoon the happy couple departed for London where the honeymoon will be spent. The func- tion throughout was of a private character.

div.head: RELIEF COMMITTEE.
div.p: THE RELIEF COMMITTEE.
The weekly meeting of this Committee was held at the Town Hall. on Wednesdiy 'afternoon, under the presidency of Mr. H. Wade Deacon, J.P., C.C. There was a good attendance.

Mr. T. Craik (assistant secretary) read the minutes of the Catering Committee, held that day, which stated that accounts amounting to .£125 had been passed. A proposal that the hot pots should be prepared in the several centres was lost by a large majority.—Councillor Christie moved the adoption of the minutes and remarked that he hoped there was truth in the report that the col- liers would soon come to some arrangement with the masters, and that the labours of the committee would quickly end.—Councillor Hodgkinson secon- ded the motion.—Carried.

Mr. Craik also read the minutes of the Finance Committee, accounts amounting to .£125 135.2 d. had been passed tot payment. Tha credit balance at the bank was £531 4s. sd. The committee further reported that the donations received and promised amounted to .£lB4 7s. 41. and the weekly sub- scriptions amounted £197 15s. 41. The actual subscriptiehas received, however, had been for the first week £l9l 5:4. 2d. and second week .£lB4 178.9(1.—Councillor F.Ndl moved the adoption ot the minutes, and said he thought the weekly subscrip- tions received very satisfactory, but there was a possibility that there might be a demease rather than an increase,since they were led to believe that Pilkingten's works would be entirely stopped at the end of the week. The subscription from these works £l9 per week, and this might be taken away. The speaker explained that accounts amounting to £215 9s. 4d. had been passed since the moyement started, and the withdrawal of this sum from I the bank would reduce' the credit balance to r £315 158.1d.—Mr. Joseph Harrison, district manager lof the United Alkali Co., seconded the motion. He considered they were in a Very satisfactory position I with £3OO at the bank and a guarantee of .£l9O per ' week, while they were only spending £l4O a week. He concurred with Mr. Christie in the hope that the strike would soon be ended. The reports in the newspapers tended to show that by the end of the month the colliers would be in again. If that were the case they would quickly have all the 'works if not in full work, pretty generally in work, and no doubt they would all be very pleased when they could tell the workmen to suspend their weekly guarantee.—Councillor Davies could not see that the labours of the Committee would speedily 'end because it would be impossible for ti,e men to all begin work immediately the Masters and col- liers came to settlement. Besides they would have to work a week before they received any wages so that at the soonest the labours of the, Committee could not flaish for another three weeks.—The Chairman explained that the subscriptions received had not equalled the promises because no doubt some of the subscribers were away from home. He believed they would receive the full amount.—The minutes were passed.

After some daiscussion, during which it was stated that the applications for relief were" becoming raort. numerous daily, it was resolved to distribute 900 hotpots on Sunday. East Sunday 750 hotpots were provided. _ _

Alderman Williamson said Superintendent Keigh- ley had asked him to mention that he had received applications for coal and to suggest that tickets for coal should be distributed in deserving cases.—The Commissioners considering the mildness of ih weather and the expense that would be involved. decided to adjourn the discussion of this subject for a week.

In a conversation with our representative at the close of the meeting, Mr. Morrison stated that only about 1,200 of the emplo36s of the United Alkali Co. were totally idle. At the present time the Co. were weekly paying £5,000 in wages, being about £2.000 less than is usually paid when the manufactories are in full work. It should be remembered, how- ever, that Tharsis Copper Works are stopped and at other places are on short tithe. The Reli-f Committee are distributing about 800 gallons of good soup per day, so that no family need to starve.
PRAYING FO It THE QUEEN.

An Ex-Highland pillie, recounting his experiences when at Balmoral, mentions that it was when her Majesty rode across th. Grampian Hills and afterwards past the Castle of Fiegue, the residence of Sir Thomas Gladstone, that a halt was made, and the Queen being thirsty, she stooped and drank from a spring of crystal w4ter which bubbled from a grassy spot among the heather. The well is now covered by a beautiful fowl. ten of granite, which bears the following inscription : , Rest. stranger, on this lovely scene And drink andnray for Scotland's Queen.—Victoria. The fountain stands in the glen of lnvermark. A good deal of amusement has been created by the following couplet Pencilled below the above, and supposed to has.° been written by an English tourist : We'll pray for Queen Vlctoriahere, But go and drink her health in beer. OF RUNCORN.

On Saturday, September 16th, was solemnized at St. Margaret's Church, Anfleld, the marriage of Mr. R. W. Pierpoint, of Runcorn with Miss Lydia Bliss (Lillie) eldest daughter of dr. E. Revell, of LiYer pool. The officiating clergy were the Rev. John Wakeford, vicar of the parish, assisted by the Rev. Horace Stephens, vicar of Godley, Hyde, cousin or the bride. The problei%. he said, "is not to be solved by creating new induci tries and workshops for a special class of unemploY,e, but by absorbing them into the industries &real, existing. div.head: QUEEN'S SE RVAN TS.
div.p: THE QUEEN'S SE RVAN TS.

'I he term " servant " as applied to those who serve the Queen is, says a writer in the Newcastle " Weekly , Chrohicle," very bread in its application. The Queen's ministers are her " servants." The Carl Rosa Opera , Troupe, atter singing at Balmoral, were pertnitt• dto • designate themselves as " Her Majk sty's SServante." But e it is in its more limit d and usual sense that I use the word here. The widest known of all the Queen's ser- vants was John Brown, Her Majesty's late Highland attendant, to whose memory her latest " Leaves from the Journal of a Life in the Highlands" is dedicated John Brown's birthplace is " The Bush," a' farm 'yin, to the north of Balmoral Castle, a road much frequent d ' as a drive for visitors. He was first employed in the stables at Balmok al, where Prince Albert found him,and, ' kecognising his excelleet qualities, promoted him to thes , post of "guile," an attendant upon gentlemen when 1 hunting and fishing. In 1849 he was chbsen by the Queen and Pkince to go with Her Majesty's carriage. In 1 1851, he began to lead the Queen's pony in their frequent ' excursions over the hills. He, together with Jchn Grant, head keeper, and also a much trusted servant, always accompanied them on those expeditions, taken incognito, in which the Queen and Prince Albert so delighted. Born in this region and his forbears before him for many generation', Jeihn Brown was well-known and respected throughout the Highlands. "Favourite servants," said a Deeside Highlander to roe, "generally gain their place by flattering the weaknesses of their employer and by underhand measures. But it was not in that way that John Brown gained his high place in the confidence of the Queen. He was honest to blunt- ness. Spoke his mind out to high and low." John Bright said of the Queen that she was the most truthful and straightforward person he had ever known. And, being such, she holds at their true value those high qualities in others. To her truthfulness is a diamond whose .priceless value she is ahle to discern even in the rough. For John Brown occasionally "spoke his mind" to hie royal mistress as to others. The Queen is fond of sketching, and on one occasion was preparing to sketch in the neighbourhood of the Glaesalt Shiel, where she had spent the night. Things had gone a little awry that morning. The royal mind was slighly out of sorts,shar- ing in that respect as in others the tendencies of our t common humanity. One table after another was fetched from the Shiel to the chosen spot for sketching,but none suited. The last table was brought and cast aside. The Shiel could furnish no other, and the servants were in despair. In the crisis they appealed to John Brown. Honest John Brown took up one of the rejected reties. carried it out, and set it down with decision in the royal presence. Her Majesty looked up. '• They canna' mak' one for you," said John Brown. The statement was incontrovertible ; they could not. The Queen laughed; the clouds vanished, and the table proved to be of the exaet height for ketching. Did Her Majesty appear in a comfortable old cloak for her drive or other exercise, John Brown was liable to remark with a plainness that wOuld send a shiver down the back of a well trained courtier, " And what kind of a thing is that you've got on the day ?" To this straightforwardness of speech and mind were united great kindness of heart and a desire to oblige. His fellow-servants liked him and trusted him—a good test—and when he came to his high place in the confid- ence of the Queen, he did much for their comfort. " A true Highlander," I have heard more than one say of him, and with a Highlander's loyalty. Highland loyalty is almost proverbial. It was put to its supreme test one might say, by the hapless Stearte. It will be remem- bered that when Prince Charlie was in hiding, at the time known in Scotch history as the " Forty-five," £30,000 was put upon his head, and though hundreds ef these people know his hiding-place, none would betray him. And yet they were living in great poverty in their miserable huts: And said one to me who knew John Brown, " I believe be would have stood between the ' Queen and a bullet any day." Such fidelity is rare, but it is to he found, and it is not limited to time or place. When O'Connor rushed up to the Queen's carriage, pistol in hand, in 1872, it was John Brown's promptness in seizing him that saved the Sovereign's life. But his province was oftener to ward off impertinence than danger. Once when the Queen was returning from a visit to the Dowager Duchess of Athol, her carriage was recognized at an inn. It was evening; a crowd gathered and one enterprising individual turned a bull's eye lantern upon the Queen. Thereat John Brown stepped between her and the glare ; to guard against such imper- tinence is one of the duties of the Queen's personal attendant. One of the Queen's horses fell lame one day as she was driving through Ballater, her carriage stopped in the square, and she sat there while a change of horses was brought from the neighbouring stable. A crowd quickly gathered, and a woman, a summer visitor, advanced, and, leaning against the carriage, stared directly into the Queen's face. Her Mejesty lowered her sun-umbrella between herself and the impertinent visitor when John Brown appeared, and without mincing matters ordered the woman back. Sometimes a bystan- der comes to Her Majesty's relief on Such occasions. Last summer an amateur photographer attempted to get a " snap-shot "at the Queen as see was sitting in her carriage at the Ballater railway station, but his camera was knocked out of his hand by someone who knows Her Majesty's repugnance to being photographed at every ' corner. John Brown's duties were manifold, not to be exactly defined; he was to be always at hand, always ready to perform the service of the moment. All John Brown's brothers have come into the Queen's service. Donald Brown is at Osborne, Hugh Brown is keeper of the kennels in the Horne Park at Windsor, Archibald Brown is a page in the royal household, James Brown is the shepherd at Balmoral, and William Brown lives in the house built by ;the Queen at Balmoral for John Brown, and which she has given to the Brown family in perpetuity. It is a large house of graniteswith stables attached. John Brown never occupied it in his lifetime, but his body rested there before burial. John Brown's suedessor as " Highland personal atten- dant "Is Francis (or Francie) Clark, his cousin. They are sons of sisters. Gark caine into the Queen's service in 1870. He looked alter the dogs, their Seeding, exer- cise, and general welfare. He rode with John Brown in the attendant's compartment in the Queen's railway carriage, and served occasionally when John Brown was off duterfor a day's sho,ting, &c. A house for him is al- es about to be built on the estate. The Queen's thought- ful sympathy is illustrated by a slight incident told me in connection with Frannie Clark. Somewhat recently and suddenly he lost by d ath a much-loved sister, who lived at Balmoral. He was driving with the Queen when the news was told her, at a cottage where she was call- ing. She at once entered the carriage, and ordering " Home immediately," gently broke the news to him her- self on their arrival. All the Queen's Scotch attendants wears a kilt. She is fond of the dress. She used tc wear the tartan her- self before her widowhood, and I obserszed that among her gifts to her grand daughter, Princess Marie of Edinburgh, was a velvet dress of Royal hunting Stuart tartan. In fact, pieces of goods of the Balmoral and Victoria as well as Stuart tartans, always form a part of her wedding gifts to her family. The daughters of the Prince of Wales when young were gowns of Bal- moral tartan, and the Queen's ladies-in-waiting make great use of this tartan for wraps. The Princes always wear kilts when at Deeside. With them it is a dress familiarized by being worn when they were boys, though as much cannot be said of the German Princes, who are also expect' d to wear it when at Balmoral. Her Majesty's Ind an Empire is roprestnted in her household. There are four of these Indians; her. Indian secretary, Haft Abdul Kairm ; her personal attendant, who " gives his arm to her coming downstairs," &c. ; and their servant and their cook. A special part of the castle is assigned to them, where are their kitchen and other apartments. Their fend is prepared by their own cook in accordance with Hindoo customs and prejudices. The atmosphere of their portion of the castle is said to be redolent of curry. The Indian secretary assists her Majesty in her study of Hindustanee, and all four accompany the Queen abroad as well as to Osborne and Windsor. ' ' The Queen is said to be very patient with her servants though she likes no better than the rest of us to" tell ever and over' how she wishes anything done. Her two wardrobe maids are both natives of Balmnral, and one has been irk her service thirty years. Both, to- gether with the dresser., must he present at a dinner or State toilet. It is one of the duties of these maids to cut out of the newspapers the paragraphs that her Majesty in looking them over, has signified her desire to keep. These are pasted into albums and dated, and can be turned to when wanted.
PAINFUL DEATH. OF WIDNES WOMAN.

DRINKING CARBOLIC ACID FOR PORTER. Yesterday afternoon week, Mr. F. A. Jones coroner, held an inquest at the Golden Bowl Hotel Moss Bank, touching the death of Mary Ann Ilanrahan, aged 35 years, wife of Lawrence Hanrahan, chemical labourer of Moss Bank Road. The evidence showed that the woman had been teetotal until the Saturday previous when she broke the pledge, and she had since been drinking heavily. On the Thursday evening, at half past six, Margaret flanrahan went home and heard a voice upstairs as of something breaking. She found her mother lying on the bed, and she said " Maggie, run quick for Mrs. Griffin; it is not porter." A t-roken cup was lying on the fire grate and there was a strong smell of carbolic acid, and Mrs. Griffin, on arriving administered salt and water to the woman but it had no effect. The woman died shortly afterwards. Two of the children of the deceased had had small cox in the suner, and the carbolic acid was left by the Corpora- tion officials when they disinfected the house.—Dr. Hutchinson who had made a p )st mortem examination, said the woman had died of carbolic acid poisoning. She had taken enough to kill tnree persons. The organs of the woman showed thht she was of intemperate habits. The jury returned a verdict of "death by mis- adventure."
