div.head: wAttniNGTON ADJoITI:NED LICENSING SESSIONS.
div.p: wAttniNGTON ADJoITI:NED LICENSING SESSIONS.

Sir,—All who look at the result, so far as can be as- rertaire d at present, of the Licensing gessions on Thurs. day,tnest s-e that much wa accomplished in the highest interest of the people of ihis town. First,it is clear that the time has arrived when the majority of our magis- trates have awakened to a sense of their responsibility, and wisely done their dory in the interest of the public at large. Second, the folly and shame of certain mem- bers ot the Watch Committee who love the interest of drink traffic more than the welfare of its victims, have been clear to all. The Watch Committees of all ether towns and cities have not acted with such folly and stolid opposition against the praiseworthy efforts if the police authorities and the general body of the magis- trates. In the third place, but not the least for good, there is the wise decision of the Bench against the per- nicious practice of drinksellers to ruin the children by tempting them with gifts of money and sweets. And it ist be hoped that a strict watch will be taken by all who wish to se the rising g,neration saved from the evils of the drink traffic.—Yours faithfully. Warrington, 22nd September, 1893.
R. STOREY.

div.head: ALTAR V. TABLE.
div.p: ALTAR V. TABLE.

Sir,—ln the Parish Magazine " Dawn of Day," circula- ted here at Runcorn and elsewhere,for this month, I find an article on the " Fabric of the church," in which the writer says :—" Within Vie sanctuary there stands no images nt heathen deities, but there does stand an altar.' Why, sir, the cross on the so-called super-altar is but a relic of Paganism, in existence centuries before Christ's advent—see Hyslop's "Two Babylons." Da the Church of Rome it is worshipped with Latria, i.e., divine or supreme worship. Churchmen know that there is no such word as altar in the communion office, but there is what Christ Himself called a " table "—John 13c. 28v. The Church mentions no altar but " the altar of the cross " (see "Homily on Repentance," part two). Her eighty-second canon prescribes "a decent com- munion table" for the Lord's Supper (not for eight o'clock morning breakfast, alias to mass, fasting). The word altar was expunged from her prayer book and " table" substituted, the obvious aim of the reformers being to sweep away the mass and re-introduce the communion. "Tile only priests under the Gospel, de- signated as such in the New Testament, are the saints, the members of the Christian brotherhood "—Bishop Lightfoot. I ask, is it honest of Bishop Jayne and the vicars under him, who have subscribed to the Articles, arid vowed t) drive away false and erroneous teaching, to allow suet' a magazine to be in their midst ?—Yours truly, Frodsham, September 20, 1893.

div.head: ROBERT FOULKES.
div.p: ROBERT FOULKES.
THE DUKE OF ARGYLE AND THE IRISH.

Sir,—lf you will kindly insert the enclosed letter in your valuable paper I shall be much obliged and I think it would be doing a good public service at present con- sidering the fierce attack maiie by the Duke of Argyle on Mr. Gladstone and the Government of Ireland Bill. Being an Irishman, and knowing as I well do the Duke of Argyle and his narrow-minded ruling of his own town of Inverary, I am cot surprised one bit at his attack on everything Irish. In 1861 I went to Inverary to live in the service of a man named Peter McGeehen, who was a general dealer in hides, skins, wool, ke, in a pretty large way; and, although then a boy I was sur,:rised to find my master and his business, stable, Sm., crammed up in a back lane, not wide enough for two wheelbarrows to pass, with the county gaol at one end, the other outlet being into a Square which was full of empty herring barrels. Both sides of this passage vvas the leasehold land of a gentle- man named Cromby, and it was known as " Cromby's Land," and contained about 20 houses. I was not long in the town before I found out the res.son of McGeeheies living in such a place, viz., that it was the only place he could get a house as there was only Cromby's Land and two other spot ii (about six houses), that was 'IA the Duke's propertc. and he (the Duke) would not allow art Irishman to live in any of his houses, and would not even allow one of his t-nanti to lodge an Irishman, for if he did so and it came to the notice of the Duke's Fa-tor," or agent, no matt ,r what part of the town or estate he held his house or crolt he was at once eject-d. Although Inverary is an impirtant (county) ti-iwn, especially in the herring fishing season, with its county gaol, assize court, provost hailies, Ste., yet the only Irish householdrs in the town were five :—viz., Peter McGeelien, Michael McGurty, Peter Gibbins. Philip D'Coine and Philip Kelly. All of these were crow&d to- gether in " Crom by's Land' for the reason already stated, and I und-rstand th .t since that time the Crom- by family's lease has expiri d, and that before the Duke would renew it they had to evict every Irish family, who were then unable to get a house in the town and had to go to Locligilphead, Greenock, and other places, so that the Duke not only cleared them out of Inverary, but almost out of Argyleshire, as Oban and Lochgilp- head are the only other towns in the county they could get any place to live in-1 am, sir, yours faithfully, HUGH O'DONNELL. Simm's Cross, Widnes.

div.head: THE. COAL WAR AND ITS VICTIMS.
div.p: THE. COAL WAR AND ITS VICTIMS.

Sir,—While in no way presuming to adjudicate as between masters and men in this most lamentable dis- pute. I wish to offer a levy remarks upon the wider as- pects of the contention. Which ever of the contending parties is to blame for the beginning and continuancs of this deadly strife, our sympathy must be mainly, if not entirely, with the innocent victims. It goes without saying that those who are out of work by reason of the dearth of coal should receive whatever help can be given. But over /sod above this comes the question—one of more perma- nent if not more pressing moment—viz. :—Ought any set of men, for purely selfish motives, be permitted to retain the power thus to paralyse the trade of the dis- trict, and reduce our labouring population to the verge —and in some cases the fulfilinent—ot starvation ? We boast of this as a free country, with free trade, and vet were a miner willing to work for what the masters offer, to save his family from starvation, his very life would be endangered. The collieries are in a state of siege arid many of the lieges cannot follow their lawful pursuits by reason of intimidation and fear of bodily harm. surely this is a state of matters that a suffering com- munity will not long tolerate. Every workingman has a nerfect right to ceas‘, working himself—if his action affects only himself—and he has the right also of corn- timing, with this object, with his fellow-workers. But question the right of any man, or combination of men thus voluntarily to subject their families and other in- nocent persons to the privations at,eridant upon a strike like this. If majorities must rule, I think the rest of the community would be within their rights in demand- ing unrestricted freedom of labour in this case. Meanwhile tte miners will find that they have no monopoly in coal. This commodity is now pouring into Liverpool from other countries. The trade so foolishly thrown up by Lancashire and Yorkshire has gone to Belgium, and may, perhaps, stay there. And for this the miners are starving themselves, their families, and fellow-citizens!

By the way, what share have the delegates in this privation? Has anyone ever heard of, or seen ow., applying for a soup ticket? Can it be that it is with them a case of bull-pup ? You know the story cf the eon who was training a bull-pup, pursuading his father to go on his knees and pretend to ffght the dog. The -son, when the dog seized the father's nose, told him to be hard—" Be hard,father, it'll be 'th ma kin' o'th pup" ! It is easy to be " hard" when the suffering is vica- rious.

But seriously, I think society ought to seek for some means of safeguarding its workers from a rgcurrence of this mist deplorable state of things. • Government undertakes to defend us from foreign enemies, but here we have a state of war causing death and privation to the lieges. Any attempt to prevent the getting of this great necessity of civilized life ought to be as sternly repressed as a foreign invasion. Hundreds of our un- avoidably unemployed would be glad to work at the wage refused by the miners.—tam, Sir, yours,
JOHN PEERS.

div.head: COAL STRIKE.
div.p: THE COAL STRIKE.

Sir,—ln a working experience of 60 years, and the greater part of that time in coal and iron operations, I never knew of a drop ot 25 per cent, or an advance of more than ten per cent, at one. time. The advances from 1858 were in small sums at intervals extending over years. H it was a necessity warranted by the st. ts f trade that expenses all round must be curtailed, ai.o cvery possible penny saved—including mores wages and Oficial salaries—it would come easier if the reduc- tion came down in a similar way to which the advance went up ; it would not be making so urge a wound at libCP. Reductions are galling and terribly so, when the current wage by its smallness scarcely suffices for the xecessities of tie day. It has been bad generalship on

the masters' part, and it has alienated the sympathy of the public generally, who think that they are making an unreasonable and unfair demand in asking for what appears now to be I7i per cent., or 3s. 6d. in the pound on current rates. When, I would ask, did wages go up to that amount at one bound ? They may have done 80, but I have no recollection of such an occurrence, and to reduce wages by such a sum seems cruel. I know nothing of the exigencies of the case. I have it from a standpoint which possibly may not be a true one. On the other hand, is it wise to prevent pumping and keeping ventilation intact and general repairs of roads and other necessary work being done,so that when the dispute is settled or arrangement come to, the mines may be in safe order for commencing work ? Neglect of this kind may cause permanent stoppage of many a concern. This I look upon as a loss of common wealth. For all wealth is in a sense national, and no man has a right to more wealth than he can judiciously use for the benefit ollothers as well as himself, and the man who 'spends thousands a year on his own amusements and pleasures deprives his fellow-man of his just rights, and is a public robber this is not popular doctrine,l am aware, but is, I think, only commonsense and common justice. I,on the other hand, deprecate the assumption of authority in the lan- guage used by some of the strike leaders—such for in- stance, as the passing of a resolution to this effect "That no pit in this federation shall commence work until this dispute is settled." Such a resolution sounds to me tyrannical, and why, may I ask, provided the wages in dispute are given, should not work commence and be carried on? Another piece of assumption is this: "If work is carried on at such a place,they must not ask me to be responsible for what may happen." The "what may happen" may likely mean outrage—which may follow resumption of work. Resolutions and language such as tnis is far from dignified, and the dignity of . labour consists in, among other things, the use of tem- perate and dii,-,,nifed language. Ur.dignified and pre-1 sumptuous latwuaze can only he excused on the score of , the excitement aud iiritation attendant upon the • t st now going on, and the war racing between aital and labour. It may be said that I do ant feel the pinch. , hut I do. I and thousands of others are involuntarily , idle for the want of ca,. I know a rather long stn-;t near me, and all the men in the street but two were idle last week from the same cause. Some are men who . have no trade and no union, and know not where to turn for a moutiful of bread, and the distress amon., such is pitiful in the extreme. Personally, I live in an , expensive house, the requisite of a small trade carried on by may daueliter. The strike and the anticipation of it has stopped the trade for many weeks, but the ex- penses go on, and it is but little cons,lation to us to know that thousands of others are in the same boat. Some will survive the storm,but many will be swamped. Living in hones of better times, we grin and bear it.— Yours respectfully, 483, Aston-road, Openshaw, Manchester.
CYMRO.

div.head: NuTES ON GAMES AND
div.p: NuTES ON GAMES AND
ATHLETICS.
RUGBY FOOTBALL..

Widnes and Warrington, during the past few seasons, have invariably played very close games, the meetings last year resulting in a victory for Warrington at War- rington by a goal to nil, and of Widnes at Widnes by a try to nil. The match of last Saturday between the two teams was again only won by Warrington by the narrow majority of a try to nil. Warrington were minus their captain and also Boscow, so that they were considerably handicapped in that respect. Widnes and Warrington bad not previously been defeated this season,so that each side did their level best to keep their record unspoiled, and no doubt the scambling play was very largely due to their eagerness to score. Eleesom performed very well in his unaccustomed p.altion of full back, and Potts among the three-quarters had the credit of scoring the winning point. James Bate already shows that he is in brilliant form, and should again gain county honours this year, unless he has the same misfortunes that he had last year. Among the forwards Jolley and Berry were about the best. Alford., on the opposing side, was an excellent player, and put in some very good work for Widnes.

To-day Warrington commence their fixtures for the Lancashire Rugby, League, when they meet Broughton Rangers away. They will have to put their best foot forward as the Rangers have been going stronger this season than they have for a long time. It appears that they have a new patterned jersey, of formidable ap- pearance, which it is suggested has terrified their oppo- nents, and made their courage fail. Warrington will, therefore, have both this formidable jersey and also a considerably more formidable team to meet, than the one they have beaten so easily of late years. However, despite the narrow victory of last Saturday, Warrington have done some good things already this season, notably beating St. Helens Recs. away from home, and they should repeat their drubhings again, which they ,have administered upon the Rangers of late years.

Respecting the question of compensation to players for loss of time, which was discussed by the Union last week it is considered significant that in Lancashire the. went solid for compensation to players for loss of wages— Swinton, Oldham, Salford, Broughton Rangers, Warring- ton, Wigan, Rochdale Hornet, Mossley, So. "These," says a correspondent in a contemporary, " are the kind of clubs in Lancashire who may be expected to go solid with the Yorkshire organisations when it is a case of combining for any purpose to which the old school of the Rugby Union may be opposed. It is quite possible that if tht wishes of a body of clubs like the Lancashire and Yorkshire Seniors are ignored on this broken-time bll3l- - they may ere long formulate demands .of a still more advanced character, and if again thwarted an offensive and defensive alliance between them might prove a very awkward movement for the Rugby Union authorities to tackle."

The question was brought to a head, however, on Wednesday at the meeting of the Union in London. A proposition for the granting of remuneration for loss of time was submitted and defeated by 282 to 136. It is R question which requires considerable consideration, and as it was brought up perhaps without sufficient thought, its being kept over for another season will not be a bad thing.

The removal of J. 11. Crompton from Runcorn to the Bradford Club was consented to at the meeting of the Rugby Union at London, on Wednesday. This was quite a novelty in the way, of removals, since the transfer of a good player's services is now looked upon almost as a crime. On the .Bth inst. Crompton wrote to the Bradford Club stating he was coming to live in the town for business reasons, and offering his services to the club. The Bradf -ird Committee replied asking him to get his transfer from the Ru.ncorn Club, and on the 13th,Runcorn wrote saying that the transfer was granted. The senior Competition Committee approved of it, so that the crack Cheshire mau is now a fully-qualified Bradfordian. Croinpton's services have proved so valu- able to Runcorn that we should imagine the latter's committee must be fully satisfie I of the genuineness of the business reasons" whet they agreed to his trans- fer to Bradford.

div.head: ASSOCIATION.
div.p: ASSOCIATION.

The match on Tuesday night between Warrington Association and the well-known Everton Combination team was witnessed by a good number of spectators. The Combination champions, of course, very easily beat Warrington,but liVarrington played an exceedingly good game, especially in the last half. Everton had their full combination team in which were Jardine, who fre- quently figures between the sticks for the league team,and Arridge, the ex-Bootle man and also Welsh international. The game, of course, was an exhibition game, and the Evertonians frequently caused roars of laughter by the clever manner in which they puzzled their opponents. They could easily have scored more than four goals had they felt so inclined. On the other hand, the Warring- ton team worked well, and once or twice were really dangerous! They were handicapped by not having the services of Forrest,their usual goal-keeper,but Carter who took his place proved himself a really reliable goal-keeper and madv some marvellous saves Of the hacks, Mather was Cat, best by a long way,although Francomh was very useful for his long kicking. In the Warrington team there were the following members of the defunct W.A.F.C., Mather, Philips and Norman,. so that the Cricket A.F.C., has gained considerably by the old club's break-up.

The St. Elphin's P.C., if rumour speaks aright, are II very ambitious, as it is said that they are endeavouring ' to get Preston North End to give them an exhibition, game. If North End come there will no doubt he a " monster" gate. The Association clubs of the district have now joined the Liverpool District so they are under the aegis of the English Association.

div.head: GYMNASTICS.
div.p: GYMNASTICS.

The Warrington Gymnasium was opened for the , season this week, but unfortunately as yet not many have joined the classes. Mr. Kinsley, the excellent con- ductor last year, has been engaged for this season, and a successful season i; anticipated. The ladies' ordinary class was opened on Monday evening, but only a few put in an appearance. The gentlemen's ordinary class is opened every Tuesday and Friday evenings, the boys' class is held each Wednesday and Saturday afternoon and the special ladies' class on Thursday afternoon from 2.30 to 4 p.m. The season extends from September to May. and those intending to join the classes should do so at the beginning of the session. It is considered prob- able that Wm ring,ton will again enter the Challenge Shield Competition, but the entries will not close until early in November.

The Rev. Father Lennon, of Blackburn, on Monday visited his estate at St. Helens, where colliers, without even asking his permission, had excavated many tons of surface coal. The rev, gentleman was indignant oifind that the dealers had purchased the coal to make a profit and threatens legal proceedings. Ile ordered all work to cease and the holes to be tilled up, hut allowed the colliers to take home for their own use the remaining coal which lay upon the land.
'IHE EXAMIN EP, SATURDAY, SEPTEM BIER 23, 1893.

div.head: WARRINGTON SLAUG tiTE Lt HO S ES.. VI. HOW ABATTOIRS ARE MANAGED.
div.p: WARRINGTON SLAUG tiTE Lt HO S ES.. VI. HOW ABATTOIRS ARE MANAGED.
(By " CLEO.")

, After what has been written I will take it for granted that the question " Should private elaugh- [er-houses be abolished," with which I prefaced the open,ng paper is answered in the affirmative. That being so it now behoves me to give practical illustra- t ion of howabattoirs aremanagedatid howthe present system and its co-existent evils can be swept away. Birkenhead and Manchester abattoirs are models in their way, but being used chiefly in the large wholesale trade they will not come under the same category as the future abattoir in Warrington,which will be designed to meet local and district consump- tion. Fortunately a friend of my own who is in the business and is conversant with all the details of the management of the Edinburgh abattoir, kindly furnished me with full particulars and the necessary documents to enable me as he said to " stir the authorities to be up to the times and have one slaughter-house under 'their own supervision for the whole town. A per- usal of the byelaws show how stringent are the arrangements dealing with matters pertaining to public health,rqually as regards supervision Of the animals and the cleanliness of the place, and also to the exclusion of outsiders and of casual jobbers and to the prevention of cruelty. By byelaws 29 and 30 the superintendent is directed to attend par- ticularly to the enforcement of cleanliness and of ' good order within the slaughterhouses, to see that everything offensive is removed within the short- est possible time, and to see enforced the enact- ments regarding diseased and unwholesome butch- er meat, and blown or stuffed butcher meat and the effectual prevention of cruelty to animals. A proper supervision of the men employed within the slaughter house is safeguarded by byelaw No. 8 which s.ava that the fleshers shall enter the names of their several servants in a register to be kept in the superintendent's office, and to amend the list from time to time, those persons whose names are so registered to have free access within the gates of the slaughterhou.se at all proper times. When any flesher shall require extra hands temporarily 'he shall not be at liberty to employ any other than one of the licensed jobbers or supernumeraries who, by byelaw 22, have to wear distinctive badges and when not employed have to attend in a house of call provided for their use and must accept of whatever employment within the slaughter-houses, in their respective department, as may be offered to them. The granting and withdrawing of the jobbers' licensee is in the hands of the superintendent. The management of the entire establishment rests with the Markets Committee of the Town Council, the executive officers being the Borough Treasurer, the Borough Surveyor and the Superintendent of the slaughter house, the duty of the Superintend- ent being limited to carrying out the byelaws and seeing that the place is conducted according to the regulat ions. . _

'The killing booths are of two sorts, those rented fieshers, and the common booths available to others who, however, have to pay double dues on the animals they bring in These dues are revised every three years but the following may be taken as the average payable by fieshers renting a booth, viz. : For each head of cattle, sixpence ; pig, threepence ; calf, threepence, sheep or lamb, one penny. All the hides, skins and tallow have to be sold within the slatighter house twice a week and the corporation makes a considerable sum by allow- ing goods of that description to be brought into the slaughter house market on payment of one penny for each hide, twopence per score of skins and two- pence for every cart of tallow. Another source of revenue is the dues from the tripery within the abattoir. where the Corporation employ a number of women to clean tripe, &c. Fleshers renting booths do not pay for this work but they pay a trifle on every sheep or calves' head they get cleaned in the tripery. Fleshers net renting booths pay for the other work as well. The Corporation retains all the manure, blood, hoofs and spurs, tallow, ox-feet parings,tleAlings,and other ref use, and the proceeds ,of the sale of these commodities form their largest , source of revenue. On the other hand,the Corpora- tion pay the wages of the general cleauers and la- bourers, and the wages of the cleaners, &c., at the tripery, and provide the straw for the cattle sheds, water, coal, gas, and other furnishings. The dues payable by the fieshers are fixed at every triennial period. They cannot be called exorbitant,more than probably they amount to much less than they would otherwise have to pay for rent, rates, and repairs if they had places of their own to maintain. The fieshsrs themselves find this central establishment exceedingly convenient, and they would most pro- bably offer greater resistance to any effort, that might be made for its discontinuance and for the erection of private slaughter houses, than will !he Warrington flesher when the Corporation come to insist on the discontinuance of the private slaughter houses and on the erection of a public abattoir. The same, or to all intents and purposes the same, arrangement holds good all over Scotland. and I know several towns, not one-tenth of the size of Warrington, which are all equipped with first-class abattoirs. They are compelled by Act of Parliament, to have them. The Oeneral Police and Improvement (Scotland) Act, ' 1862. renders private slaughter houses illegal,and so satisfied have the public been with the good effects I or this system that after thirty years' experience legislation has not only confirmed that Act,but has strengthened it by the "Burgh Police (Scotian I)Act 1892." I have already in part I quoted the clause of the Act under which Warrington and other cor- porations are handicapped.but as it will be interes- r ing to give it in juxtaposition with the Scotch Act will here repeat it. Clause 169 of the Public Health Act. of 1875 says :—" Any urban autho- rity may if they think fit, provide slaughter houses, and they shall make byelaws with respect to the management and charges for the use of any slaughter houses so provided. For the purpose of enabling any urban authority to regulate slaughter houses within their district the provi- sions of the Town's Improvement Clauses Act 1847, with respect to slaughter houses shall be incorpor- ated with this Act." Section 284th of the "Burgh police (Scotland) Act, 1892." enacts that "If the Commissioners have provided under any former Act, or resolve to provide and establish,and do pro- vide and establish, shambles or slaughter houses,no person shall thereafter slaughter any cattle or beast. or scauld or dress the carcases of any slaughtered cattle, or cause the same to be done, within the boundaries of the borough' elsewhere than within te said slaughter houses, under a penalty of five pounds for each ~ffence." That is the law. I do not wish here to dilate on the merits of the one or the demerits or the other. Warrington has the power to erect an abattoir, but on the question of whether Warrington has the power to directly com- pel the older licencees of private slaughter houses to close these houses and utilize the Corporation prernises,should such liCensees be injudicious enough to refuse to do so, my opinion might not be worth much. Indirectly, Warrington has this power, for it can easily be proved that the slaughter houses are a nuisance and a danger to health, and, as it would be impossible owing to their situation, to abate the nuisance. the houses would, therefore, have to he closed. But first of all an abattoir would have to be available.

Does an abattoir pay? The demands of health the claims of morality, the pleadings of humanity may have fallen on dull ears but when the .£ s. d. argument is adcltibed all is attention. Well, an abattoir does pay and pays handsomely. The Edin- burgh abattoir pays .£l,OOO every year into the general city funds by way of an annuity, and after paying that sum and a large sum in interest and contributions to the sinking fund as well as the general expenses of management there is an aver- age balance in hand at each year end of about .£l2O. This annuity may well be taken to represent the old market dues and tolls which the ezigenlies of modern civilization have diminished to vanishing point. In stri king contrast to this we have the Chair- man of the Markets Committee of the Corporation of Warrington, that same Warrington once famed all England over for its markets which put Man- chester markets in the shade, publicly lamenting in the Council Chamber that their receipts are ebbing by rapid flows year by year, that they are but a ghost of their former selves and that no one knew how or where it will end or how to turn the tide, And this with a lawful remedy at hand. Where base all the large market dues of ancient Warring- ton vanished to? Only one answer can be forth- coming. These, what were once legitimate town ' property, have vanished into the pockets of private individuals. They should he public property still, more especially since, the additional mite of ex- pense incurred could not result in an increase of the price of meat, as it is notorious that the long con- tinued cheapness and ever cheapening price of cattle has not resulted in a corresponding cheap- ness in the price of meat. To show how and where this highly desirable establishment could be carried am in wnrrington I shall devote next week's article,which will be the last

div.head: HA RYES r FESTIVALS.
div.p: HA RYES r FESTIVALS.

WESLEYAN CHAPEL, WESTON POINT. The harvest thanksgiving services were IP-Id on Sun- day, when sermons were preached by the Rev. W. Ar- rowsmith and Mr. I. Hayes. On Monday evening an- other service was held, conducted by the Rev. J. Hanby.
GOSPEL UNION MISSION, WIDNES.

The harvest festival in connection with the Gospel Mission, West Bank, was held on Sunday, when appro- priate sermons were preached by Mr. J. B. Hartley (MancheSter). In the afternoon a service of song was rendered in a creditable manner by the choir mid scholars.
TRINITY WESLEYAN.CITAPEL, FRODSRANI.

• The annnal harvest thanksgiving services were held at Trinity Wesleyan Chapel, on Sunday. Sermons were preached morning and evening by Mr. J. W. Allcock, of Didsbnry, ta large congregations. Special hymns and anthems were ably rendered by the choir, and Mr. T. Nickson. of Birmingham. gave a solo with t..lling effect at each service. The collections for the day realised £6 Us. 10d.
HOLY TRINITY CHURCH.

The harvest thanksgiving services in connection with Holy Trinity Church were held on Thursday evening. The church had been decorated for the occasion, and leaked very 'pretty. Special music was excellently ren- dered by the choir. There was a very large congregation. The Rev. Robert Catterall. M.A., rector, of St. Mary's, Crumpsall, was the preacher for the occasion. Collec- tions were taken in aid of the Holy Trinity day schools for which £3O is required. ST. MA kY'S CFIURCH, WIDNES.

The harvest thanksgiving services were continued on Sunday. In the mo-ning, the Rev. J. Moore, who is assisting pro tem, in the work of the parish, occupied the Pulpit, and a special service was held in the afternoon for the Bible Classes and Sunday school scholars, when an anpropriate address was given by the Vicar (the Rev. W. flodzson). At the evening service the church was crowded to excess, and an eloquent sermon was preached by the Rev. A. H. Rhodes, curate of Claughton. The total collections amounted to about £ll.
" ST. PETERS CHURCH.

The harvest festival at St. Peters Church, Birchall- street, was commenced on Thursday evening. The church had been tastefully decorated with fruit, flowers grain and vegetables by a committee composed of the following, ladies Mrs. Percival, Mrs. Bamforth, Mrs. TI. Taylor, Miss Edgar, Miss Dagnall. Mrs. Blease, and Mrs. Richardson. Mr. TI. Taylor, P.C.M., made a mini- ature haystack. There was a very good attendance. The preacher was the Rev. T. T. Madden. M.A., vicar of St Luke's, Liverpool, who delivered an appropriate sermon. The collections which are to he devoted to the church boundary wall fund realised £353.

ST. JAMES' CHURCH. The harvest thanksiiving services in connection with the above church were held on Thursday night. In the abencecf the Rev. J. B. Meredith, who was advertised to preach, but was unable to be present on account of ill- ness,the Rev. W. A. Wickham, vicar of St. Andrew's Church, Wigan, was the preacher. The attendance was good, and there was a large choir assisted by four instru- mentalists. During the evening, the anthem "He shall dwell in the light," by Sir Joseph Stainer,was effectively rendered by the choir. Thfl offertory was on behalf of church expenses. The decorations, which consisted of flowers, fruit.kc., were set out in very good taste by the ladies of the congregation. It is expected that the new rectory for St. games' Church.which is to be in Wilderspool Causeway,opposite to the church, will be opened before Christmas, and that the present rectors, will be sold.
THELWALL CFRJRCFI.

The Harvest Festivals at All Saints Church, Thelwall, were held on Saturday and Sunday. The church had been prettily decorated with corn, flowers, and fruit for the occasion. The service on Saturday evening was conducted by the Rev. Richard Greenall. M.A., rector of Grappenhall. The anthems "Ye shall dwell in the land" (Sir J. Stainer), and "The Lord is loving unto every man" (Dr. Garrett) were sung by the choir. The Rev. T. Pym Williamson, vicar, was the preacher at the Sunday morning service, and the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, M.A., vicar of Holy Trinity, Warrington, preached at the afternoon service. The Rev. Wilfred J.Stanton, M.A., also preached in the evening. A collection was taken at each service and the proceeds were divided between the Society for the propagation of the gospel in foreign parts and the schools.
BEWSEY-ROAD WESLEYAN CHAPEL.

Large congregations assembled both morning an 3 evening at the harvest thanksgiving services at Bqwsev- road Wesleyan Chapel on Sunday. The preacher at morning service WAS the Ray. Owen Watkins, who deliv- ered an appropriate sermon on sowing and reaping. The chapel had been tastefully decorated for the occasion. The front of the pulpit was draped with ferns, relieved with white flowers. In the centre a wreath of white flowers had been affixed. The gas brackets had been ,decorated with ears of corn, interwoven with flowers, and the pipes of the organ by the use of sunflowers pro- clucPd a pretty effect. Great praise is due be the follow- ing ladies for decorating the chapel :—Mrs.Watkins,Mrs. Shaw-Green. Mrs. A, FL Dunn, Mrs. Davey, Miss Wat- kins, Miss Shaw-Green, Miss Bonnell, Miss Bailey, Miss Morrie Bennett, and Miss Gertie S. Green. A special antlfem arranged from the hymn " We plough the 'fields and scatt.,r," composed by the organist, Mr, J. M. Muir I was rendered with excellent effect by the choir. The preacher at the evening service was the Rev. G.D. Mason The collections received were in evcess of last year.

div.head: PADGATE WESLEYAN CHAPEL.
div.p: PADGATE WESLEYAN CHAPEL.

On Sunday the annual h irvest festival was held in the Pacigate Wesleyan Chanel. The edifice had been decor- ated for the occasion by the Misses Bennett (Lyndhurst) Misses Bennett (Pear Tree), Misses Richarelson, Miss Morton, Miss E. Smith, Miss Ward, and otherk. In the morning _a sermon was preached_ by

the Rev. Thomas Turvev, of Didsbury Col-lee, from the words" tie shall grow like the cedar of Lebanon." At the evening service the pulpit was occu- pied by the Rev. Owen Watkins, one of the newly ap- pointed ministers of the Warrington circuit. The ser- mon wad full of witty savings, and was listened to by the large congregation. Collections were taken dur- ing the day in aid of the trust fund.

div.head: GREAT SANKEY.
div.p: GREAT SANKEY.

The annual harvest thanksgiving service was held on Sunday at St. Mary's Church, Great Sankey. This pretty little church has long been noted for the splendid display on such occasions, and this year, if anything, this display was better than on previous occasions. The sacred edifice had been tastefully decorated for the occasion by a number of willing workers and presents of corn, fruit, etc., had been freely bestowed by the neighbouring farmers and gentlemen. The following ladies and gentlemen were responsible for the decora- tions : Mrs. E. Bolton, Misses Standish, Miss Bolton, Misses Warburton, Mien Grange. Miss Daisy Owen and Miss Annie Jones, and Mr. It. Boardman, and Mr. Denton. There was a large attendance at the morning service. The prayers were read by the Rev. J. R. Jones, curate. A powerful and eloquent sermon was preached by the vicar. the Rev. E. S. Jackson, M.A. The anthem " And God said, Let the earth bring forth fruit," was admirably sung by the choir, Miss M. Standish accompanying on the organ. The sAo was finely ren- dered by Mr. W. Ireland. In the afternoon the scholars nf the St. Mary's Sankey Sunday School, and the Penketh Mission Sunday School formed in procession and pro- ceeded to the church where a children's flower service was held. The Rev. J. R. Jones conducted the service and preached a very good sermon. At the conclusion the children came forward with their offerings of flowers and laid them on a table in the chancel, and a very large number of lovely flowers were thus collected. The flowers were afterwar Is presented to the hospital. In the evening the church was crowded to the utmost, many persona being iniable to find even a standing place, and so were forced to withdraw. The musical portion of the service was of a special character, special harvest hymns being sling and an anthem, " Fear not 0 Land," was rendered in first class style by the choir. The Rev. E. S. Jackson preached a very earnest and touching sermon. After the service the people walked round and inspected the decorations. Collections were taken at all services in aid of the general funds and reached the liandsoms sum of £24 3s Bd.

div.head: WEEKLY REPOET OF THE HEAITti OF
div.p: WEEKLY REPOET OF THE HEAITti OF
WARRINGTON.

During the week, which was the 37th of the current year, the following births and deaths were registered :—Births : Warrington, 37 ; Latchford, 4; total, 41. Deaths : Warrington, 25 ; Latchford, 2, total 27. The exces,t of births over deaths was 14, The death-rate from all causes was equal to 25.4 per 1.000, against 285 the average of the previous four weeks, and against 20.9 the corresponding week e,f last year. The death-rate from the seven chief zymotic diseases was equal to 9.4 per 1.000, against 11.5. the average rate of the four previous weeks,and Against 3.8 the corresponding week of 1892. The ages of mortality were :—Warrington : 0 to 1, 2-2 ; 1 to 5, 14 ; 5 to 15. 1 ; 15 to 2.5, 1 ; 23 to 60, 4 ; 60 up ! 3 ;total. _25-2 27. The deaths included-3 from scarlet fever; 5 from diarrhml ; 2 from measles ; lfrom phthisis ; 1 from cancer; 1 from old age ; 4 from lung disease ; 1 from . heart disease ; 2 from brain disease; 1 from suicide (cut throat). The following cases of, infectious disease have been reported during the week:— Scarlet fever, 14. Meteorology .—The mean tem- perature was 54 Feb. and therefore 54- deg. lower than the preceding week. The maxi- mum temperature 09 F., was recorded on the 10th inst., and the minimum temperature 34 F., on the 12th inst. The rainfall measured .041 n. The general; direction was S.F., the reading of the anemometer ! denoting 745 miles.—JOHN LI. 0011.NALL, Medical Officer of Health,

div.head: WAItRINGTON ADJOURNED LICENSING SESSIONS.
div.p: WAItRINGTON ADJOURNED LICENSING SESSIONS.

--- THE BACK-DOOR QUESTION. The adjourned licensing sessions for the Borough of Warrington were held in the Police Court, on Thursday. The court room was crowded with spectators interested in the points to be decided. Amongst those interested in the temperance cause who were present were : the Revs. J. Yonge, J. .Kirtlan, J. Warnock, W. 11. Drummond, D. W. Roberts, E. T. Reed G. D. Mason, and E. Moore. There was a full bench of magistrues includ- ing Alderman Holmes (ha the chair) Aldermen Harrison, Sutton, Francomb, Wright, Messrs. J. i Crosfleld, F. W. Monks, H. Roberts, Z. Armitage,l James Fairclough, John Fairclougb, J. Whi ,e, J. H.I Fleming. W. Pierpoint, E. M. Croatield, T. Birchall, J. Burgess, J. Geddes, J. W. Hayward, L. Voisey, E. I J.Guast.S. Wright, Dr. Gornall and Major Ridgway. In regard to his objection to the side door at the Lion Hotel, Mr. E. Fickavance was represented by Mr. Chorl- I ton. Messrs. Walker and Co. the owners, and Mr. Joseph Taylor, the tenant of the Lion Hotel, were retire- I sented by Mr. Mattinson, Q.C., instructed by Mr. A. Browne. Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Co., were represented by Mr. Swift, barrister, of Liverpool, in- structed by Messrs.R.Davies,Kirkconnel and Co.; and Mr. Mulholland, barrister, Manchester, represented Mr. Wm. Bolton, and was instructed by Mr. Wallhead. Mr. Unsworth, of the firm of Messrs. Jenkins and Unsworth, also represented some of the license holders. THR LION LICENSE.—THR SIDE DOOR CLOSED. Mr. Mattinson said that with regard to the Lion Hotel license he had a statement to make to the bench which, he thought, would obviate the necessity for further dis- cussion in the case. The Bench would remember the position in which the matter stood a montth ago. Objection was taken to the renewal of Mr. Taylor's license on the ground that there was a side door opening into Ship-yard in relation to which it was alleged that objectionable incidents took place after nightfall. The Eench, on that occasion, intimated the opinion that it was desirable that that side door should be closed. That was a mongth ago. In the interval he found that Messrs. Walker and Sons had given the most anxious and careful consideration to the suggestions of theßench with every desire to meet any opinion which they might throw out. Mr. Mattinson was then about to refer to what took place at the previous sessions, when Mr. Chorlton said he must take an objection. The whole Of the evidence was gone into on the last occasion counsel made his Speech, and the matter was entirely closed, but if it was intended , merely to make a state- ment as to what Messrs. Walker were going to do he should have no objection. If, however, it was intended to examinetheevidence,tnaiee remarks on it and appeal, to the Court &gain for some further consideration, then he should say at once that be objected on behalf of Mr. Pickavance, aS the whole of the evidence was gone into and the case cloeed atthe last hearing. 'Mr. Mattinson said his object was to makes state- ment as to what they proposed to do. Having regard to the importance of the case to Messrs. Walker, it was only right that he should state in a few sentences what their position in that matter was. Everything that had been done with regard to the door had been done under sanction. Further, it was their view, whether rightly or wrongly, that even if the suggestion of the Bench was acted upon it would make very, little difference with regard to the good order, or otherwise, existing in the passage. At the same time, they felt this—that the justices were primarily responsible for the good order of the town and for making efficient arrangements with regard tc;thatprder. If it were the general sense of the Bench that something substantial ought to be done in the direction of closing the door in that passage, Messrs. Walker would not for a moment think of opposing the opinion of the Bench. Be had, therefore, a suggestion to make, and he hoped it would meet with the unanimous assent of the Bench. It was quite' clear from the evidence which was given (and he had had an opportunity of reading the shorthand writer's notes) that the objectionable incidents to which reference was made were incidents which took place after nightfall. Be thought about a dozen instances were given of alleged misconduct in the yard, and in every case, save one, it was after nightfall that the misconduct took place. That being so, he had tendered certain advice to Messrs. Walker, which they, had accepted, and by it he thought that the wishes of the Bench would be entirely met, and that any possibility of trouble or disorder would he obviated. It was this—that Messrs. Walker undertake absolutely to close this door in Ship-yard at six o'clock every night.. He made that suggestion to to the Bench. It cut off five hours to which, in the ordinary course of events, they would be entitled—five hours at night, when there was a risk of the description of men referred to coining out of the house and forget- ting themselves.

Mr. Cherlton—said he would at once, on behalf of his client, Mr. Pickavance, most thoroughly decline to accept such a suggestion. Oc public grounds the side door was objected to because there were other entrances to the vaults from Bridge-street and from the Lion Hotel yard, and entrances which lead from back streets were of a character to allow people to enter or leave without being under the proper/ supervision of the police. As for closing the entrance into Ship-yard at six o'clock at night he was sure it would not in any way do away with the nuisances to which Mr. Pickavance objected. The Clerk : It will be necessary to call some evidence as there are gentlemen on the Bench who were not onat the last meeting.

At the request of Mr. Monks Mr. White, the magis- trates clerk, read the resolution passed by the Licensing Committee, expressing their intention to close all back entrances that were used for sale of drink. Mr. Monks drew attention to this as relative to the question under consideration,

Alderman Sutton : But the resolution is In DO way binding upon the Bench. It was passed at a meeting of magistrates and not by the Bench. , Mr. Mattinson : I don't wish the question to be dis- cussed simply in regard to our case. If tho Bench are • going to lay down any general rule regarding back doors my clients do not wish to offer any objections. Alderman Harrison: What kind of entrance is that leading from Ship-yard? Mr. Mattinson : It is a very ample one. Alderman Harrison: Could a horse and cart pass through it ? Mr. Mattinson : Well, there are three or four steps, you know.—(Laughter.) The Bench then decided to retire and consider the case It was feared at first that all the magistrates present could not get in the room into which the magis-• rates usually retire,and an order was given for the court to be cleared while the consultation was hell in the court room. Just as the" public " were somewhat un- ceremoniously being bustled out of the court, someone discovered that the Bench could be accommodated in their own room.

... _ Just as the magistrates were about to retire Mr. R. Davies suggested that before they gave in their, verdict they should bear a few of the cases which would arise out of the instruction which had been given for the closing of backdoors. He represented cases in which this question would be bmught up, as did also his learned friend, Mr.Swi ft, whom he had instructed on behalf of Messrs. Greenall and '.30.

Mr. Swift upheld Mr. Davies's suggestion. Mr. MAttinson said he did not wish his case to be tried in conjunction with others. And as the point to bq de- cided was only a stnall cne, he did not care to lose the time waiting for other cases to be heard.

The Bench then retired and were absent for about half itn hour, Upon returning Alderman Holmes said the decision of the Bench was to confirm the resolution which they adopted on the llth September—that was that the side door at the Linn Hotel be closed permanently. MT. latattinson : Very well, we undertake to do so.

div.head: OTHER LICENSES.--.AN AMICABLE ARRANGEMENT. –
div.p: THE OTHER LICENSES.--.AN AMICABLE ARRANGEMENT. -

Mr. Unsworth asked the magistrates-ti)--t-aVe-t-hT;se which he represented next. This would facilitate buii- fleas as his client (Mr. Wm. Atherton) was prepared to give the undertaking required by the bench that the side door would not be used for the sale of beer.

Mr. A. Browne objected to this. The cases, he said, were so intermixed that it would be better to take the usual course. Mr. Mulholland said he Appeared on behalf of Mr. Owen Jones, and he was prepared to give the same undertaking. Mr. Jolm Crosfield remarked that such an undertak- in be given to cover all the COWS. •

Mulholland said he appeared for several cases,and the licensees he represented were quite prepared to accede to the wishes of the majority of the bench as expressed in the last case. He would suggest that upon an undertaking being given in the court by responsible gentlemen, that the wishes of the liench would be met, the licenses may be safely renewed for the present year. The police would then be able to report to the next annual licensing sessions as to the way in which the wishes of the bench had been carried out. He did not think the bench wanted any more than that. Mr. Monks said that was what was intended. Further than that, the bench had appointed a :silb-comtnittee consisting of six magistrates, to confer with any licensee or owner of publie-house property, with a view to con- verting or .adapting the premises. '
Mr. Mulholland said that, so far se he knew, there was no licensee there who was not prepared to accede to the wishes of the bench.

Mr Swift said he appeared on behalf of eight of the full-licensed houses, and of two of the olf-licerses, an,l in regard to the " off " cases, he at once gave an undertaking in the terms of their worships resolution, namelv, that the backdoors should not he used for other than domestic purposes. With regard also to the point mentioned by his friend. Mr. McConnell—(laughter)— he begged pardon' Mr. Mulholland.— Mr. Mulholland I am not at all offended. Mr. Swift : Well, lie is a good-looking man. (Laugh- ter.) A Voice : Which Mr. Swift Both. (Laughter.) . . . .

, Mr. Swift said that although he represrntoritl,e licen- sees, he really represented Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Co.. the owners of the property, and no their part he might 'assure their worships that they wished to entirely meet the reasonable wishes of the magistrates

with regard to police supervision and back doors and side entrances. It had been impossible, however, upon such short notice as they had had—the notices having only been served within the last eight or nine days—to , submit any proposition that would be likely to suit both parties. He was very pleased to hear that their worships had nominated a committee of the ben& for the purpose ef conferring with the representatives of the licenses and the owners. He might say that he was in agreement with his friend Mr. Mulholland in saying that if the licenses were granted that day he would give an assurance on, behalf of his clients and the owners that during the year every effort would be made by conferr- ing with their 'worships and by appointing a surveyor, to find the very bast method to be adopted. It seemed to him that a satisfactory arrangement might be come to long before the next licensing meeting came round; while a prolonged inquiry in every case that day would not result in any usetul purpose. Alderman Holmes said the bench accepted the proposi- tion. The bench also wished to call attention to the practice of some license holders giving coppers to chil- dren as an inducement to them to come for seer, and also ' to the tendency of off-licensed housta to become places I for the sale of beer 'only. Mr. Robert Davies said he represented the licensee of a , house belonging to the Bedford Brewery Company, and lie was quite prepared to give the same undertaking as Mr. Swift and Mr. Mulholland. He believed that, look- ing at the gentlemen on the bench, their requirements would be reasonable, and he felt sure that, by this time next year, they should have very little friction. If, in some cases, it was impossible to alter quite satisfactorily allowances would, no doubt, be made.

Mr. Monks said they were alive to the difficulties that presented themselves, and personally he was of opinion that the Committee might be able to solve some difficul- ties which might be insuperable to the owners as between themselves, tie could speak for half of the Committee that they would act in a reasonable spirit. Alderman Sutton said that what was understood was that the clients of the gentlemen there that morn- ing would fall in with any reasonable suggestion the coin- mittee. might make.

In the course of some conversation it was explained that meetings of the sub-committee of magistrates would be held during the corning year, and the licensees would have an opportunity of coming belore the committee and conferring with them as to meeting the objections of the Ma gistrratas.
The licenses were then all renewed subject to the un- dertakings entered into.
_A WINE LIUENSE REFUSED.

George Frederick Catcherside applied for a wine license for the Hone and Coloniel 'lea Company's shop, Hersemarket-street. Mr. Browne objected to the appli- cation on behalf ol Mr. Allen of the Pelican. His objec- tion was that the applicant was not the holder of the shop.—Cross-examined by the Chairman the applicant said he was the managing director, of the Company and was responsible for the conduct of the shop, as he was for 12 other shops in Birmingham.—As the applicant was not the occupier of the shop the Clerk ruled that a license should not be granted him, and a decision in accordance with this was given.

div.head: MUSICLICENSES.
div.p: MUSICLICENSES.

Joseph Horlock, Rope and Anchor Inn, Buttermarket- st.,applied for a music license. Mr.A. Brownie appeared for the applicant and said that m an objection had been raised at the last meeting because of a piano which was played in the room nearest the street, and thus causing crowds of people to assemble, his client had consented to remove the piano.---The Chief Constable said he did not wish to retract one word he had said about Mr. Horlock a fortnight ago. If the piano was removed, a nuisance of which he had complained would be removed. 'But he also wished to say that he did net care to see the place thronged and t 3 hear of telegrams being taken in and out, as had been complained of.—Mr. Browne explained that his client had never had telegramssent to him of a betting charac- ter. He had never made a bet in his life. But he had found out that a customer had been receiving the tele- grams complained of and, as Inspector Spinks knew, that man had been forlsidden to enter the place.—The Chief Constable said he could undorstand the applicant not being up to his business at 'first, as he was a young man from the country—(laughter)—and had formerly been a coachman.—The Bench reserved their decision.— William Bolton, of the Exchange Inn, Horsemarket-at., applied for a music license.—The Chief Constable said the police had no complaint against Mr. Bolton.—The Bench reserved their decision.—James Keenan, Walker. St., applied for a music and dance license for St. Paul's Infant schools, and Miss Eliza Young applied for a music license at the Shakespeare Inn.—After a short consulta- tion the Bench granted all the applications except that of Mrs.. Young...
• Mr. Monks sal.] that he wished to say on behalf of the• sub-committee of the Licensing committee that they would look after the conduct cf the houses which had music licenses.

The Chief Constable said he also wished to say that he and his staff weuld do their best to work with the com- mittee' and also to carry out suggestions made by the ! Watch Committee. He hoped there would be harmony between the police and these two committees. Until the recent question of authority between the Bench and 'the Watch Committee, he had thought the two bodies. were working amicably together.

div.head: HOUSES OBJECTED TO.
div.p: HOUSES OBJECTED TO.

div.head: WIDNES REVISION COURT.
div.p: WIDNES REVISION COURT.

On Wednesday evening, Mr. J. T. Foard, barrister, commenced the revision of the Parliamentary and municipal voters' lists for the divisien and borough of Widnes. The Court was held in the Council Chamber of the Town Hall. Mr. H. B. Shores repre- sented the Liberal party,and Mr. R. Madge, assisted by Mr. W. 0. Evans and Mr. J. H. Woodnorth, ap- peared for the Conservatives. There were also present Mr. H. S. Oppenheim (town clerk), Mr. T. Ctaik (assistant town clerk), and Mr. Goff (assist- ant overseer). SERIOUS DECISION AGAINST CONSERVATIVE AGENT.

At the outset Mr. Shores said he wished his honour's ruling on an important point. Mr. Madge and himself had taken an opposite course with respect to the service of declarations. Ile had deemed it expedient and in conformity with the Acts of Parliament to serve the de- clarations upon the Town Clerk of Widnes.' Mr. Madge bad served the declarations upon the Clerk of the Peact.. He asked his honour to regard Mr. Madge's declarations as invalid.—Tne Barrister said his view was that frr borough registration the declaration must be served Upon the Town Clerk, and for county registration upon the Clerk of the Peace. He was open to hear any argument to the contrarv.—Mr. Madge said he had left his de- clarations with the Clerk of the Peace in accordance with the practice that had been usual for years in the neighbouring borough cf Bootle, and he believed in Sluthprt for although they were municipal boroughs, they were in Parliamentary County dlvisions.—The Barrister said the law most specifically stated that all boroughs were to be treated in one war, and that de- clarations for a borough must be served upon the Town Clerk.—Mr. Madge said his Honour's decision against him would put him to some inconvenience. M. Shore's objection on a technicality would not help him (Mr. Shores) very much, because he should bring the people to court.—Mr. Shores : But there are a number of peo- ple who cannot COMP up—that is the point. Mr. Shores said he could refute Mr.Mirigr's statement with reference to the custom in the municipal boroughs,because he had : letters from Darwen, Blackburn, Accrington, and Prest- wich, which stated that the custom was to serve the de- clarations upon the Town Clerk.—The Barrister: It is satisfactory to know that the practice of Bmtle is most universal : but it does not go further than that. I must decide against Mr. Madge.
RENT BOOKS NOT EVIDENCE.

Mr. Shores supported the claim of Thomas Duffy for an occupiers vote in respect of 38, Oxford-street. The applicant produced a rent book commencing Atsgust 3rd 1892. Rut he stated that he had been the sole suport of his mother and had paid the rent since the death of his father nineteen months ago.—Mr. Madge said his information was that the name on the rent book was Margarct Duffy the mother of the a pnlicant.—The applicant admitted that his mother's name was placed on the rent book when his father died.—Mr. Goff (assistant overseer) said the landlord had returned Duffy as the tenant.—The B mister said any name might. be put nn the rent book for a variety of reasons. A rent hook was really no evidence at all. The question wag, who is the real substanti4l tenant. fie allowed the claim.: The court was then adjourned. CONSERVATIVE LOSSES.

The Court was resumed on Thursday morninsr. when the Itevisine Barrister confirmed his decision with res- pect to the Conser'vativo declarations. The regult was that a considerable number of Conservative claims were struck off ,the claimants not appearing.

A REVEREND CLAIMANT. 'rho Rev. R. G. Hughes claimed through Mr. Shores for a lodger vote in respect of 72 Frederick-st. He stated that he occupied three rooms in the hons. r d paid 154. per week exclusive of board.—Mr. Mad,go ir.quired if he had any receipts.—Mr. Hughes replied that he did not keep receipts.—The vote was allowed.

These Mortgages are being issued by the Runcorn Improve- ment Commissioners for the purpose of paying for the Water- works which they are purchasing from the Runcorn, Weston, and Halton Waterworks Company, under the powers of the Runcorn Commissioners Act, 1893. The secur ty for the Loan will o,mprise a Mortgage of the Water Revenue, and the District Fund and General District Rate of Runcorn. Besides the present Loan the Commissioners ere authorised by the Runcorn Commissioners Act, 1893, to borrow upon the security of the Water Revenue, (a) such a sum as may be required for the purpose of paying the taxed cost of that Act, and (8) with the al proval of the Local Government Board such further moneys as may be neeessary in relation to the Commissioners Water Undertaking. The present Loan and such other Moneys as may be borrowed under the powers of the said last mentioned Act will all rank together as a first charge upon the. Water Revenue alter re-payment of Working Expenses. The Water Revenue is estimated to produce at the present time after payment of Working Expenses £2,600 per annum. So far as relates to the District Fund, and General District Rate, the present LORI, Will he subject to a prior charge of £12.115 13s. 5d and Interest for moneys previou4v borrowed by the commissioners under the powers of the Itunc,orn Improvement Act, 182, and the Library Acts and will rank pin passu with any moneys which the Commissioners mar heresfter borrow under the powers of the Public Health Act, 1875. The amount of the moneys which may he borrowed under the last mentionot Act, inclusive of £l5O (part of the said sum of £12,116 13s. sd) already borrowed under the Library Acts previously mentioned, cannot, howeveriexceed two years assessable value of the district. The present rateable value of the district is £58,131 9s. Od., assessed for rating purposes at £52.779 lls. 6d., and the General District liatefor the curt% nt year amounts to two shill.ngs and tenpencein the 2. As the Manchester Ship Canal traverses the river front of the Town of Runcorn, a great increase in its rateable value may be reasonably expected. The population of Runcorn, according to Population Statistics, was in the year 1881, 15,126. and in the year 1891, 28.050. The Mortgages will be issued in multiples of £lOO, tuad will be registered in the name of the proprietor. Interest will be calculated from the 30th day of September, 1893. and will be payable, hslf-yeirly by warrant on the 31st March and 30th Se, tember in 'each year; the first payment heing due 31st March, 1894. THE FATALITY TO A RUNCORN MAN AT LOSTOCK. ' On Friday afternoon, Mr. H. C. Yates, coroner, held an inquiry at the Lion and Railway Hotel, Northwich, respecting the death of Samuel Find- low. Owen Findlow, of Runcorn, said the deceased was his son, 25 years of age, and had resided at No. 48, Seweli-st., Runcorn. Deceased was a ship- wright, and was employed by Mr. McCulloch, con- tractor at Messrs. Bowman, Thompson, and Co.'s new bleach works at Lostock Gralam. Deceased was not accustomed to work at great heights; but he did not know whether he had ever suffered from giddiness.— Philip Handley, joiner, lodging at Greenall-road. deposed that he also worked for Mr. McCulloch. Shortly after two o'clock on Wednesday, decealed and he were work- ing on the first storey of a new bleach chamber which was being put up by Mr. McCulloch for Messrs. Bow- man, Thompson and Co. at Lostock. He was working at one end of the chamber when deceased called and asked him to come and look at a, scarf end which did not fit very well. The chamber was covered in with planks, and deceased had removed one of these to enable witness to see the scarf end. After calling to wit- ness, deceased turned round, and stopping back- wards, fell through the hole in the flooring which he himself had made by removing the plank. He had evidently forgotten that the, plank had been taken away. Witness tried to save him, but failed. Deceased fell to the ground, a distance of about 19 feet.—Albert Carter, a joiner, residing at Anderton, said he was working about 15 yards away from the spot where the accident occurred. He found deceased lying on the ground unconscious. There was a wound about an inch and a half or two inches deep on the back of his head, from which blood was flowing. A doctor was sent for, but the man died in about ten min- utes. In his fall, the deceased's head had come in con- tact with aniron column about half-way down. He was a very quiet and steady man.=,The Coroner having briefly summed up, the jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death." On Sunday afternoon the remains were interred in the Runcorn Cemetery amidst numerous manifestations of regret. The deceased had been connected with the Holy Trinity Church, and was held in high esteem by the members of the congregation. As a mark of respect to his memory the funeral procession was joined by the officials of the church, the choir, and representatives of the workshop where he was engaged. There was a large muster of friends. The service was conducted by the Rev. Dr. Preston, assisted by the Rev A. W. Riley. In the chapel the choir sang a psalm, and the hymn com- mencing" The labourer's task is o'er." At the grave- side the hymn " Jesu, lover of my soul," was feelingly interpreted. The collections at Holy Trinity Church, morning and evening; which realised £5, will be handed over to the widow arid children. His Excellency the Earl of Glasgow has given his assent to an electoral reform bill conferring the Parliamentary franchise upon women.
